articles.title: Marcos takes criticism personally, highlights work's importance in Gary V podcast
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. admitted that he takes criticism on the job personally, believing that being affected by public perception reflects the importance that he places on his work.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 2:12am

President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. admitted that he takes criticism on the job personally, believing that being affected by public perception reflects the importance that he places on his work.
During the podcast of singer Gary Valenciano on Monday, Marcos was asked whether he is able to separate the criticism he receives from who he believes he is.

“In a sense, no, because I take my work personally. It’s important to me—I get happy when I get it right, I’m sad if I [don’t], and if people do something wrong you get angry because I take it personally,” Marcos said on "Unshaken with Gary V."

“I think if I don't take it personally, you’re not doing everything that you can. ‘Yung talagang lampas na, you know, you go the extra mile kasi it’s personal eh, it means something for you,” he added.
Marcos said it is normal to be affected emotionally, explaining that acknowledging public feedback shows he values criticism and as he remains driven to improve his performance in office.

“Masusugatan ka talaga (You will really be hurt) but you have to be willing to do that, otherwise, you are not doing enough. It has to be hard, if it’s not hard, you’re not doing enough — you’re not working hard enough, you’re not thinking about things enough, you don’t care enough. Because if you’re caring enough, it hurts if it doesn’t go right or if there’s a problem,” the President said.
“It has to be personal, but then there’s a three-minute rule that I have. So pag nagalit ka na (if you get angry), ‘Okay, it matters to me, so let’s find out how to fix it,” he added.
Marcos said he does not let his emotions drive his decisions when resolving issues, which is something that he hopes other people, more importantly his children, would learn from him.

“What I hope [my children] would inherit from me is the ability to be objective. I’ve always followed the advice ‘Don’t make any decisions if you’re too sad, too happy, too anything.’ Just never trust your first instinct… That’s the advice that I always give: ‘Think about it for three minutes more,’” the President said.
Back from exile
In 1986, Marcos’ family fled the Philippines and was exiled to Hawaii after his father’s dictatorship was overthrown by the people’s uprising during the EDSA People Power Revolution.
He recalled being warned against returning to the country, citing threats to their family’s security.
“I remember they were warning us, kept warning us, ‘Don’t try to go home because it’s the security [that] is the problem, people are going to come after you, nobody likes you anymore,’” Marcos said.
He shared that he can still remember well his arrival in the Philippines from Hawaii at the end of October 1991, being the first member of the Marcos family to arrive.

“I arrived at the airport, and there were thousands of people cheering us on. And I thought, ‘Okay, it’s not true what they’ve been telling us.’ That’s why I wanted to come home, I’m with Filipinos again. I'm back home and it feels natural,” Marcos said.
The President said that at that moment, he felt like “natural” again. He noted that while he knew his life wouldn't be easy, it felt much more familiar than living in a foreign country.
“The reaction of the people was certainly not what I expected,” Marcos said.
“But there were thousands of people, and they were enthusiastic upon my return. Talagang nagulat ako (I was really surprised). I didn't think that it would be like that,” he added. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: No 10 insists RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws its bombers from base
articles.summary:
A dozen B-1s stationed at Gloucestershire base redeployed over concerns about possible threat from Iran

Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the

blocks.text: Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is secure a day after the US air force suddenly withdrew a dozen B-1 bombers that had been stationed at the Gloucestershire base over security concerns about a possible threat from Iran.

The prime minister’s spokesperson, speaking during a scheduled briefing, said “yes” when asked if the military site was safe – contrasting with the concern the US military revealed during the hasty redeployment the day before.

Pointing to comments made last week by the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, the official said there were “tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world”.

Aircraft trackers reported that an entire squadron of 12 B-1 bombers based at Fairford had redeployed from the British base to the US on Sunday, a rapid movement that the Pentagon confirmed on Sunday evening.

US officials told the New York Times commanders had received new information about an Iran-backed plot against the base, which has been on high alert for more than a week. Some of the bombers left so quickly that refuelling aircraft had to be scrambled to support their flights to the US.

UK sources said they were not aware of a new terrorism threat to the base and that they would be surprised if Iran had the capability to orchestrate a fresh threat, a week after five men from London were arrested in the small hours of the night having driven to a village near the base in white vans with an unclear purpose.

The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said on Monday that the redeployment of the bombers was not tied to the arrests and tried to downplay any discrepancies with the UK. He said the US was confident in the security of all its bases and “with the Brits, we’ve worked very closely a long time, including on this investigation, and they couldn’t be more cooperative”.

Downing Street’s comments were the first made by the UK in the light of the US withdrawal. No comment was made by the Ministry of Defence or Gloucestershire police when asked if there was any additional threat to residents near the base. Other UK officials indicated they had not been briefed on US thinking.

RAF Fairford has already been on high alert for several weeks amid heightened US concern that Tehran could try to instigate an attack on the base, which was used for US air force bombing runs against Iran earlier this year. Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that the base was a legitimate military target.

The hasty redeployment arguably represents a victory for Iran, forcing US bombers to retreat without any kind of attack taking place, though some experts said Washington was engaging in a wider redeployment that could lead to a scaling up of operations against Iran after the US midterm elections in November.

It is unclear what level of threat Tehran could pose to a base in the heart of the UK, though Iran has destroyed US planes on the tarmac during fighting this year. Missiles fired from Iran may be able to reach the UK but would belikely to be shot down first, and a drone attack would be a high-risk operation close to the base.

Experts said the size of the airbase meant it was difficult to protect from a short-range drone attack, perhaps similar to the attempt to bomb Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig airport in Germany in August, which the country’s authorities attributed to Russia.

But there was caution that there remained a lack of information. “Airfields are hard to defend, but the US could be making a point or just being very cautious,” said Matthew Savill, an expert with the Royal United Services Institute.

Developments in the UK have not so far matched the apparent level of US concern. The five men from London were arrested in Whelford, next to the base, on suspicion of carrying explosives, but they were not charged.
No explosive devices were found in the search of the vans or the men, though a barrel of petrol was recovered. All five were released on bail a day later.
The US president, Donald Trump, said afterwards that he was surprised they had been allowed out on bail. “We know everything about them, we would not have released them,” he said.

The prime minister, Andy Burnham, has been more muted. He said last week that there were “strong indications that Iran played a part” in the incident, but developments in the British investigation, led by counter-terrorism police, have been limited.

A sixth man, a dual UK-Iranian national, was arrested in London on Thursday on suspicion of preparing acts of terrorism, but he was also released on bail on Saturday. Investigations into the circumstances surrounding the events in Gloucestershire were continuing, counter-terrorism police said.

articles.summary:

Investigators believe that the co-pilot who tried to take control…
articles.byline: Jason Burke in London and Stephanie Kirchgaessner in Washington

blocks.text: Investigators believe that the co-pilot who tried to take control of a plane from Dubai to Tel Aviv last week originally planned his attack for July but postponed the hijacking, possibly because a friend was among the crew, regional and Israeli officials have said.

The evidence of prior planning suggests that Hamam al-Hammami, 29, may have specifically sought employment with an airline that flew to Israel in order to carry out the attack on last Wednesday’s flydubai ‌flight FZ1073, experts believe.

Police and security agencies in at least six countries are scrambling to piece together the background of Hammami, an Omani national, and his intentions, as well as to establish if he acted entirely alone.

Hammami allegedly used an emergency crash axe kept in the cockpit to launch a surprise attack on the pilot approximately two hours and 20 minutes after takeoff. The plane was carrying more than 180 passengers – almost all Israeli – and crew on a routine flight.

Israeli media have quoted from Hammami’s statements to interrogators since being transferred to United Arab Emirates custody on Thursday to report that he planned to crash into Ben Gurion airport near ⁠Tel Aviv, or possibly another high-profile target nearby.
The flight’s captain, Smit Machchhar, said on Saturday that shortly after Hammami had left his seat to pray, he felt a “big blow” to the back of his head.

In a phone call with Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, on Saturday, Machchhar said: “The blows kept coming … That’s when I realised that it’s not the aircraft, it’s the other guy who was in the cockpit with me.”

Despite his injuries Machchhar was able to unlock the cockpit’s security door to allow passengers to overpower Hammami. A reserve flydubai pilot travelling on the flight took control of the aircraft and landed it at a regional airport in north-western Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi authorities.

blocks.caption: Capt Smit Machchhar was visited on Sunday in hospital in the UAE by Hamdan bin Mohammed Al Maktoum, the crown prince of Dubai. Photograph: Hamdan bin Mohammed/X/Reuters

blocks.text: The investigation into Hammami has now spread to more than eight countries. Authorities in New Zealand and Australia are probing reports that the co-pilot studied in both about 10 years ago.

Hammami, who has an Omani father and a Syrian mother, is thought to have been employed by Oman Air from 2018 to June 2025, but left the airline after being moved to a desk job out of concerns that he had developed extremist views. He was then hired by Royal Air Maroc, the Moroccan national flag carrier, but did not obtain permission to fly and gave up his job there.

Shortly afterward, Hammami was hired at the state-owned flydubai, which has needed pilots as it expands rapidly. The airline conducted checks for a criminal record but not for evidence of radicalisation, officials have said.
A key question for investigators is when Hammami began to formulate his plan to attack a plane full of Israelis or target Israel.
Netanyahu has claimed Hammami had undergone “radical Islamist indoctrination” and was clearly suicidal, without giving details.

blocks.caption: FlyDubai conducted checks on Hammami for a criminal record but not for evidence of radicalisation, officials have said. Photograph: Fadel Senna/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Nine hours after the attack, a post was made to an online social media account in Hammami’s name praising Ayman al-Zawahiri, a former al-Qaida leader, as well as a militant responsible for a lethal suicide attack on US troops in Afghanistan in 2009. A second post contained religious imagery.

An analysis of Hammami’s X account by a company that uses AI to measure the toxicity of individuals’ social media accounts found dozens of misogynistic posts, including public threats against women. The analysis by Accountability! – which recovered Hammami’s deleted account by scraping internet archives, and reviewed almost 3,000 posts and responses – found repeated use of slurs against women, and a “consistent pattern” of use of terms meaning “whores”, and “filthy feminist”. The researchers also found homophobic slurs directed at men.

“Beyond offensive language, the analysis surfaced explicit conditional threats of physical violence … including repeated imagery of stomping on a woman’s head and making her ‘a lesson for others’,” the analysis found.

“Online toxicity isn’t just corrosive, it’s a warning sign. This pilot was telling the world who he was in his posts. Had anyone in charge been listening, nearly 200 people might never have been put in danger,” said Gur Megiddo, the co-founder and chief executive of Accountability!.
Regional officials said Emirati authorities had shared information about the passengers and crew, including their nationalities, with Israel.

The Shin Bet, Israel’s domestic security agency, said the transportation ministry was responsible for vetting passenger lists from foreign flights but the transportation minister, Miri Regev, said on X that the security agencies handled flight security.
Israeli newspapers reported that a key database of foreign pilots had not been checked despite concerns raised by official reports.

The attack occurred at a sensitive time for Israel, a week before the anniversary of the Hamas-led attack on 7 October 2023 which triggered the war in Gaza, and weeks before a fiercely contested general election in which security – and responsibility for failures to keep Israelis safe – has been a central issue.
Opposition politicians have seized on the apparent lapses to attack Netanyahu, who has boasted of his ability to keep Israelis safe.

“This is exactly what system collapse looks like,” Yair Golan, the head of the opposition Democrats party, wrote on X. “A transportation minister who completely abandons our skies, and a prime minister who abandons national security.”

articles.title: Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 33: AMLC witness spills P4.4 billion 'suspicious' bank transactions
articles.summary: The nine-hour impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday, including a one-hour lunch break, saw the proceedings tackle their biggest sum yet--P4.4 billion.

blocks.text: The nine-hour impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday, including a one-hour lunch break, saw the proceedings tackle their biggest sum yet—P4.4 billion.

This came after Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura of the Anti-Money Laundering Council testified that the Anti-Money Laundering Council recorded P4.4 billion in covered and suspicious bank transactions under the names of the Vice President and her husband, Manases Carpio.

Senator-judge Raffy Tulfo, meanwhile, asked the Senate impeachment court to admonish its spokesperson, lawyer Reginald Tongol, for telling the media that the impeachment trial verdict would be out by December 16.

Presiding officer Chiz Escudero said that Tongol’s announcement was based on a pre-trial order or the court schedule agreed by both parties, although he clarified that it was simply a math equation and would not necessarily reflect the situation on the ground.
Tongol was quick to echo Escudero and said that the date was only a logistical projection hinged on the pre-trial order calendar and that he appreciates the correction of the Senator judges.

With that sidelight out of the way, Escudero allowed Buenaventura to testify on the bank transactions of the Vice President and her husband, saying the laws did not design AMLC as a passive institution.

“Section 8A [of the Anti-Money Laundering law] protects AMLC information against leaks, indiscriminate publication, and other unauthorized disclosure. It cannot be construed to disable the AMLC from performing the very investigative and litigation functions that Congress simultaneously preserved, or from complying with the lawful and particularized subpoenas subject to judicial safeguards,” Escudero said.

Escudero later ruled that bank accounts of the Vice President and her husband in foreign currency can be presented as evidence in the impeachment trial, overruling the objection of Senator-judge Imee Marcos.
Escudero said the confidentiality afforded to foreign currency deposits does not exempt them from the reporting and inquiry provisions under Republic Act No. 9160 or the Anti-Money Laundering Act.
Private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia highlighted prosecution witness Buenaventura’s 85.75% Bar Exam score, noting that he ranked 10th in the 2015 Bar Examinations.

Divinagracia said the AMLC’s official Bar Exam rating is 5.75 percentage points higher than the score of a lawyer whom she and Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense counsel Mark Vinluan know. Vinluan moved to remove the remark from the record, which the court granted.
On July 14, it was Vinluan who touted during his cross-examination of state auditor Roderick Wamil that the Vice President passed the Bar on one take and scored 80% on her Bar Exam.
But despite this seemingly light moment initiated by Divinagracia, AMLC’s Buenaventura later said he skipped lunch because he was nervous.
Buenaventura proceeded to testify that the Vice President had over P10 million in over-the-counter withdrawals and check encashment in December 2024.
These include:

items: P2.371 million in an over-the-counter withdrawal reported by Land Bank of the Philippines-San Pedro on December 5, 2024
P1.7 million in a check encashment reported by Metropolitan Bank and Trust Co.-Davao/Ecoland on December 20, 2024
P5.969 million in a withdrawal reported by BDO Unibank Inc.-Davao Rizal on December 20, 2024

blocks.text: In addition, Buenaventura said the husband of Vice President Duterte withdrew a total of P41 million from two banks in a single day, specifically on August 6, 2024.
Of the P41 million, P23 million was withdrawn from BDO Unibank Inc. (BDO), while P18 million was withdrawn from Philippine National Bank (PNB).
Buenaventura also said that multiple bank accounts under Duterte's name were flagged by banks over alleged links to graft and corruption, drug trafficking, and malversation of public funds.

The AMLC official said at least two transactions of the Vice President involving premium payments to Mercantile Insurance Company Inc. in July and November 2019 were reported by the banks as suspicious transactions.

This is on top of the August 1, 2024 transaction with Philippine Savings Bank and a December 5, 2024 transaction with BDO Life Assurance Company Inc., which were also reported by the banks as suspicious transactions due to “drug trafficking and related offenses” and “malversation of public funds and property," respectively.
Billions
The AMLC official then dropped the biggest amount of the day: the P4.4 billion worth of covered and suspicious transactions recorded under the bank accounts of the Duterte and her husband.
Buenaventura said the value was reduced to P4.4 billion from P6.7 billion, which the AMLC official testified in the House justice panel, after a correction was made by one of the subject banks, BPI.
Of the 4.4 billion, he also testified that P1.63 billion accounted for inflows, while P1.3 billion was for outflows.
He also said there were P1.4 billion worth of covered and suspicious transactions with undetermined inflows and outflows.

Outside the courtroom, the Vice President’s spokesperson, Paolo Panelo, said the reduced amount of covered and suspicious transactions flagged by AMLC shows that those figures cannot be trusted. https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/topstories/nation/1004848/sara-duterte-camp-questions-contradictory-amlc-bank-transaction-data/story/?just_in
From China to PH
The money trail, as testified by Buenaventura, however, went beyond Philippine shores.
Buenaventura told the Senate impeachment court that Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company in which the Vice President’s husband has business interests, received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.
Throughout Day 33, Vinluan kept on harping that AMLC reports are confidential even if the Senate court already ruled otherwise.

Vinluan even cited that the defense won’t let such a violation of the law go unchallenged, and that anyone who would peruse AMLC reports, including journalists, could face jail time as provided by the Anti-Money Laundering law.

House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas, however, said such threat does not have weight because the AMLC report disclosures, including those revealed before the House justice panel hearings on the impeachment complaints against the Vice President, are all legal.

“We were exercising our duty as members of the House. We were exercising our duty, which is to initiate all impeachment cases. Remember that it is very clear in the Constitution that the House of Representatives has the exclusive power to initiate all impeachment cases,” Luistro said.

“On behalf of the prosecution team, kami po'y naninindigan na walang nilabag na batas, either the Anti-Money Laundering Act during the House proceedings, and we feel the same way now amid the ongoing impeachment trial and the reporting of the media being a free press since the impeachment is imbued with public interest,” Luistro added.
No closed doors for bribery allegation

Before the day ended, Luistro also said the House prosecution panel has yet to decide if it will drop its bribery charge in its impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte, House lead prosecutor Gerville Luistro of Batangas said Monday.

“I wish to confirm what the other members of the prosecution said: that there are serious inclinations [to drop the bribery charge]. But the fact that we are not yet manifesting it formally before the [Senate] impeachment court only means that the prosecution is not yet ready to officially withdraw this Article,” Luistro said in a press conference.

“There are considerations we are addressing, and this is what we meant when we said that while there are discussions…serious inclinations towards withdrawing Article 3, until we are yet to tell it to the impeachment court, it does not become official,” Luistro added.
Finally, the House prosecution panel said that the Vice President should explain why a business linked to her husband is taking Chinese money.

“This has serious national security implications. We have to understand that this Chinese remittance is crucial, given China’s aggressive position, including firing water cannons at our Coast Guard personnel, in the West Philippine Sea. This has to be investigated more thoroughly,” House prosecution team adviser and ex-Surigao del Norte Rep. Ace Barbers said in a press conference.

“Para saan itong perang ito? Who is the direct beneficiary? Is this hush money so that the Vice President will be mum on the Chinese aggression against us in the West Philippine Sea? Is this in exchange for any favor? Whoever gave this money, this raises questions that merit investigation,” Barbers added. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: UK threatens to expel Israeli diplomats after closing of East Jerusalem consulate
articles.summary:
Tit-for-tat expulsions expected after relations deteriorate as a result of UK ban on goods from illegal settlements

The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British…

blocks.text: The UK has threatened to expel one Israeli diplomat for every British diplomat forced to leave Israel as a result of Israel’s decision to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem later this week.

This could means as many as 27 Israeli diplomats being expelled from the UK, a step that would arguably mark the lowest point in British-Israeli diplomatic relations since the formation of the state of Israel.

The mass expulsion threat – more reminiscent of British-Russian diplomatic relations – was first reported by the Israeli newspaper Ynet, citing a message sent to Israeli officials. The UK Foreign Office said it would not comment on speculation, rather than denying the report outright.

Israel has threatened to close the UK consulate in East Jerusalem in protest at the UK decision to ban trade with goods from illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank and to impose sanctions on British firms that aid support or facilitate the construction of further illegal settlements.

The Foreign Office has been advised informally by the former UK attorney general Dominic Grieve that Israel is acting unlawfully if it closes the consulate on the basis it is sited in East Jerusalem, which is recognised by the United Nations and most of its members, including the UK, as being occupied Palestinian territory.
Israel’s foreign minister, Gideon Sa’ar, has said that Britain’s ‌decision to impose sanctions was “morally distorted” and accused Britain’s ruling Labour party of being hostile towards the country.

The consulate, which Israel’s foreign ministry has said will close on Thursday, is separate from the UK embassy based in Tel Aviv and has a distinct diplomatic role, covering East Jerusalem, the rest of the West Bank and Gaza. It is located in the Sheikh Jarrah neighbourhood of East ​Jerusalem.
An Israeli diplomatic sources said: “There is no reason for us to respond to speculation about decisions that other countries may or may not take in the future.
“We have already demonstrated that any step taken against Israel will be met with an appropriate response, and that will continue to be the case.”

The UK national security adviser, Jonathan Powell, travelled to Jerusalem last week in an effort to persuade the Israeli government to rescind or defer the closure of the consulate but the talks failed.

It has been reported that Powell opposed the decision of the UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, to press ahead with the settlement trade ban decision, fearing that it might play to the advantage of the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, in the national election on 27 October as he seeks bolster his case that only his brand of leadership can bring Israel security. There is no evidence as yet that the UK decision has yet played very big in the campaign, but tit-for-tat expulsion of diplomats may make the issue more high profile.

The ‌incident highlighted growing frustration among Israel’s longtime allies over its settlements in the occupied West Bank, viewed by much of the world as illegal under international law. In his statement to the UK parliament, Milband said settler terrorists, supported by Netanyahu’s, government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank, Israel disputes this.
after newsletter promotion

Israel has also said it is to revoke the credentials of Dutch diplomats from the country’s mission to Palestine, in response to the Netherlands’ ban on imports from illegal Israeli settlements. Israel’s military occupation of the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza means diplomats need Israeli accreditation to operate in Palestine. The decision also in effect bars them from Israel-controlled East Jerusalem.
France and Canada, which also joined the UK in the settlement trade ban, have not had action taken against them.
Miliband received a very warm reception at the UK Labour party conference last week during a speech in which he highlighted his decision to get tough with Israel over illegal settlements.

UK-Israeli relations have deteriorated steadily during the war in Gaza begun by Hamas’s 7 October 2023 massacre of Israelis as the UK became increasingly critical of the way in which Netanyahu seemed prepared to tolerate the death of thousands of Palestinians in a bid to render Hamas inoperative, a task both the Conservative and Labour governments thought was unachievable through his methods.

The UK has rescinded a large number of arms export licences to Israel as a result and Miliband has spoken of evidence of war crimes in Gaza. He has declined to accuse Israel of genocide on the grounds that he believes this is a matter for international courts alone to determine.

articles.title: Denmark: Data of millions compromised in hack
articles.summary: The breach by the hackers was through the legitimate login credentials of a local company, initial findings suggest. The data of some 8.8 million registered people was compromised.

image.caption: The hacker has not yet been apprehended [FILE: March 12, 2024]Image: Loïc Déquier/PHOTOPQR/SUD OUEST/picture alliance

blocks.text: Denmark's national registry was hacked in an incident the authorities described as "extremely serious."

Hackers secured access to personal information on millions of people, the country's digital affairs ministry said on Monday. The compromised information included names, addresses and social security numbers, known in Denmark as national registry numbers.

The data of some 8.8 million registered people was compromised. This figure exceeds Denmark's population size because it includes people who have already died or emigrated, the Danish authorities said in a statement.

The breach by the hackers was through the legitimate login credentials of a local company, initial findings suggest. The hackers have not yet been identified. The means they used to gain access has since been cut off.
The ministry said it was first alerted to an "anomaly" in the system "during September."
Information of deceased, emigrated people included

Denmark has a population of roughly six million people. However, its national registry includes information of eleven million people, which includes the data of those deceased or people who have moved abroad and don't live in Denmark anymore.
Christina Egelund, Denmark's digital affairs minister, said the incident's full extent will investigated by the authorities.
"This is an extremely serious incident," Egelund said. "We are in the process of tracking the exact extent of this incident with all those affected."

blocks.caption: Minister Christina Egelund called the breach 'very serious' [FILE: May 3, 2024]Image: Kristian Tuxen Ladegaard Berg/IMAGO

blocks.text: Danish news agency Ritzau reported that the register includes information on church membership, details of legal incapacitation and restrictions on legal capacity.

articles.title: Merz, Macron seek tougher EU measures against unfair trade
articles.summary: Emmanuel Macron and Friedrich Merz have written to Ursula von der Leyen, calling for tougher EU mechanisms against unfair trade practices by other states. They name no names but seem to have China or…

image.caption: Merz and Macron suggested that the EU should have the power to exclude countries from single-market access more quickly in extreme situations [FILE: July 17, 2026]Image: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron sent a joint appeal to the European Commission on Monday, calling for tougher EU measures against unfair trade practices by other states.
They said that the existing instruments at the EU's disposal were no longer sufficient.

The appeal did not name any specific country but it seemed most clearly tied to Chinese trade policy, the EU's vast deficit with China, and its dependence on certain key raw materials. The other apparent candidate would be the US, not least under the current unpredictable trade policy stewardship of tariff-loving President Donald Trump.
It also came just a few days before the EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, is set to visit Beijing.
How China is upping pressure on German businesses
What did Merz and Macron say?
The joint letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for two new measures to be introduced in Brussels.
One would aim at ensuring diversification and preventing companies from becoming too dependent on suppliers from individual companies.
The other would allow another country to be excluded from access to the European single market on an expedited basis if exceptional circumstances made this necessary.

Merz and Macron wrote that this could be used in cases "where third countries deliberately seek to undermine the restoration of a level playing field and fair market conditions through political or economic means, leading to serious and systematic distortions of our single market."

The French and German leaders, both struggling to balance economic growth and public spending, said the EU's struggles to maintain global competitiveness and its dependencies on certain suppliers of core materials led to "geoeconomic risks."

"The open and rules-based trading system is being massively compromised by the instrumentalization of trade, systemic market-distorting practices and global macroeconomic imbalances," they wrote. "All this undermines the level competitive playing field for our companies, our position as a sovereign core industrial producer and our capacity for innovations, which leads to increasing dependencies and geoeconomic risks."
Tungsten prices rally as China limits exports
Appeal comes ahead of EU China visit, and EU leaders' summit

Monday's letter is what's known in EU diplomatic circles as a "non-paper." These are nonbinding, informal documents shared between EU member states and institutions that are supposed to propose ideas and initiate discussions without officially committing to a position.

It recommends authorizing the Commission to exclude a country from single market access in extreme situations if it sees the need — currently a complicated process that would take some time to arrange and requires approval from member states.

It suggests reversing this process: allowing the Commission to take the step independently, but with member states then having the chance to block it with a qualified majority vote, which the EU currently defines as a vote by a minimum of 55% of member states that also represents a minimum of 65% of the bloc's total population.

The EU's trade deficit with China is vast and growing. The EU put the figure at around €360 billion (roughly $400 billion) in 2025, though China's statisticians reached a more modest tally of $292 billion.

The bloc is also particularly dependent on China for a number of raw materials, not least rare earths, and is increasingly reliant on both the US and China for high-tech imports and services, particularly in computing and the so-called AI sector.

The EU's trade commissioner, Maros Sefcovic, visits China this week for talks, ahead of an EU leaders' summit next week, on October 15-16. Sefcovic said earlier this year that he hoped to see "tangible results by October" on the question of trade with China, although whether these will materialize is an open question.
Beijing has warned that it could retaliate with changes of its own after learning of the EU's plans, if it perceives a need to.

Senator Panfilo Lacson on Monday posted an image on X (formerly Twitter) of Senator Vicente "Tito" Sotto III sitting in a dimly lit room furnished only with a monobloc chair and table and a gas lamp.
"Poor Senate President Pro Tempore Tito Sotto," Lacson said in the caption.

Lacson's post with the image, which appears to be AI-generated, came after media reports that the office—which Sotto was moving into as the Senate President Pro Tempore—had been stripped of furnishings and fixtures, including floor tiles, light bulbs and the toilet.
The office was previously used by Senator Jinggoy Estrada, the former President Pro Tempore who is currently detained on plunder charges.

articles.title: Norway seeks temporary ban on smart glasses amid privacy concerns
articles.summary: Norwegian authorities say a ban on the use of smart glasses could apply to places where "privacy is particularly important," like health-care facilities or fitness centres with changing rooms and…

image.caption: Meta Smart Glasses use built-in artificial intelligence, cameras, speakerphone, microphone and touch controls, providing real-time support for disabled and able bodied users wherever they go. (Shane Fowler/CBC)

blocks.text: World

Norwegian authorities say a ban on the use of smart glasses could apply to places where "privacy is particularly important," like health-care facilities or fitness centres with changing rooms and showers.
Norway's government is proposing parliament enact a temporary ban on AI glasses in some places

A trip to the park. A day at the beach. A workout session at the gym. All in public spaces where smart glasses can snap photos, record conversations or stream video online — without people in the line of their lenses and microphones knowing about it.
Norway's government wants to get a handle on both the promise and peril of AI glasses and is proposing that parliament enact a temporary ban on them in some places.

It's the latest sign of growing concern in many countries about new technologies that are fundamentally changing the way people live. Some governments have banned the use of social media by children and young teens.
Norway's government said the proposal for the temporary ban will be made to parliament, the Storting, "as soon as possible."
Where to draw the line?

Norwegian authorities say a ban on the use of smart glasses could apply to places where "privacy is particularly important," like health-care facilities, or fitness centres with changing rooms and showers. A major focus is spaces where children congregate, such as schools, kindergartens, playgrounds and youth clubs.
But it could extend to public concerts and sports events, plus parks, beaches, museums and shopping centers.

A temporary ban would give authorities time to decide what types of devices might be affected, and debate whether permanent regulation is needed. The government was quick to note that it was not proposing a total ban and said such devices should still be allowed in some places and for private use.
The government also said it was considering exceptions to a ban for vulnerable groups, so that "socially beneficial uses" of smart glasses could be permitted in some circumstances.

items: Should municipalities ban smart glasses in pools and change rooms?
Kids and young adults are addicted to screens. New research argues it may be a public health concern

blocks.text: Privacy advocates hail Norway's move

Adam Smith, a technology advocacy officer at Britain-based Privacy International, said Norway's move was "a welcome protection against big tech's greedy attempts to extract ever more data, often in absence of any thought for the privacy or rights of others."
"No reality exists in which people expect to be secretly surveilled going about their daily lives," he said.
One effort to rein in the use of AI glasses has run aground — in the home of Silicon Valley.

California's governor last week vetoed legislation that would have penalized the use of smart glasses to record people without their permission in places like changing rooms, doctor's offices and other spaces people generally consider private.
Meta glasses: the good, the bad and the creepy | Hanomansing Tonight
Despite Meta's assurances, some businesses clamp down

Meta, the company behind Facebook, WhatsApp and Instagram that has rolled out AI glasses with eyewear vendor Ray-Ban, encourages respect for privacy and advises customers on how to use the glasses responsibly.
"Respect people's preferences. Not everyone loves being photographed. Stop recording if anyone expresses that they would rather you not," Meta wrote on its site.

The tech giant based in Menlo Park, Calif., says a light on the glasses indicates when recording in underway, and if the glasses detect that the light has been blocked or physically tampered with, the camera is automatically disabled.
Despite such advice and assurances, some privacy advocacy groups cite a growing backlash against AI glasses.
Hans Anders, a prominent eyewear retailer in the Netherlands, has suspended sales of the Ray-Ban Meta glasses.
Would you wear AI smart glasses? Big tech is betting on it

"This decision follows the ongoing public and political debate surrounding smart glasses and the questions being raised about the conditions under which this technology can be used," Hans Anders said in a statement, suggesting that it plans to await the outcome of the debate before making a final decision.

In Britain, the UK Cinema Association said in August it was introducing policies to prohibit or restrict the wearing of camera-enabled smart glasses, citing concerns about privacy and film piracy through the use of such technology.

Medical transport plane flying from Bermuda to Boston crashed off coast of Massachusetts early Saturday

Six people are presumed dead after the US Coast Guard on Sunday suspended its search…

blocks.text: Six people are presumed dead after the US Coast Guard on Sunday suspended its search for survivors of a medical transport plane crash off the coast of Massachusetts early the previous day.

The aircraft, which was flying from Bermuda to Boston, lost contact with ground authorities at about 2am on Saturday, and the Coast Guard located a debris field near the island of Nantucket later that day.

“Suspending a search is not an easy decision,” Coast Guard Rear Adm Matthew Lake, commander of the agency’s north-east district, said in a statement. “We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts.”

The aircraft – a Gulfstream G100 operated by Canadian company Latitude Air Ambulance – took off from Bermuda at 12.41am on Saturday, carrying a patient, a family member and a four-person crew. The patient and family member were identified as citizens of Bermuda. The crew was identified as Canadian citizens.
In its own statement, Latitude acknowledged the Coast Guard’s decision to suspend the search for those who were aboard what the company described as Heartbeat 104.

“Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search and rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient’s family escort, who were aboard Heartbeat 104, are presumed to have died,” the company’s statement said.
Air traffic controllers had difficulty communicating with the flight in its final moments.
“You’re coming in blind? Is that what you said?” a controller asked the pilot at about 12.46am. “Are you declaring an emergency, or no?”
According to a recording captured by LiveATC.net, the pilot’s response was not audible.

The plane reported electrical failures as it neared Nantucket, according to radio transmissions. Data from the website FlightAware shows the plane descended thousands of feet within three minutes and disappeared from radar shortly after about 1am local time.

Latitude said it will “cooperate fully” with US National ⁠Transportation ​Safety Board (NTSB), the Transportation Safety Board ​of Canada and other authorities on recovery efforts and an investigation into why the plane ​crashed.

articles.title: Sara Duterte spox on alleged China money: What if it was used for classrooms?
articles.summary: Accusations that Vice President Sara Duterte has links to China because she allegedly received funds from the Chinese are without basis, her spokesman said on Monday.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 12:32am
Accusations that Vice President Sara Duterte has links to China because she allegedly received funds from the Chinese are without basis, her spokesman said on Monday.

Atty. Paolo Panelo said this after the prosecution in Duterte's impeachment trial offered evidence that she allegedly received funds from China, an allegation former Sen. Antonio Trillanes IV made at a press conference on Friday.

"May donation ng Chinese government sa Tapangin at Malasakit [Foundation], and the Vice President is one of the trustees. Awtomatikong agad na sinusuportahan ng Chinese government si Vice President?" Panelo said.
"What if it was used to build classrooms? Or what if it was used for charitable purposes at may resibo?" he added.
Panelo said there are rules on the admissibility of evidence, and this is why Trillanes opted to hold a press conference instead of testifying in the impeachment court.

"To jump to a conclusion as Senator Trillanes did, na this proves na sinusuportahan ng China si Vice President at parang malaking national security concern yan dahil vice president, walang basehan yan, eh," Panelo said.
"Kaya kailangan dumaan talaga dito sa impeachment court. Kaya tayo may rules of evidence, kaya tayo may rule of law," he added.
Defense Secretary Giberto "Gibo" Teodoro, over the weekend, asked Trillanes to submit evidence as regards the alleged ties between China and the Vice President because of national security concerns.

"Wala naman siyang tinatakbuhan na kahit anong kaso. Di naharap niya naman lahat. Nakita niya naman. So, kung merong investigation, eh di mag-investigate kasi confident siya na nasa tama siya," Panelo said. –NB, GMA News

articles.title: Marcos shares childhood dream of becoming musician or scientist in Gary V podcast
articles.summary: President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. shared on Monday his childhood dream of becoming a musician or a scientist, revealing that he even studied music for a couple of years abroad.

blocks.text: Published October 6, 2026 12:16am
President Ferdinand “Bongbong” Marcos Jr. shared on Monday his childhood dream of becoming a musician or a scientist, revealing that he even studied music for a couple of years abroad.

“My sister [has] always said, ‘The two dreams in your life were to be an astronaut, because of the science, and to be a rockstar.' It’s true, I would’ve done anything to fly in space, and I would’ve done anything to have a life in music,” Marcos said in the podcast “Unshaken with Gary V” of singer Gary Valenciano.
Marcos said that despite having a father who was a Philippine president, he initially never thought of becoming one himself.
He recalled being teased about becoming the next president as early as three or four years old.

“I’ve been hearing it all my life, and maybe that’s part of the reason I resist. I think I first heard it when I was three years old [or] four years old… and I always said, ‘Of course not, I’m not going to be, I’m going to be something else,’” Marcos said.
He pointed out that seeing his father’s life was one of the factors why he never thought of becoming a politician when he was young.

“The funny thing is.. I knew I wasn't going to be is a politician. I absolutely said, ‘That is one walk of life that I am not going to go down,’ because I saw how difficult it is from the sacrifices that my dad had to make, my mom had to make, and the other people had to make around them,” Marcos said.
Dream
Growing up, the President said that he always had an affinity for mathematics and science, which led him to dream of becoming a scientist.
“I said, ‘I’m going to be a scientist. I want to be a scientist.’ I dreamed of working in a lab in a white coat and doing really important research… and maybe teach a little bit,” Marcos said.
Meanwhile, his dream of becoming a musician was inspired by his mother’s fondness for music.
Since childhood, Marcos recalled how their household was always filled with music, which molded him into becoming musical. This interest eventually led him to study music abroad.
“The other thing that really was always there is music. And my mother, because she is so musically minded, we always had music in our house,” the President said.
“... When I was studying already abroad, I started studying music… I studied music for years,” he added.
Marcos shared that he learned how to play the flute and the saxophone, and played in an orchestra and a school band.
At present, the President said that he still carries his deep appreciation for music.

“If you took music away from me, I don't know how I would manage. I just don't know how I would get through the day… There’s two things that can change my mood. Music is one of them, the other one is my children,” Marcos said. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Pentagon stops using Anthropic AI tools months after blacklisting company, BBC told
articles.summary: It labelled the company a "supply chain risk" earlier this year, but multiple sources said Anthropic's Claude model was recently widely used.

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Defence secretary Pete Hegseth has publicly criticised Anthropic's boss Dario Amodei
ByKali HaysTechnology reporter in San Francisco and Daniel BushWashington correspondent
The US Department of Defence is no longer using Anthropic's AI tools, an official has told the BBC, months after it designated the company a supply chain risk on national security grounds.
The Pentagon "has ceased the use of Anthropic products", the department official said in a statement.
Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth labelled Anthropic a supply chain risk in February, and announced that the Pentagon would stop using it by late August.

But multiple people familiar with the matter told the BBC that as recently as last week Anthopic's Claude model was still used by the department in research, analysis and intelligence gathering as well as in military operations against Iran.

It was viewed as a critical tool for sorting through vast quantities of information, the people said. They include former US defence officials and contractors who have worked closely with the Pentagon specifically on AI.
A spokesman for Anthropic declined to comment when asked about the Pentagon's statement.
The details of the defence department stopping all use of Anthropic's tools have not been previously reported.
Anthropic had been used by the US government and military since 2024 and was the first advanced AI company to have its tools deployed in government agencies doing classified work.
But earlier this year, the Pentagon pressed it to remove its safety guardrails from Claude and give the military unfettered access to its AI tools.

When Anthropic refused, citing concerns of mass surveillance and autonomous weapons, Hegseth designated the company a "national security supply-chain risk" - a law typically reserved for companies based in countries that pose a threat to the US.
Anthropic said the move was "unprecedented and unlawful" and has sued the Trump administration in an effort to overturn the designation.
As this legal fight has played out in the courts, the Pentagon has signed contracts with other major tech companies, including Google, xAI and OpenAI.
OpenAI tools have been more widely adopted in recent months in some military departments, according to two people familiar with AI use in the defence department
The Pentagon's statement to the BBC on Monday came after multiple people said in interviews that Claude was still being widely used in recent weeks.
It was embedded in a larger data platform used by the Pentagon called Maven Smart System, multiple sources said.
Maven, which is operated by Palantir, is the Pentagon's primary platform for organising intelligence and other data.

Lauren Kahn, a senior research analyst at Georgetown's Center for Security and Emerging Technology said that because Claude was deeply integrated into Maven it would have been difficult to remove it quickly from the system.
"The fact that it took the Pentagon until now to remove all use of Claude from across the system is indicative that these things are not just plug and play," she said.
"Once they become integrated it can be painful to remove them," added Kahn, a former US defence official.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Trump recently met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei at the White House

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Trump recently met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei at the White House

The BBC spoke with defence contractors who specialise in AI and have worked closely with the Pentagon, as well as former US defence officials and others familiar with the Pentagon's use of artificial intelligence. Several spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to speak to the media.
When Hegseth initially ordered Anthropic to be phased out of government, "there was concern with moving beyond Anthropic to OpenAI" and other tools, a former senior US defence official said.
Hegseth set a six-month deadline to phase out Anthropic on 27 February, one day before the US and Israel attacked Iran.
Pentagon employees continued to use Anthropic's Claude tools, including its powerful Mythos models, "throughout the whole period of the controversy" with the company, one of the people said.

Claude was used in particular for intelligence gathering and analysis, including through Palantir's Maven system, several sources said. Palantir, a leading defence tech firm, was founded by the billionaire ally of President Donald Trump, Peter Thiel.
'There is a possibility of human extinction,' former Anthropic employee says about AI
Sources familiar with the way the technology is used said analysts and other defence officials rely on Maven to access and organise visual data, including satellite imagery and drone footage.
The data was then fed into Claude and other large language models for tasks such as identifying potential military targets.

Officials frequently used the technology when compiling one-page briefs that were passed up the chain of command, according to a source who was given a demonstration of Maven by Palantir earlier this year.
Recent private demonstrations of Maven for government officials have also included Claude, another person familiar with Maven said.
The Maven system is deployed "across the entire department", Cameron Stanley, who leads AI work within the defence department, said during a demonstration of Maven earlier this year.
Maven is also used by some US allies to share intelligence with the Trump administration.

A current defence department official touted Maven's role in intelligence sharing in the war with Iran during a private briefing with industry leaders in Washington last week, according to a former US official who participated in the meeting.
Anthropic's clash with the Pentagon comes as relations with the White House appear to be warming. Trump met with Anthropic boss Dario Amodei twice at the White House last week.
After one of the meetings with Trump and other technology leaders, Amodei said he still had concerns about risks posed by AI.
"How we address those risks is still under discussion," Amodei told reporters at the White House, as Trump stood by his side, but "if we work with the president, we can win safely".
Trump then proceeded to praise Amodei, saying he was "great" and "fantastic."

articles.title: Norway plans temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places
articles.summary:
Camera-enabled Meta spectacles are already restricted in UK and US because of fears about covert recording

Norway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places, amid…

blocks.text: Norway is planning a temporary ban on smart glasses in some public places, amid rising global concern at the spread of the AI-enabled recording devices.

The Oslo government is planning a bill to prevent the use of the camera-enabled spectacles in parks, beaches, museums, shopping centres, schools, daycare centres, healthcare facilities, gyms and public events, although private use would still be allowed.
There is already a growing patchwork of restrictions on the use of the glasses including in UK and US courtrooms and in pubs, cinemas and restaurants where owners have raised privacy fears.

Torgeir Micaelsen, Norway’s minister of digital affairs, said he was “worried that ‌new, powerful technology is being introduced where people risk being ‌photographed, filmed or audio-recorded without knowing it”.
“We do not want a society where people worry about being recorded without their knowledge, photographed or filmed in places and situations where they are accustomed to not being monitored,” he said.

Norway’s Labour party, which heads a minority government, needs the support of other parties to pass the proposed ban. It said it plans to submit a bill “as soon as possible”, while tasking an expert group with drawing up permanent regulations on the issue.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta sells “smart” versions of Rayban and Oakley glasses that allow users to film, take photos, make phone calls, play music and execute AI prompts. It has sold at least nine million pairs of the Rayban versions since the start of 2023.

In the UK restaurateurs such as Jeremy King, who created the Wolseley and Delaunay restaurants, and pub chain Wetherspoons have already said they do not want customers using the devices. Cinemas said in August they have begun introducing policies to ban or restrict the use of smart glasses citing both privacy and film piracy concerns.

Last week the governor of California, Gavin Newsom, vetoed legislation that would have penalised citizens for using smart glasses to record people without their permission in changing rooms, doctors’ offices and other spaces people generally consider private. The state already has laws governing unlawful recording.
after newsletter promotion

In France, the child welfare group E-enfance said it had this year received about 20 reports of women being filmed without their knowledge using glasses fitted with a camera, the majority of which involved Meta smart glasses. It said the incidents often followed the same pattern: a young girl or woman approached in a public place, filmed without her knowledge, with the clip then posted on social media in the form of a prank or a street interview.

Meta has stressed that each pair of glasses is fitted with a tamper-proof LED light that blinks white when the user is recording or taking pictures. It advises users: “Not everyone loves being photographed. Stop recording if anyone expresses that they would rather you not.”
Meta has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Glasgow city council reaches pay deal with union to avert fire-and-rehire plan
articles.summary:
‘Strong and fair’ proposal to be taken to members’ ballot after previous offer led Unison to walk out of negotiations

Glasgow city council has reached an agreement with the trade union…

blocks.text: Glasgow city council has reached an agreement with the trade union Unison over pay and grading, averting one of the UK’s biggest ever fire-and-rehire exercises.

Talks between the council and the GMB, Unite and Unison unions previously broke down when Unison refused to ballot its members on a new pay and grading system, designed to resolve historical equal pay issues.

The collapse of talks prompted the council to contact 23,000 workers, its entire non-teaching staff, at the end of last month to inform them they were at risk of being dismissed and reappointed, many on less favourable terms. The move led to significant backlash from opposition parties, unions and council employees.
The original proposal that led Unison to walk out of negotiations would have resulted in wage cuts for 11% of staff, but on Monday the council agreed to protect their pay for three years.

Unison said many issues remained unresolved and that negotiations would continue, but that it would now ballot its members this month. The council has agreed to continue negotiating on issues including the equality impacts of the new pay structure.
Ricky Bell, the leader of Glasgow city council, said he was “delighted that we have been able to reach agreement with Unison” and “remove the unpalatable prospect of fire-and-rehire”.

“This is a strong and fair deal,” he added. “Both GMB and Unite have already agreed to take it to their members and, with all three unions now engaging with their memberships, we are moving closer to the outcome we have always wanted to achieve: ending pay discrimination in Glasgow city council once and for all.”

Bell emphasised there was no further money to come as part of the package, but said he looked forward to seeing the outcome of the union ballots. He thanked the Scottish government for additional support to help “unlock [the] agreement”.
Chris Sermanni, Unison’s Glasgow city branch secretary, said: “Unison stood firm because Glasgow’s workers deserved better than what was originally put on the table.
“That position has secured significant movement. There’s now a path for Unison members to give their verdict without the immediate threat of dismissal and re-engagement hanging over them.
“The period ahead will be used to keep fighting to give the whole workforce the information they need to make their decision.”
The ballot will last four weeks, with a timeline to be laid out in the coming days.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro poised to win Brazilian presidency after shock first-round victory
articles.summary:
Progressive voters and supporters of incumbent president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva left reeling after far-right surge

Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential…
articles.byline: Tom Phillips and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro

blocks.text: Flávio Bolsonaro is in pole position to win Brazil’s presidential election, after a far-right tsunami propelled him to a shock first-round victory over the incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, leaving progressive voters reeling.

The 45-year-old rightwing candidate received 56.1m votes to Lula’s 53.8m – 47.03% to 45.16% – meaning the 80-year-old leftwinger has a mountain to climb if he is to bounce back in the second round on 25 October. Never, since the return of democracy to Brazil in 1985, has the first-round runner-up managed to turn the game around and win the second ballot.
“Miracles are possible in politics. But I don’t see that happening,” the political scientist Miguel Lago said of Lula’s chances of snapping back. “I don’t see Flávio losing this election now.”
The far-right surge was a triumph – albeit an incomplete one – for the Bolsonaro clan and its 71-year-old patriarch, Jair Bolsonaro.

The disgraced ex-president, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election to Lula, saw four relatives elected to congress. His 44-year-old wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, won a seat in the senate, as did his second son, Carlos Bolsonaro, who is 43. Bolsonaro’s youngest son, 28-year-old Jair Renan Bolsonaro, and the ex-president’s 62-year-old brother, Renato Bolsonaro, both won seats in the lower house of congress.

blocks.caption: Supporters of Flávio Bolsonaro celebrate the first-round results in Porto Alegre on Sunday. Photograph: Sílvio Ávila/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Across Latin America’s biggest democracy, key congressional and gubernatorial races were also won by staunch Bolsonaristas including Tarcísio de Freitas, who was re-elected as the governor of São Paulo state, and Sérgio Moro, who was elected governor of the southern state of Paraná. Both men were ministers during Bolsonaro’s 2018-22 government.

Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) will now boast the largest caucus in the senate with 28 of its 81 seats. Combined with the seats of other hard-right parties, that number rises to 43, giving the movement an upper house majority.

Meanwhile, pro-Lula senate candidates, including the former environment minister Marina Silva, the leftwing veteran Benedita da Silva, and the centrist former planning minister Simone Tebet, suffered bitter defeats.
Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, two young Bolsonarista social media warriors, became the best-voted congresspeople in Brazilian history, securing more than 3m votes.

blocks.caption: Nikolas Ferreira, a 30-year-old congressman from Minas Gerais, is seen as one of the most influential members of the Bolsonarista right; he has more than 5 million followers on Instagram. Photograph: Alan Lima/The Guardian

blocks.text: “We are experiencing a revolution … The far right is growing in a very consistent way, election after election,” said Lago, calling the election the worst for progressive and moderate centrist parties since the late 80s.

Lago believed Lula had managed to interrupt the advance of Bolsonaro’s populist movement in 2022, thanks to positive voter memories of his first two terms, from 2002 to 2010. Back then, a global commodities boom allowed Brazil’s first working-class president to fund major social welfare programmes that helped millions escape poverty. “But it was just an interregnum,” Lago said.

Control of the senate should allow pro-Bolsonaro politicians to approve an amnesty for their movement’s charismatic leader, allowing the former president to emerge from the Brasília mansion where he is living under house arrest and reassert his leadership of the far right.

“I think he will be freed and I think he will be very important during Flávio Bolsonaro’s [presidency],” said Lago. “Flávio will be running the country and [Jair] Bolsonaro will be doing what he has always done: leading the revolution.”

The senate majority may also help Bolsonaro’s third son, Eduardo Bolsonaro, return from self-imposed exile in the US. The 42-year-old, who has close ties to Donald Trump’s Maga movement, was sentenced in absentia to four years in prison earlier this year for coercion – the result of his lobbying the Trump administration to interfere in his father’s coup trial. Eduardo Bolsonaro reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.

blocks.caption: Eduardo Bolsonaro, seen here at the Conservative Political Action Conference (Cpac) in Buenos Aires in 2024, reportedly hopes to become foreign minister if his brother wins the presidency.  Photograph: Juan Mabromata/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Trump, who has been accused of trying to sway the election in Bolsonaro’s favour, has yet to comment on Sunday’s result, although writing on his Truth Social network, he praised the speed of the vote count. But the US president will be delighted by the strong rightwing showing, a major boost to his attempt to expand the conservative “orange wave” sweeping Latin America to its biggest democracy and economy. Recent years have seen a succession of pro-Trump presidents win power in the region, from Costa Rica, Honduras and El Salvador to Chile and Colombia.

One of Trump’s most enthusiastic regional cheerleaders, the Argentinian president, Javier Milei, celebrated Bolsonaro’s “historic” victory against “the communist Lula”. “The American continent belongs to citizens who want to live in freedom,” Milei wrote on X.

The prime minister of Israel, Benjamin Netanyahu, wished Bolsonaro “good luck in the final” and celebrated his “great victory”. He wrote on X: “I look forward to restoring the extraordinary friendship between Israel and Brazil.”

blocks.caption: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said his Workers’ party ‘will launch a new campaign’.  Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Speaking after Sunday’s result was confirmed, Lula put a brave face on what analysts called a catastrophic night for the left. “From tomorrow we will launch a new campaign: [and in] a campaign with only two candidates we will be able to show the difference between our proposals for Brazil,” he said, vowing to expose his rival’s “dark past”, which involves well-documented ties to members of Rio’s underworld and corruption allegations, which Bolsonaro has denied.

But the mood at Lula’s post-election event was reportedly funereal and Bolsonaro goes into the second round as the firm favourite. He is likely to be boosted by the migration of votes from the election’s other rightwing candidates – Ronaldo Caiado, Renan Santos and Romeu Zema – who, between them, won more than 5.5m votes.

Santos quickly announced he would endorse neither candidate, considering both Lula and Bolsonaro to be “crooks”. Zema has vowed to vote against Lula’s Worker’s party (PT) in the runoff, while Caiado has yet to declare his intentions.

Lula’s best hope may be convincing some of the record 33 million Brazilians who did not vote to turn out next time. “He will need to mobilise these apathetic voters who, in a sense, have already abandoned politics, which will be an extremely difficult task,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right.

Rocha has spent recent months interviewing undecided voters and identified “a great deal of voter apathy, especially among those who are not aligned with Bolsonarismo, and who could potentially vote for Lula”.

Although Flávio Bolsonaro has held political office for more than 20 years, “for undecided voters, his main positive characteristic is this idea of ‘renewal’, despite his possible involvement in corruption and with paramilitary groups,” Rocha added.

Lago believed only a dramatic shift from Lula’s campaign – such as changing the candidate, or a severe scandal involving Bolsonaro – could change the election’s outcome. But he was doubtful that would occur.

articles.title: Republican Ken Paxton admits forces in DC control his Texas Senate campaign
articles.summary:
‘I don’t control message or what we’re doing,’ scandal- hit state attorney general reportedly says at private event

Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general

blocks.text: Ken Paxton, the Texas attorney general chosen by Donald Trump to run as the Republican candidate for a Senate seat, admitted in private that his campaign was being controlled by outside forces in Washington DC.

Paxton, who is locked in a competitive race with the progressive Democrat James Talarico, told people at a fundraising event in September that he had never felt such little control over his campaign because of outside influence.

“I’ve never been in a race where I felt less control over the campaign and, like, what issues are going to matter because it’s all coming – you know – from D.C.,” Paxton said, according to an audio recording obtained by Politico.
“I don’t control message or what we’re doing,” Paxton said.

An unnamed attender told Politico that Paxton never explicitly said he was referring to Trump’s team controlling his campaign messaging but that Paxton’s comments arose during a conversation about the national political environment.
Paxton’s campaign adviser Nick Maddux said in a statement, “Campaigns don’t coordinate with Super Pacs, and that’s obviously what AG Paxton was referring to.

“AG Paxton is thankful for the support and knows how important Texas is to keeping the majority which is why he’s on the ground every day talking to Texas, raising money, and taking his message directly to the people including with his statewide television buy that started over this past weekend,” Maddux said.
Earlier this year, Trump chose Paxton to run against Talarico, a political newcomer who Democrats hope will flip Texas’s longtime red senate seat to blue in the midterm elections next month.

Though Paxton has been a well-known conservative figure in Texas for years, he has also been embroiled in a series of scandals. Paxton was impeached in 2023 on allegations including bribery and abuse of public trust – though he was later acquitted. Paxton’s wife, Angela Paxton, also divorced him on “biblical grounds”, citing adultery.
Polls show Paxton and Talarico neck-and-neck, with Talarico having a small lead over the Texas attorney general.

A Fox News survey found Talarico at 51% and Paxton at 49% among likely voters. A New York Times/Siena College poll found Talarico at 51% and Paxton at 45% among likely Texas voters. A Marist University poll indicated Talarico had 50% while Paxton had 44% among registered voters.
Paxton’s latest comments are the second reported critical remarks the Texas attorney general has made about outside involvement in his campaign.
Last week, the New York Times reported that Paxton admitted that Trump’s Republican National Convention for the midterms “dropped” his polling numbers.

Asked whether the convention had negative consequences, Paxton replied: “So to be honest with you, the numbers – when we did that convention – it dropped our numbers. Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”
Maddux told the New York Times that Paxton’s reported comment was “manipulated nonsense from The New York Times to create a story that doesn’t exist”.
