articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is hot meat?
articles.summary: Hot meat refers to “the carcass or parts of carcass or food animals which were slaughtered from unregistered or unaccredited meat establishments and have not undergone the required inspection,”…

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 10:31pm
Authorities recently seized 11.5 metric tons or P5.19 million worth of Chinese meat products in Pasay City that did not undergo the proper inspection.
Meat products that were processed in unregistered facilities or illegally transported are tagged as “hot meat.”

Hot meat refers to “the carcass or parts of carcass or food animals which were slaughtered from unregistered/unaccredited meat establishments and have not undergone the required inspection,” according to Republic Act No. 9296 or the Meat Inspection Code of the Philippines.
“It also includes undocumented, illegally shipped, and unregistered carcasses, parts of carcasses, and meat products coming from other countries,” the law added.
Among the illegal meat products seized in the Pasay City operations are peking duck, whole pigeon, lamb, yellow chicken, and black chicken.
How about frog meat?

All meat products, including frog meat, meant for commercial sale or import must meet NMIS safety, inspection, and documentation standards, according to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and Department of Agriculture’s National Meat Inspection Service (NMIS).

“Imported meat must come from foreign meat establishments that have undergone the required evaluation and are compliant with Philippine requirements before they are authorized to export to the country,” the NBI and NMIS said in a briefer.
Meat found unfit for human consumption is disposed of accordingly by the NMIS.

“The inspectors shall mark, stamp, tag, or label as ‘Inspected and Passed’ or ‘Inspected and Condemned’ all such products found to be unadulterated or adulterated as the case may be. Condemned meat Products shall be destroyed for food purposes,” the law stated.

Meanwhile, imported meat products that did not meet Philippine import requirements shall be refused entry and sent back to the country of origin. They can also be disposed of “at the expense of the importer or owner to protect public health and the local animal population.”
Individuals caught selling, transporting, or receiving uninspected "hot meat" or violating meat safety laws face up to 12 years in prison and fines of up to P1 million under Republic Act No. 9296.
Violators convicted by the court may also be compelled to pay restitution to affected consumers. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Euro plummets against US dollar: has the next financial crisis begun?
articles.summary: The euro has fallen to a 17-month low against the dollar. That will make inflation worse in the EU, where political worries and concern over French debt are already troubling investors. Is a fiscal…

image.caption: The difference between French and German government 10-year debt yields reached their highest level since the eurozone debt crisisImage: LUNAMARINA/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: The euro hit a 17-month low against the dollar in early trading on Monday, as concerns over eurozone debt, particularly in France, compounded existing investor concerns over global government bond yields and rising oil prices.
The euro has been sliding against the dollar for much of 2026, down around 5% since the start of the year. It reached $1.12 on Monday, the lowest level since early in 2025.

Ricardo Amaro, lead eurozone economist with Oxford Economics, told DW that the general slide can be attributed to a repricing of investor expectations regarding US Federal Reserve policy in terms of higher interest rates in the face of rising global bond yields.
However, he said the latest sell-off was prompted in particular by concerns over France, where "investors positioned for higher fiscal risk."
The France problem

The sell-off in French debt gathered pace last week as doubts grow over its long-term viability. French 10-year government bonds — the cost France must pay to borrow money within 10 years of the debt being issued — rose to a 5% yield before easing slightly.

France has long had underlying fiscal problems. Since President Emmanuel Macron came to office in May 2017, public spending has climbed while he has brought in deep tax cuts. As a result, the country's national debt has increased by well over €1 trillion ($1.12 trillion).

France's debt-to-GDP ratio now stands at almost 118%. It consistently posts unbalanced budgets. Its annual budget deficit is now regularly more than 5%, above the 3.4% rate when Macron came to office.

For many investors, wider concerns over low eurozone growth levels and surging energy prices have contributed to a renewed focus on France, with many retreating to perceived safer options, such as German government debt.
The difference between French and German government 10-year debt yields reached their highest level since the eurozone debt crisis last week, a closely-watched measure of EU financial stability.
What can the ECB do?

The resulting pressure on the euro and on other government bond markets, including Italy's, means there are calls for the European Central Bank (ECB) to take action to prevent concern over France turning into panic.
Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid said in a note on Monday that at one point last week, the spread between German and French bonds had become so wide that a "mini-panic" was at hand.
"The big question is whether this is the start of a new euro sovereign crisis or whether markets have already overshot," he said.

blocks.caption: There is pressure on the European Central Bank to take actionImage: Jana Rodenbusch/REUTERS

blocks.text: Ricardo Amaro said the situation presents a challenge for the ECB because it needs to act without making things worse. "Sounding too hawkish would also add to pressure on France's bond yields, which became an important driver of euro weakness," he added.
He expects policymakers to continue monitoring currency developments between the US dollar and the euro, but to stop short of trying to influence the market for now.
What is at stake?

Uncertainty abounds due to both political and economic pressures. France has been beset by political crises in recent years, where passing annual budgets has become a major test of government stability.

Although the 2027 budget has been agreed, with reforms aimed at reducing the deficit, the right-wing National Rally remains well-placed ahead of the 2027 presidential election, in which Marine Le Pen is likely to be the lead candidate.

Concerns over French economic policy in the event of Le Pen winning the presidency are spooking investors, similar to how the rise of the populist AfD in Germany has raised questions over the future direction of the bloc's key economy.

Much of the political instability has been driven by voter anger over the high cost of living. In Spain, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has just called a snap election after measures to deal with the country's housing crisis were voted down in parliament.

blocks.caption: Political crises in France and Spain are fuelled by economic issuesImage: Cheng Min/Xinhua/picture alliance

blocks.text: Amaro says a weakening euro could compound the underlying problem of inflation.
"Sharper euro weakness would reinforce the inflationary shock at a time when inflation is already expected to stay high into 2027," he said.

A weaker euro would increase the cost of imported goods, particularly those that are priced in US dollars. Global commodities such as oil and gas are priced in dollars, meaning soaring energy prices would likely rise further, as would US imports.
The next financial crisis?

With memories of the sovereign debt crisis that afflicted the EU in the early 2010s still fresh, many observers are beginning to wonder if the moves on French debt could be indicative of a new crisis in the eurozone.
Some, such as Geoffrey Yu, a senior strategist with BNY, believes such concerns are misplaced. "Comparisons to 2012 are well off the mark," he said.

However, Amaro says the fact that further interest rate hikes are expected from the ECB this year, combined with the worsening inflation outlook, makes this a situation which needs to be managed and monitored very carefully.

"Euro weakness shouldn't be interpreted as an isolated development," he says. "If triggered by growing concerns about France's fiscal outlook, then the ECB would certainly want to thread that carefully given risks for the eurozone."

articles.title: Sara Duterte camp questions contradictory AMLC bank transaction data
articles.summary: The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday questioned the contradictory covered and suspicious bank transactions discussed in the impeachment trial compared to what was discussed during the…

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 10:26pm

The camp of Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday questioned the contradictory covered and suspicious bank transactions discussed in the impeachment trial compared to what was discussed during the earlier probe by the House Committee on Justice.

On Day 33 of the impeachment trial on Monday, the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) said P4.4 billion worth of covered and suspicious transactions were recorded under the bank accounts of the Vice President and her husband, Manases Carpio.
But this is far from what the AMLC presented during the April 22 hearing, wherein transactions totaling P6.7 billion—classified as covered and suspicious—were recorded under the couple’s names.

“Nagkaroon po ng system error, base na ito mismo dun sa abogado ni Atty. Mans Carpio, na itong meron daw P2 million transaction na na-report ng BPI bilang 2 point something billion. Kaya po lumobo ng P6.7 billion ,” said Paolo Panelo, the vice president’s spokesperson.

(There was a system error, based on the lawyer of Atty. Mans Carpio, where a 2 million transaction was reportedly reported by BPI as 2 point something billion. That is why it inflated to P6.7 billion.)

“Kaya yun po yung sinasabi natin bakit hindi pwedeng i-share lang bigla ng AMLC yung raw data nila dahil kailangan mong i-verify yan, kailangan mong alamin kung ano yung konteksto ng mga... ng mga transactions bago mo isisiwalat,” he added.
(That's why we are saying why AMLC cannot just suddenly share their raw data—because you need to verify it, you need to know what the context of the... of the transactions is before you disclose it.)
Of the P4.4 billion, AMLC executive director Ronel Buenaventura also testified that P1.63 billion accounted for inflows, while P1.3 billion was for outflows.
He also said there are P1.4 billion worth of covered and suspicious transactions with undetermined inflows and outflows.

When asked whether the contradictory amounts are “fatal” to the case, Panelo said this only shows how raw data from the AMLC can be inaccurate, noting that the Bank of the Philippine Islands owned the mistake.

“What I'm saying is, when it was presented in the House Justice Committee, it was presented like it was 6.7 billion and... From what I understand, at that time, the House Justice Committee was already aware that BPI, included in the AMLC report, is the explanation na out of the 6.7 billion pesos, 2.2 of that, BPI is claiming is an error,” he said.

“Tapos ngayon, siyempre wala na silang choice para aminin na meron ngang nagkaganon. Kaya ngayon, ang pinapalabas nila, 4.4 billion. It's not fatal or anything; it's just a demonstration of how raw data from the AMLC can be misleading or inaccurate,” Panelo added.

(And now, of course, they have no choice but to admit that something like that actually happened. So now, what they are making it appear to be is 4.4 billion. It's not fatal or anything; it's just a demonstration of how raw data from the AMLC can be misleading or inaccurate.)

In a statement on May 4, 2026, BPI said, “As a Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP)-supervised institution, Bank of the Philippine Islands adheres strictly to all applicable laws and regulations, including those governing bank secrecy, data privacy, and consumer protection."
BPI also said it “complies with required reporting and regulatory engagements through the proper authorities, and provides relevant clarifications when necessary.” —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Student reportedly loses hand from police grenade amid France's education protests
articles.summary: A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday, a local official said, on ‌the eve of a national demonstration by the pupils' union…

image.caption: Firefighters arrive to extinguish a fire in front of Jean-Louis Cyffle high school in Nancy, France, on Monday, on the sidelines of nationwide protests by high-school students over learning conditions. (Jean-Christophe Verhaegen/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

A teenager's hand was blown off as high-school protesters clashed with riot police in northern France on Monday, a local official said, on ‌the eve of a national demonstration by the pupils' union against underfunding, overcrowding and dilapidation.
Security officials concerned about organized protest scheduled for Tuesday in Paris
Up to 500 schools in France to remain closed amid student protests

The regional newspaper La Voix du Nord said the 15-year-old lost his hand and part of his lower arm after picking up a police stun grenade that then detonated, in the town of Lens as the wave of school protests entered its third week.
François-Xavier Lauch, prefect of Pas-de-Calais, declined to comment on the exact ​circumstances, saying some 200-250 protesters had been hurling objects at police.

Six months out from ​an election to replace President Emmanuel Macron, his government and the far-right National Rally, spearheaded by presidential front-runner Marine Le Pen, have accused hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) lawmakers and mayors of stoking the protests, an accusation the LFI denies.
Rights groups accuse police of using heavy-handed tactics against minors including batons, tear gas and other riot-control weapons.

Among several investigations into police methods, authorities ⁠are examining the case of a 16-year-old who suffered an eye injury after ‌police fired rubber bullets into a crowd of protesters, according to his friends.
The LFI, headed by presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, denies encouraging violence and accuses the government of politicizing the issue and neglecting pupils' interests.

The protests have put more pressure on a government trying to narrow a budget deficit as investor concerns about states' finances grow, briefly pushing the yield on France's 10-year bonds to a 24-year ⁠high over five per cent last week and raising the likely cost of future borrowing.
Some 400 to 500 high schools were closed or partially closed as demonstrations and blockades showed no sign of abating ahead of Tuesday's nationwide protest.
The protests began in September in Paris, focusing on the deprived suburbs, before spreading. The government says they ‌have been hijacked and morphed into urban violence.
"Our priority is to restore order," Maud Bregeon, spokesperson for the French government, told CNews television.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked and 78 teaching staff had been injured in the demonstrations.

On Monday, BFMTV showed images of police and students clashing in Lille in northern France, tear gas being used ​in Toulouse in the southwest, and a fire being lit as people tried to break into a school in central Paris.
Union official 'appalled'

Carole Zerbib, head of the vandalized Lycee Vauquelin in Paris, said it had been attacked ⁠by a "very determined" group wearing hoods and masks who had tried to break through the entrance door and then lit a fire, forcing the school ⁠to be evacuated and classes suspended.
"It was very violent and happened very quickly," she said, adding that she did not believe the attackers were ⁠from the school.

Since ⁠last Monday, 5,000 people, 85 per cent of them teenagers, have been ​arrested and dozens injured. Teachers and members of the public have been attacked, while damage to property is estimated in the millions of euros.
Bregeon said the ​government would fast-track a bill on Oct. 27 ⁠to make youngsters found to have damaged property, or their parents, financially liable.
Security officials fear that Tuesday's organized protests in central Paris in particular could bring further violence amid concerns that far-left and anarchist groups could try to take them over.
Sophie Binet, head of the CGT labor union, told TF1 television on Monday that her members would attend Tuesday's demonstrations to protect the students.
"We've been appalled by what we have seen over the past 10 days and by the unprecedented crackdown that the ⁠government has organized," she said.

articles.title: Iran’s oil minister resigns as country’s economic crisis worsens
articles.summary:
Departure comes amid large drop in oil receipts, rampant inflation and shrinking economy

Iran’s oil minister has resigned days after allegations that an intermediary trust selling Iranian…

blocks.text: Iran’s oil minister has resigned days after allegations that an intermediary trust selling Iranian oil abroad owed millions of dollars’ worth of export receipts to the state.

Mohsen Paknejad’s departure comes as Iran grapples with a dire economic situation, including inflation running at 85%. An overall drop in oil receipts has led to a massive shortfall in foreign exchange earnings and one of the biggest drops in the value of the rial since the Iranian revolution in 1979.
The Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he had accepted the resignation of Paknejad, who had given personal reasons for going.
The rial is trading more than 10% lower than a month ago, largely due to the US naval blockade preventing Iran from selling oil, the mainstay of government receipts.

Emergency government meetings over the weekend to combat the crisis have yielded little tangible progress, and there are growing reports that the professional middle class, notably teachers and nurses, are resigning in large numbers because their salaries are not keeping up with price rises. The central bank says its role is not to defend a specific rate, but manage fluctuations.

Iran’s economy contracted by 10% in the first three months of the year. Despite concerns that continued sanctions may lead to protests, Iranian diplomats are not planning any new concessions after a proposal to speed the process of nuclear negotiations was rejected by Donald Trump a week ago.

blocks.caption: Masoud Pezeshkian said he had accepted the resignation of Paknejad. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

blocks.text: Iran has been using informal networks known as “trustees” to bypass US sanctions and repatriate oil revenues. A report last week by the Farhikhtegan newspaper alleged that a trust set up on Paknejad’s watch to recoup income from Iran’s overseas oil sales owed the state-owned National Iranian Oil Company nearly $2bn (£1.5bn) in revenues. Three individual trustees awarded oil contracts allegedly owe hundreds of millions of dollars each to the NIOC.

Some of the leaks behind the reporting may reflect a power struggle inside the oil industry. Reza Sepahvand, a spokesperson for the parliament’s energy commission, has announced the launch of an inquiry.

Although Iran’s oil export problem, and its impact on foreign exchange reserves, is primarily caused by the US naval blockade on Iran’s oil exports, reports of lax management or possibly corruption will do little to bolster confidence in government at a time when most Iranians are going through an unprecedented squeeze on their standards of living.

It is claimed the difficulties were regarded as so serious that they were conveyed by one security official to the president and then before the US attack on Iran in February to the supreme Leader himself. The president apparently took up the complaint with the oil minister but no satisfactory response was received.

In an attempt to shore up public confidence in the government’s strategy, ministers have been seeking to rebut Donald Trump’s claim that oil is now flowing through the strait of Hormuz at near pre-blockade rates.

The number of attacks on ships trying to use the strait’s southern route close to the Oman shoreline has risen in recent days, including four attacks in the past 48 hours. It was also reported that Saudi Arabia’s east-west pipeline had been forced to close again after a further attack.

Reuters reported last week that the seven-day moving average of the region’s crude oil exports reached 18.5m barrels a day on 1 October. About the same amount was exported before the US-Israeli war with Iran began.

The dollar traded at 269,000 tomans (a toman is 10,000 rials) this week, a record high, and has risen 12% since 9 September. The minimum monthly wage of 166m rials is worth about $66. Food inflation is 130%.

Alireza Zakani, the mayor of Tehran, has announced he is freezing the price of 12 basic items including sugar, rice, oil and detergent for six months. There has been scepticism about how these price controls will be enforced, but he claimed the national government was going to study his plan. Ministers also said a second rise in public sector wages was likely.

Mohammad Sharifi Moghaddam, the secretary general of the Nurses’ House organisation, stressed the scale of the squeeze on living standards: “Nurses have explored all possible avenues – logical, legal, professional, and every type of protest or critical path – to achieve their demands.

“The current healthcare system has shown no regard for the issues and demands of the nursing community.️ Nurses have come to the conclusion that it is more cost-effective and less damaging to their wellbeing to stay home and receive a salary of 25m tomans.”

At the same time, repression of mainstream dissidents has continued, with the summoning of the leadership of the Reform Front by the ministry of intelligence to explain criticisms it had issued during the crackdown on protests.
The front has already written to the government calling for transparency about corruption at a time when people are facing pressure from inflation, high prices and falling living standards.

articles.title: Military aircraft with 32 people on board crashes in southern Nigeria
articles.summary: Rescue teams are searching the crash site after the military aircraft went down in southern Nigeria. The fate of those on board remains unclear.

image.caption: The plane involved in the crash is similar to the one in the picture (FILE: August 10, 2026)Image: Steven Mohr/SNS/picture alliance

blocks.text: A military aircraft carrying 25 passengers and seven crew members crashed in southern Nigeria, authorities said on Monday.
Nigerian President Bola Tinubu later said all 32 people on the plane had died in the crash.
The aircraft was on a routine mission to Lagos, Nigeria's economic hub, when it crashed in the Igbokoda area of Ondo state, Aviation Minister Festus Keyamo said in a statement.
Wreckage located
Keyamo said the aircraft disappeared from radar at around 9 a.m. local time (7:00 a.m. GMT) and was later found to have crashed about halfway through its journey from Edo state to Lagos.
He said the wreckage had been located near a naval base.
The Nigerian Air Force identified the aircraft as an ATR-42 and said an immediate search and rescue operation had been launched.
A video circulating on social media showed a small crowd gathered near a river as rescuers searched the area by boat.
Locals told AP news agency about what they had heard and seen.
"The plane cleared some trees. We found some body parts, some clothes and shoes," one of the locals said.

articles.title: Iran poised to exploit security vacuum as US leaves Iraq
articles.summary: The end of the US military mission in Iraq leaves the Kurdistan region facing a severe security vacuum. As Erbil grapples with deep internal divisions, Tehran is well positioned to make strategic…

image.caption: Iraqis last week celebrated the departure of final US forces after more than two decades of conflictImage: Ahmad Al-Rubaye/AFP

blocks.text: The end of the US military mission in Iraq has created a dangerous security vacuum for the semi-autonomous Kurdish region.
Politicians in Baghdad celebrated the withdrawal, with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi officially declaring October 1 a "Day of Sovereignty and Independence."
Tehran, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and Iranian-backed Shiite militias also cheered the move.
But in Erbil, the capital of Iraq's Kurdish region, the mood is markedly more anxious.

Having relied on Washington's protection for two decades, the Kurdistan Region of Iraq (KRI) now faces intertwined crises, including mounting pressure from Baghdad to centralize power and escalating military threats from its neighbors, most notably Iran.
Why Iraq can't escape the US and Iran
A strategy of containment

The immediate threat to the Kurdistan region isn't a full-scale military invasion, but rather a slow, calculated chipping away of its autonomy, said Hesam Dastpish, a Middle East analyst based in Brussels.
He describes Tehran's overarching strategy toward Erbil as hostile and heavily focused on containment.
The Islamic Republic ultimately wants to strip the KRI of its political clout, reducing it to a purely administrative body, the expert stressed.

"Tehran's goal is to turn the Kurdistan region into an institution with absolutely no room to maneuver," Dastpish told DW, pointing to Iran's repeated strikes in the region, supposedly targeting camps of Iranian Kurdish opposition groups.
Salahuddin Khadiw, a political analyst based in Mahabad in Iran's Kurdish region, said that neighboring states don't necessarily want to wipe out Kurdish autonomy completely.
Instead, he underscored, Tehran envisions a "controlled and weak" Kurdistan.

By dealing separately with the rival power centers in Erbil and Sulaymaniyah, he argued, Iran has maintained influence across the KRI while seeking to prevent any single Kurdish authority from emerging as a dominant power on its western border.
Internal fragmentation remains a fatal flaw
Despite the external challenges, the Iraqi Kurdish region's most critical vulnerability comes from within.
The legacy of the 1990s civil war lives on through the deeply entrenched rivalry between the two main ruling factions: the Kurdistan Democratic Party (KDP) and the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan (PUK).

Hiwa Mahmoud Osman, an analyst on Iraqi and Kurdish affairs in the Middle East, pointed out that Tehran leans heavily on this internal friction. "Iran has spent decades mastering political influence inside Iraq," he told DW. "The Kurds' biggest hurdle is their own fragmentation. Without a united front, foreign powers simply have more room to operate."
What will the US troop withdrawal from Iraq mean for Kurds?

Ardeshir Pashang, a Middle East researcher in Tehran, warned that if Kurdish leaders fail to patch up their political quarrels, this disunity could ultimately lead to the collapse of the Kurdistan region as a political entity.
The opposition dilemma
A particularly thorny issue is the presence of Iranian Kurdish opposition outfits taking refuge in the KRI.
These groups, which have historically clashed with Iranian state forces, are now under immense pressure to disarm and relocate.
Their presence provides Iran with a convenient pretext to launch drone and missile strikes across the border, said Dastpish.
But he doesn't expect Erbil to offer "total surrender," as maintaining a balance with these groups is crucial for the KRI's domestic legitimacy and foreign relations.
Kasra Gharadaghi, a political science researcher based in Florida, argues that these groups are now more vulnerable than ever.

If Iran was able to strike their sanctuaries while US forces were still fully deployed — culminating in a 2023 border security pact between Baghdad and Tehran — Erbil's leverage is now practically non-existent, giving Tehran significantly more power to force concessions, he said.
Iranian Kurds in Iraq face war fears, exile
Dollar diplomacy is America's hidden weapon

While American troops may have left, Washington's leverage in Iraq has not entirely disappeared. It has simply transitioned toward global financial networks. Gharadaghi describes this as a "realignment of power," where the US, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia act as natural counterweights to Iran's growing reach.

Osman echoed this view, highlighting Iraq's deep financial reliance on the US dollar. This economic tether allows the US Treasury to indirectly influence Baghdad's internal affairs, right down to ensuring salaries are paid to KRI civil servants.
Khadiw similarly characterizes this strategic pivot as America transitioning from a "military balancer" to a "powerful economic observer."

But as internal and external pressures mount, the analysts said, Iraq's Kurdish region may have little choice but to heal its internal divides and present a united front to preserve its autonomy and limit Iran's strategic gains in the region.

articles.title: Trust in the German Constitutional Court is eroding — how can this be stopped?
articles.summary: Germany's top court, which turned 75 this year, is losing the population's trust, surveys show. Some say reforms in the way it picks candidates would help, to also accept candidates nominated by the…

image.caption: The Federal Constitutional Court is Germany's supreme court, based in KarlsruheImage: Bernd Weißbrod/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Federal Constitutional Court — Germany's equivalent of the US Supreme Court — still enjoys the most trust among the population of any branch of government, but that trust is slipping, according to recent surveys.

A new survey by the pollsters YouGov, commissioned to mark the 75th anniversary of the founding of the court, found that about two-thirds (66%) of Germans trust the Federal Constitutional Court. This was significantly more than the other major branches of the country's government system: The Bundesrat, the upper house of the German parliament, scored 47%, the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag 38%, and the Federal Government itself 29%.
But other surveys show those figures were significantly higher just a few years ago: One study from 2025 by the Allensbach Institute found that trust in the court was as high as 81% in 2021.

Exactly why this has happened remains a matter of conjecture: As a possible explanation, some analysts have pointed to the decisions the court made to allow the government to curtail certain freedoms during the COVID-19 pandemic — which precipitated many protests.
That period also saw an overall drop in trust in all the branches of government, and this decision, some argued, showed that the court was not an independent arbiter after all.

blocks.caption: President Frank-Walter Steinmeier spoke about the importance of the Constitutional Court during the anniversary ceremonyImage: Uli Deck/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Can the Constitutional Court be 'too political?'

Christine Landfried, former professor of political science at Hamburg University, thinks the criticism that the court can be too political doesn't really make sense. Its purpose was always ultimately to make political decisions — but ones based on a legal argument, rather than a political debate.

"A constitutional court always deals with political questions," she told DW. "But the way that decisions are arrived at should follow legal arguments and legal methods. That's different from politics."

The court was founded in 1951, in the aftermath of World War II, to make sure that the laws of the newly founded West Germany adhered to the constitution, or Basic Law, which came into effect in 1949. Over the years, it has had to interpret the tenets of the Basic Law (democracy, human dignity, the rule of law) into many political questions: What happens to citizens' data? Should the government protect the climate? How much money should unemployed people be paid?
The importance of a plural court
Former Constitutional Court judge Gertrude Lübbe-Wolff thinks that the problem is not that the court is too political, but that its composition does not reflect new political realities in Germany.

As things stand, there is an agreement in the two houses of the German parliament, the Bundestag and the Bundesrat, that the main parties each propose a certain number of candidates for the court's two chambers, or senates. The Bundestag and the Bundesrat each pick half the judges for the two eight-seat senates.

That agreement was fractured, however, last year thanks to a campaign against an the candidate Frauke Brosius-Gersdorf, nominated by the center-left Social Democratic Party (SPD) whose position on decriminalizing abortion and other issues were deemed by some as too liberal. The campaign — driven by populist and unproven claims on social media — caused some parliamentarians from the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) to withdraw their support, before Brosius-Gersdorf herself withdrew her candidacy.

Though this affair may have damaged trust in how the court's judges were selected, Lübbe-Wolff argues that maintaining the court's plural composition is "extremely important for sensible and balanced decisions that are broadly accepted by the public," she told DW.
How a routine vote blew up German politics
German Constitutional Court vs the US Supreme Court

Unlike US Supreme Court judges, many of whom are familiar names whose opinions and party affiliation are widely known, the people who sit on Germany's Constitutional Court are not famous at all. But they are nominated by different parties in parliament, and their political affiliations are usually known to those who care to follow the nominations.

But a key difference to the US Supreme Court, Landfried points out, is that while in the US, the judges only have to agree on a decision, but each can write their own reasoning, the German Constitutional Court makes an effort to produce a joint reasoning for each decision, or a majority reasoning if some judges disagree. "The Federal Constitutional Court acts much more as an institution," she said. "It's considered very important that this or that senate made a decision, and not that individual judges are in the foreground."

Lübbe-Wolff's new book, entitled "Does the Federal Constitutional Court need (more) Reform?" contains a few ideas for how the court could be improved to make it less dependent on the choices of the political parties. One suggestion: Instead of having the different parties in the parliamentary committee propose candidates, the seats on the Constitutional Court would be advertised like any other job, and people would apply, and then have the committee decide on who to accept. This would, Lübbe-Wolff argues, maintain the democratic principles behind the court selection while reducing the influence of party politics. Austria and Switzerland both already have similar systems.
Landfried likes this idea. "That would mean party politics is not such a big part of the selection," she said. "Very good people could apply who haven't been chosen by the party."
Should there be AfD candidates for the court?

Lübbe-Wolff also believes that, for the sake of plurality, the Bundestag should allow candidates put forward by the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) to be considered for the Constitutional Court. Germany's domestic intelligence agencies consider some sections of the AfD extremist and hostile to the constitution.

Indeed, the recent YouGov survey found that, among supporters of the major political parties, AfD supporters had by far the least faith in the court: Only 34%, compared to around 80% for both the CDU and SPD.
How much of a neo-Nazi party is the German AfD?
Nevertheless, some constitutional courts at the state level have already accepted AfD nominees into their ranks, notably Bavaria and Baden-Württemberg.

Now Lübbe-Wolff believes that the wider array of parties in the German parliament mean that the AfD and the socialist Left Party should also be allowed to propose candidates. "It used to be that the CDU and the SPD could simply decide between themselves which judges to elect," she said. "Today they always need votes from the Left Party too, because the AfD has become so big." She calls this imbalance a "structural problem."

But she believes that there are enough safeguards in the selection processes to ensure that no candidate for the Constitutional Court would hold views that were directly hostile to the constitution. "I think there are people who I believe are close enough to the AfD that the party could put them forward, but at the same time stand reliably on the foundation of the constitution," she said. "I think there are people of a younger generation in that category, but they don't want to out themselves."

Landfried is not sold on the idea. "For me, sections of that party is hostile to the constitution, it is partly right-wing extremist," she says, though she doesn't believe that all AfD voters are far-right. "But I have my reservations, and I wouldn't agree with that proposal."

Landfried is concerned that, because of Germany's Nazi history, the federal constitutional court should be especially wary about allowing people who potentially have far-right sympathies a place on the body that is, more than any other, meant to safeguard German democracy.
Edited by Rina Goldenberg

articles.title: What China's new military foothold in Laos means for Southeast Asia
articles.summary: Beijing says its new Laos facility will train pilots. Analysts see a broader signal: China's growing military presence in mainland Southeast Asia.

image.caption: The two communist nations said the Ban Keun center was aimed at training Lao air force pilotsImage: Vantor/REUTERS

blocks.text: China has opened a new military training and logistics facility in Laos, extending Beijing's security presence deeper into mainland Southeast Asia and potentially giving the Chinese air force its first dedicated foothold overseas.

The China-Laos Joint Support and Training Center at Ban Keun Airport, north of the capital Vientiane, formally began operations late last month alongside the new China-Laos Friendship Aviation Academy.
Beijing says the center will primarily help train Lao air force pilots and will be jointly maintained and operated by the two countries.
The opening adds to China's still relatively small network of overseas military facilities.

Beijing established its first foreign military base in Djibouti in the Horn of Africa in 2017. A Chinese-funded expansion of Cambodia's Ream Naval Base was formally inaugurated last year, giving Chinese forces access to a facility strategically positioned near the South China Sea.
Laos and Cambodia are widely regarded as China's closest political partners in Southeast Asia, and military cooperation with both has expanded substantially in recent years.

"The two institutions … are not directed against any third party and aim to help further deepen practical cooperation between the two militaries and contribute to maintaining peace and stability in the region," said the Chinese Defense Ministry in a public statement.
Could Ban Keun become a permanent Chinese base?
The facility's infrastructure gives Beijing the option of expanding its military use in the future, Hunter Marston, director of the Southeast Asia Program at Australia's Lowy Institute, told DW.

"The focus may well be on joint training, but it has the potential to become a more permanent base. Should Beijing choose to use it as such, it has ample political leverage over Vientiane to demand exclusive access in the future," he added.
Laos has become heavily dependent on Chinese investment and financing during the past two decades. Critics have frequently accused Beijing of engaging in "debt-trap diplomacy."
The International Monetary Fund estimates Laos' public debt at around 81% of GDP last year, with China by far the largest bilateral creditor.

blocks.caption: China opened its first overseas military base in Djibouti in 2017, reflecting the Horn of Africa nation's strategic importanceImage: Xinhua/IMAGO

blocks.text: In 2020, China's state-owned China Southern Power Grid acquired a reported 90% stake in Electricite du Laos Transmission Company, which operates much of Laos' electricity transmission network.
A more durable Chinese military presence in Laos would also add another dimension to the strategic competition between Beijing and Washington in Southeast Asia.
The United States still enjoys far more extensive military access across the wider Indo-Pacific, particularly through alliances with the Philippines, Japan and Australia.

Beijing has historically lacked comparable overseas facilities. But Ban Keun, alongside Ream, could gradually reduce that disadvantage by giving the Chinese military additional locations from which to train, maintain equipment and potentially preposition supplies.
It is a particularly ominous development for Vietnam, Euan Graham, a senior fellow at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, told DW.
Hanoi and Beijing retain close party-to-party and economic relations, but they remain rivals in the South China Sea, where their competing territorial claims have repeatedly generated tensions.

Vietnam has also traditionally viewed Laos and Cambodia as strategically important buffers along its western flank and has worked for decades to maintain considerable political and military influence in both countries.

"Hanoi has always perceived the Indochinese peninsula as within its sphere of influence, offering a buffer against external aggressors, especially given Vietnam's narrow midriff," said Graham. "Now, it faces an alarming possibility of strategic encirclement by China. The new air base in Laos will certainly complicate Vietnam's defense planning."
Laos: A country in the grip of the Chinese?
Strategic importance should not be overstated
Other analysts caution, however, that geography places clear limits on Ban Keun's military value.

Collin Koh, a senior fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies at Singapore's Nanyang Technological University, told DW that China could gradually expand its presence at the facility.

Beijing could deploy more personnel, particularly advisers and instructors, as well as trainer aircraft and eventually more advanced aircraft, while also using the site to preposition equipment and supplies, he said.
But the "operational usefulness for the PLA's projection of military power in Southeast Asia is constrained by the landlocked nature of Laos."
Unlike Ream, Ban Keun provides no sea access, while Chinese military aircraft already operate from substantially larger and better-equipped bases in southern China.

While Vietnam will closely monitor Ban Keun for its potential role in any future South China Sea conflict, the site's geography doesn't give the Chinese military a significant operational advantage, said Koh.

Simon Creak, an associate professor at Singapore's National Institute of Education and a historian of Laos, noted that Vientiane has maintained a policy of non-alignment since adopting its current foreign policy in 1986.

"It has not had similar joint facilities in the past despite boasting close political and military relations with Vietnam, as well as China and Russia … and any mention of foreign bases in Laos typically recalls the CIA's bases during the Indochina Wars," Creak said.
Still, he believes it's "highly unlikely" that Laos will adjust its formal foreign policy settings or its longstanding effort to balance relations with Vietnam, Thailand and China.

articles.title: Hundreds of Australians, including war veterans, are being buried in unmarked communal graves
articles.summary: Exclusive: Guardian Australia investigation reveals state governments use shared graves to bury those deemed too poor to pay for funerals. ‘It’s unspeakable,’ one relative…

blocks.text: Vietnam veterans, rough sleepers and other impoverished Australians are being buried in unmarked communal graves often holding four or more people, a practice relatives have described as “unspeakable” and “a disgrace”.

A Guardian Australia investigation has identified more than 100 unmarked graves across New South Wales, and some in Queensland, that are being used by state governments to bury those deemed too poor to afford their own funerals.

Using evidence from family, friends and the homelessness sector, together with analysis of cemetery registries and aerial imagery, the Guardian has established that the NSW government is using bare stretches of earth between dirt walkways and old headstones at Rookwood cemetery in Sydney to bury the remains of four to six strangers together in communal graves.

Among those being buried together are war veterans, cancer sufferers, people with gambling addictions and severe mental illness, and migrants from developing countries whose families cannot afford exorbitant repatriation costs.

In at least six cases, the Guardian has identified failures by authorities that meant friends, family or support workers were either not contacted or not told of the use of unmarked and common graves. The failures are likely breaches of a NSW policy designed to “avoid causing unnecessary distress to people who may have wished to make other funeral arrangements”.
Shocked family and friends say they have been left feeling robbed.

blocks.caption: Roger Davies was buried in an unmarked communal grave at Rookwood cemetery

blocks.text: “It’s unspeakable,” said Chantel Dubsky, whose brother Roger Davies, a rough sleeper, was buried in an unmarked grave with four strangers at Rookwood without her knowledge. “He should have had the opportunity to be laid to rest with his mother, his grandparents and the people he loved, at his home in Adelaide.
“He wasn’t just someone off the street – he was someone’s son, he was someone’s brother. He was my brother.”
By crosschecking names with homelessness services in Sydney, Guardian Australia has also identified a further 18 individuals in the communal graves who had experienced homelessness.
The homelessness sector is outraged by the revelations.

Two leaders in Sydney’s homelessness sector say they were never made aware of the practice of using unmarked communal graves and are not being given the chance to intervene on behalf of their clients to fund a proper burial.

A third service, the Rev Bill Crews Foundation, an inner-city Sydney homelessness charity, says it has repeatedly raised concerns with the state government about the possible use of unmarked and communal graves but has been ignored.
The Rev Bill Crews, who runs the foundation, identified three of his clients as being among those in the communal graves but said he had not been told about their deaths and impending burials.
“It’s outrageous,” Crews said. “We did not know – they would all have had a dignified funeral and a proper cremation, and their ashes would have been scattered in the sea.
The foundation regularly uses its own funds to conduct funeral services for rough sleepers when it becomes aware they have died. It was given no notification in the three cases.
“For us, it’s frustrating. Incredibly frustrating.”
Guardian Australia has also established that two veterans of the Vietnam war, who both served in the Royal Australian Navy, were buried in unmarked communal graves in 2024 and 2025.

The pair were buried despite the availability of a federal funding program run by the Department of Veterans’ Affairs to help pay for the funerals of impoverished veterans. NSW policy recommends state health authorities approach DVA in such cases.
DVA was never asked for funding for the 2024 and 2025 burials. A spokesperson said it has “not been approached to help fund the burials of destitute persons since 2020”.

blocks.caption: Aerial imagery shows new graves appearing at Rookwood cemetery between 2025 and 2026 - Nearmap

blocks.text: The Guardian’s investigation has prompted an apology from NSW Health, which has flagged changes to improve the process, and criticism from the health minister, Ryan Park, who described the failings as “unacceptable”.

In the first half of this year alone, a 17-metre stretch of earth adjacent to a dirt pathway at Rookwood has been dug up and used to bury the remains of more than 40 people in unmarked communal graves, including a rough sleeper who was well-known to most major homelessness services.
Nothing has been left to mark the 17-metre stretch of graves. Inspections of the sites of hundreds of other burials at Rookwood since 2010 show only about a dozen are marked by crosses or plaques.
The vast majority have no crosses, plaques or headstones to name the groups of deceased in each plot. There are also no signs to indicate the presence of graves.
Older sites, where the earth has settled, appear simply as long stretches of grass.
Markings are generally not used in Queensland for the smaller number of people buried under its scheme. The use of communal graves is much rarer in that state.
The situation contrasts sharply with the process embraced by Victoria, where each individual is given their own grave and a simple marking, identifying who is interred below.
after newsletter promotion
The NSW government has previously pledged to stop the use of unmarked graves for destitute burials.

blocks.caption: The site where Roger Davies was buried in 2015. The unmarked graves are beneath the grassed area to the right, between the walkway and the old headstones. Photograph: Christopher  Knaus/The Guardian

blocks.text: That came after lobbying by Barbara Davis, who was never told that her foster daughter Christine Halpin had been buried in Rookwood in 1989.

Davis and Christine’s biological daughter Jayne say they were told by the NSW government in 2013 that the use of unmarked graves would cease. The cemetery erected a “path of remembrance” that allows people to pay more than $800 to put a plaque on a rock, about 1km from some of the gravesites, but this has been used in a few dozen cases since 2020.
Christine’s gravesite remains unmarked. Davis and Jayne are both furious.
“It is a disgrace,” Davis said. “Whether you’re a prince or a pauper, you deserve a decent burial site, even just with a wooden cross with your name on it.”
In another case, a young Fijian who came to Australia to play rugby in Leeton, in NSW’s Riverina region, was buried in a communal unmarked grave after dying of cancer in 2022.

A former Leeton mayor, Paul Maytom, now president of the Leeton Multicultural Support Group, said he had previously helped raise funds from local Solomon Islander and Vietnamese communities to provide repatriation or proper burials.
He was not informed about the Fijian’s death.

“There should be a point of contact when this type of thing happens,” Maytom said. “And you should never have a situation where someone ends up in an unmarked grave, particularly when there are community members who are willing to help pay.”
A NSW Health Pathology spokesperson apologised for the failings, acknowledging they meant the dead and families and friends were not always treated with dignity and respect.

“Families and friends who have lost a loved one face many challenges managing arrangements during a time of grief, and all deceased persons should be treated with dignity and respect, regardless of their financial circumstances,” a spokesperson said.

“It is clear this has not always occurred with respect to the burials or cremations for deceased people without the financial means to pay for a funeral, and NSW Health apologises for the distress this has caused to those who have lost someone they love.”

NSW Health said it had made changes to the process in 2025 and in recent months to improve the way the funerals were handled. That includes giving NSW Health greater control, in place of police, and creating a dedicated six-person team within NSW Health Pathology to provide “alternative funeral arrangements and alternate sources of support for families and friends that may be willing to assist”.
It also flagged improving its relationships with “religious, cultural, charitable, community, and government organisations” to find funding for funerals after deaths.
Two NSW ministers, Park and the homelessness minister, Rose Jackson, said the dead and their families should be treated with respect, regardless of their financial circumstances.
“Previous arrangements have meant that this has not always been the case, and that is unacceptable,” Park said.

“Since early 2025, NSW Health has made significant changes to establish a more comprehensive and person-centred approach to ensure all deceased persons are treated with the respect and compassion they deserve.”
A spokesperson for Metropolitan Memorial Parks, which operates Rookwood general cemetery, said the NSW government did not fund it to provide grave markings for persons without means.

MMP said destitute burials were not the only burial type that used multiple interments in a single plot, and rejected any suggestion that those buried through the process were being placed between individual headstones, under walkways or in trenches.
It also said it had identified no legislation or regulation that had given effect to the government’s 2013 promise to mark graves.

articles.title: OpenAI must explain action taken to stop AI hacking Australians’ private data, chair of federal inquiry says
articles.summary:
Unions, employer groups, banks and industry experts will appear at the four-day hearings along with OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google

  • Get our

blocks.text: OpenAI must explain how they will stop their models from inappropriately accessing Australian data, the Labor chair of the parliament’s committee on artificial intelligence has warned, ahead of federal inquiry hearings which will grill the tech company alongside Anthropic, Microsoft and Google.

Independent senator David Pocock is also demanding answers, saying OpenAI “still have a lot they need to answer” about their AI agent accessing Services Australia data on Medicare and the company’s “appalling” tardiness in notifying the federal government about the incident.

The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence will hold four days of hearings this week, hearing from tech companies as well as unions, employer groups, banks and industry experts. Tuesday’s hearing will include representatives from copyright and artists’ groups, to probe issues around access to data to train AI models, as well as the Australian Broadcasting Corportation, which warned in its submission of a “cannibalisation” of journalism and demanded AI companies be subject to the same copyright, defamation and privacy rules as news outlets.

items: Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

blocks.text: OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, will front the hearing alongside Adam Cohen, the company’s head of economic policy, and Asia-Pacific national security lead, Peter Anstee. OpenAI last week apologised for the Services Australia incident and the manner in which it informed the government, saying it was “working to do better”.
But the Labor MP chairing the committee, Jo Briskey, said the company still had questions to answer.

“We have heard what happened, we understand what has occurred, and there’s some pretty problematic issues around not only the fact that these AI agents did access non-public data, but the reality was also that they took far too long to to notify us,” she said.

“We’ve seen OpenAI make its public apology to Australians. That’s important … my focus is on what do they do next? How do they assure Australians that they that this won’t happen again? And that’s a difficult question.”

Briskey said her starting point would be to interrogate how to balance the potential risks and rewards of AI, such as economic benefits as well as cyber security and defence applications. She said she would also raise concerns about online safety, scams, and how any benefits would be spread among all Australians.
“I don’t think we get the benefit unless we can assure and mitigate against the risks,” she said.
Pocock, who is also on the committee, also plans to seek more answers from OpenAI about the Services Australia incident.

“You’ve got a bunch of companies that are essentially self-regulating with Donald Trump. I don’t think many people would trust Sam Altman and OpenAI … This is supposedly a company the Australian government wants to welcome with open arms and do deals with,” he said.
“The Medicare hack stuff will be pretty well looked at through the committee process. It’s been a fairly appalling response from them.”

Altman, in an interview with Politico published on Monday, said OpenAI “believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.”
Pocock has raised alarm about the potential impacts on artists, creatives and copyrighted material and said he was still to be convinced about the technology.
“There’s still big questions over the long-term benefit of all this for Australia … Nobody has been able to answer that,” he said.

“[The government] is chasing this GDP sugar hit, but we haven’t hit the big part of the datacentre buildout yet, and we’re already [seeing] inflation going up. They want to raise GDP, but after the buildout phase, how do we get a return? Looking at how much tax big tech companies pay, it’s not much, and I don’t see how it’ll change.”

Pocock is keen to interrogate the government plans to address copyright issues. Anthropic, in its submission, suggested a form of “opt-out” model where rightsholders could request their data not be scraped; an idea SBS, in its submission, claimed was “routinely ignored or bypassed”.

Pocock said it was “hard to cop this industry saying it’s too hard to deal with rightsholders when they’re heading for multi-trillion-dollar valuations”, and said the government should “force them [AI companies] to negotiate deals.”

articles.title: Australian leaders condemn pro-Palestine vigils planned for 7 October anniversary amid Jewish commemorations
articles.summary:
Peak Jewish bodies organise ceremonies on third anniversary of attacks that triggered conflict in which 74,000 Palestinians have been killed

  • Get our

blocks.text: Jewish Australians will mark the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks on Wednesday as Labor state governments condemn pro-Palestinian vigils to be held the same day.

Peak Jewish bodies have organised commemorations across the capital cities but avoided publicising locations as community members report ongoing fears for their safety since the Bondi terror attack in December.

Hamas militants killed about 1,200 people, mostly civilians, and took 251 others hostage in the surprise attack on Israel in 2023, triggering the ongoing Israel-Gaza war in which 74,000 Palestinians have been killed.

On the night before the anniversary, people at a Melbourne event were expected to hear a first-hand account from an Israeli soldier who was in the country during the attacks. Zionism Victoria has planned an outdoor evening ceremony on Wednesday.

Sydney’s eastern suburbs will host a dawn commemoration starting at 6.29am, to mark the time at which Hamas’ attack began and an evening community event run by the Zionist Council of NSW and backed by the United Israel Appeal, the local arm of Keren Hayesod.
“United in remembrance and resilience, we stand with Israel and the Jewish people, joined by our fellow Australians against hatred and extremism,” the evening event’s description reads.

A documentary exploring experiences of Israeli trauma professionals, After Never Again, will be screened in Canberra and Perth. The film has been produced by Kehilot to Australia or K2A, a group set up to bring Israeli youth to Australia for relief from the stress of living near active conflict.

blocks.caption: The NSW premier, Chris Minns, has said the planned vigils on the anniversary of a ‘horrible and violent event were ‘obscene’. Photograph: George Chan/Getty Images

blocks.text: All details, including registration, have been kept private for events planned in Brisbane and Adelaide. JWire has reported the Zionist Council of Queensland has organised a gathering open to Nepalese, Filipino and Iranian communities.

Pro-Palestine groups have also planned to mark the day, with a gathering planned at Sydney’s town hall on Wednesday evening. An organising group, Jews Against The Occupation ‘48, said their event would not be a protest but a vigil to mark Israel’s retaliatory airstrikes on Gaza on 7 October 2023, in a post on social media.
Wollongong Friends of Palestine, south of Sydney, has planned its own vigil.

A Melbourne “sit-in vigil” is planned from 10am to 5pm outside the state library of Victoria. The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, has said police would act to “protect the public” if the event breached the state’s anti-vilification laws.
The New South Wales premier, Chris Minns, has said the planned vigils on the anniversary of a “horrible and violent” event were “obscene”, speaking to reporters last Wednesday.
“To choose that day, I think it’s designed to antagonise large sections of our community,” Minns said. “I’m obviously distressed on their behalf.”
Minns said supreme court and high court decisions on political communication prevented him from shutting down the Wednesday gatherings.
“They’re very difficult … for us to shut down static protests, particularly ones, as I think they’re describing it as a vigil, a silent vigil. We’ll see if it is a silent vigil.”

Further pro-Palestine rallies to mark the anniversary are planned in more than a dozen Australian cities on Sunday as part of a “global day of action” led by activist groups overseas. A Friday rally is also scheduled outside the electorate office of Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles.

articles.title: Trump’s former press secretary Karoline Leavitt to join Fox News
articles.summary:
Youngest press secretary in White House history left earlier this year after the birth of her second child

Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary in August, is…

blocks.text: Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down as White House press secretary in August, is joining Fox News as an on-air contributor, according to the New York Times, citing a network announcement.

Leavitt, 29, who was the youngest press secretary in White House history, left the administration after the birth of her second child earlier this year. She said at the time that she planned to spend more time with her family and take a role with the Trump-aligned Super Pac Maga Inc.
When she announced her pregnancy in December, she became the first sitting White House press secretary to do so.

During her tenure, Leavitt sought to reshape the White House media landscape. She moved to exert greater control over the press pool, the small group of journalists who closely track the president’s daily activities; created a “new media” briefing room seat, often filled by conservative commentators and pro-Trump personalities; and frequently clashed with reporters.
One of Trump’s most steadfast defenders, Leavitt emerged as a key ally for the president and regularly drew praise from him during her time in the West Wing.

articles.title: Alberta's population grew by more people than any other place in Canada, data shows
articles.summary: Alberta’s population continues to grow — and faster than almost all of Canada, Statistics Canada’s latest population estimates suggest.

image.caption: Alberta's population grew by more people than any other place in Canada since 2025, Statistics Canada's latest estimates suggest. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Edmonton·New
Alberta’s population continues to grow — and faster than almost all of Canada, Statistics Canada’s latest population estimates suggest.
Almost 76,500 more people called province home as of July 1
Alberta’s population continues to grow — and faster than almost all of Canada.

Statistics Canada estimates that more than 5.1 million people lived in Alberta as of July 1, up nearly 76,500 people — or about 1.5 per cent — from a year before, according to the agency’s latest data.
No jurisdiction added as many people over the year, data suggests, and only Nunavut and the Yukon — places with much lower populations than Alberta — grew at a greater rate.

“We're still a destination, and I think that speaks to economic opportunities,” said Jenny Godley, a professor in the University of Calgary’s anthropology and archaeology department. “Hopefully it also speaks to the openness of Alberta as a place for people to come and work and live and have their families.”

Alberta’s population has boomed for several years, but that growth is calming down, data shows. The estimated growth rate from 2025 to 2026 was the slowest since 2021, amid the height of the COVID-19 pandemic.

Data suggests the province’s natural increase — births versus deaths — stayed level. Several thousand fewer Canadians migrated from other provinces — but tens of thousands of people from B.C. and Ontario, and more people from the other Prairie provinces, flocked to Alberta.
The federal government’s new immigration policies are also a factor.

items: Canada did not see historic population decline last year, StatsCan says after second look

blocks.text: The levels plan, included in last year’s budget, aims to limit admissions into Canada over the next few years, in part to ensure immigration matches labour market needs and doesn’t exceed the housing supply. Ottawa capped permanent resident admissions at 380,000 each year until 2028, and non-permanent resident admissions — including asylum seekers and people here on study and work visas — at 385,000 this year, with a further decrease upcoming.

StatsCan data suggests more than 50,000 immigrants landed in Alberta in the past year — which is still high, historically, but roughly 8,000 fewer than the year before, and the fewest since the pandemic started.
The province also reported a net loss of almost 8,000 non-permanent residents, driven almost entirely by international students leaving, data shows.
“That has been true all across the country,” Godley said.

“[Ottawa’s] cutback has been successful in terms of reducing that pressure, a little bit anyway, on the housing market,” she said. “But it certainly does change the nature of our student body as well; our student body becomes a little bit less diverse.”

The Alberta government plans to keep pressing the federal government for "a more sustainable" immigration approach, Juliana Rodriguez, spokesperson for Finance Minister Jason Nixon, told CBC News in an emailed statement.
Strong population growth can bolster the province's economy, but "unsustainable levels" can strain public services, the housing supply and labour market, she said.

Heather Thomson, the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce’s vice president of economy and engagement, said immigration ought to align with the province's economic needs. But she said there also needs to be an awareness of who's leaving, ensuring they aren’t part of the skilled workforce.
Looking ahead, Thomson worries about how the upcoming provincial referendum — and the uncertainty surrounding it — could affect Alberta's economy.
The referendum, scheduled for Oct. 19, will pose 10 questions to voters on various issues.

items: Alberta separation too costly with too many uncertainties, warns Calgary think-tank
Alberta referendum pitches more control over immigration. Here's what you need to know

blocks.text: Only one of the questions pertains to Alberta's place within Canada. Five others focus on immigration policy, including whether the Alberta government should have more control over immigration, and whether non-permanent residents should have to pay — at least for a time — to access social services, like health care and education.

“Anytime we're talking about a level of uncertainty — whether it comes from investment, talent and just what's going to happen with a certain jurisdiction — that can pause, or delay, or put investment off altogether,” Thomson said.

“Whether people want to come live here and invest their time and their skillset in the province, or if it's an organization or a massive company that wants to come here, certainty is going to be a big part of that,” she said.

The federal government has been studying potential consequences of Albertans choosing to move closer to independence, including an incredible financial shock and mass exodus of businesses and residents from the province.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Nicholas Frew is a CBC Edmonton reporter who specializes in producing data-driven stories. Hailing from Newfoundland and Labrador, Frew moved to Halifax to attend journalism school. He has previously worked for CBC newsrooms in Manitoba and Saskatchewan. Before joining CBC, he interned at the Winnipeg Free Press. You can reach him at nick.frew@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Rainy season over for 2026 as southwest monsoon ends
articles.summary: Now, the Philippines is transitioning to the period of the northeast monsoon. But El Niño is also expected to cause hotter-than-usual conditions in the coming months.

blocks.text: BAD WEATHER. Pedestrians wait at the corner of Taft Avenue and UN Avenue in Manila on September 9, 2026, amid heavy rain brought by the southwest monsoon.
Rappler
Now, the Philippines is transitioning to the period of the northeast monsoon. But El Niño is also expected to cause hotter-than-usual conditions in the coming months.
MANILA, Philippines – The southwest monsoon or habagat is over, marking the end of the 2026 rainy season in the western portions of Luzon and the Visayas.

The Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical, and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) said on Monday, October 5, that it has observed “a gradual shift in the prevailing weather pattern” over the past days.

PAGASA noted the weakening of winds and reduced rainfall linked to the southwest monsoon, as well as the strengthening of a high pressure system over East Asia and the “southward migration” of the intertropical convergence zone (ITCZ).

The ITCZ is a belt near the equator where the trade winds of the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere meet. So far, it is the only weather system currently affecting the country, bringing scattered rain showers and thunderstorms to the Visayas, Mindanao, and Palawan.
The southwest monsoon had begun in late May, and monsoon rain subsequently triggered the onset of the rainy season in early June.
Now, the Philippines is transitioning to the period of the northeast monsoon or amihan, which is also called the cool and dry season.
The northeast monsoon typically lasts from October to February or March, causing surges of cool temperatures.
But PAGASA has warned that the strong El Niño currently active in the tropical Pacific Ocean may become very strong in the fourth quarter of 2026, and persist until the first half of 2027.

That would mean hotter-than-usual conditions and below-normal rainfall in most parts of the Philippines, according to the weather bureau. Droughts and dry spells are likely to spread in the coming months.

However, tropical cyclones can still develop within or enter the Philippine Area of Responsibility, and possibly affect the country, even during El Niño. These are PAGASA’s estimates for the next six months:

items: October 2026 – 1 or 2
November 2026 – 1 or 2
December 2026 – 1 or 2
January 2027 – 0 or 1
February 2027 – slim chance
March 2027 – slim chance

blocks.text: Other weather systems that may bring rain in the next six months include the ITCZ, shear line, low pressure areas, easterlies, and localized thunderstorms. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Greens pitch Zohran Mamdani-style $25.1bn plan to nationalise 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets
articles.summary:
Former MP and Greens Institute head, Max Chandler-Mather, says proposal for publicly owned supermarket chain will ease grocery prices

  • Get our

blocks.text: More than 200 Coles and Woolworths supermarkets would be nationalised, and hundreds of government grocery stores opened, under a $25bn plan being put forward by former Greens MP Max Chandler-Mather.

Channelling New York mayor Zohran Mamdani’s plan for publicly owned grocery stores, Chandler-Mather, the boss of the party’s thinktank, the Greens Institute, wants to use new forced divestiture laws to take over major supermarket sites and three distribution centres.
The government would fund another 424 new supermarkets and 10 distribution centres, taking about 20% of the market share of commercial operators for the new non-profit network.

Chandler-Mather says the new stores – dubbed Fair Go Grocers – would save consumers as much as 22% on the average shop, or $60 per week for a four-person household. Heavy discounts would be put in place for essentials including fruit and vegetables, bread, milk and meat.

A statutory authority would be established to set prices each month, as well as minimum wholesale rates for suppliers. Its members would include experts in supermarket operations, nutrition and food science, and farming.
The federal government would pay for capital costs including land, construction, and acquisition, and stores would be located in areas of the highest need.
After an initial $25.1bn price tag over five years, Chandler-Mather says the stores would be self-funded and not require additional taxpayer cash.
By comparison, the federal government currently spends about $24bn each year on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme.

“Kids are going to school hungry, families are skipping meals, people are cutting back on essentials, all because Labor has allowed Coles and Woolworths to jack up prices for extra profit, regardless of the human consequences,” Chandler-Mather said.
“Just like healthcare and education, food is essential to life. And just like Medicare and public schools, it’s time we had a public option for food.”

The proposal is similar to Mamdani’s plan for five city-owned and subsidised grocery stores, one in each of New York City’s boroughs, opening by 2029. Last month a local business group sued the Democratic Socialist mayor, arguing existing small grocery stores would be unable to compete.
The New Zealand Greens have a plan to nationalise 120 supermarkets and establish a new publicly owned chain called KiwiMark.

The Greens Institute commissioned pollsters YouGov to test public support for the proposal last month, with background on Mamdani’s plan for government-owned stores that cut out profits made by private corporations.

Voters were asked: Would you support or oppose publicly owned supermarkets being tried in Australia? A total of 84% said they strongly supported or somewhat supported the idea, while 16% somewhat or strongly opposed the idea.
after newsletter promotion
Support was strongest among voters aged 25-34 (88%), among Greens voters (96%) and women (88%).

Newly elected Greens leader David Shoebridge, under pressure to spur enthusiasm and attention for the party, has welcomed the proposal, saying the Greens should be focused on improving the material conditions of individuals, the environment and community.
“A publicly owned supermarket with cheaper food is wildly popular, because it makes people’s lives better,” he told Guardian Australia.
“Of course this is the sort of policy that we should be discussing right now.”
Shoebridge said Mamdani’s message about the government needing to address the needs of citizens was working.
“When I talk to people, I hear about the dread they feel heading down the supermarket aisle, the shopping trolley feels like pushing a boulder up to the checkout,” he said.
“While 99% of us are paying more for food, and many are making decisions about enough food or some other essentials, the 1% who own Coles and Woolies are laughing.”

The competition watchdog has brought cases against both Coles and Woolworths over false or misleading representations about in-store discounts, and a report released last year found they were among the most profitable grocers in the world.
The Greens allege Labor’s new laws banning supermarkets from excessive pricing are ineffective and have not resulted in lower costs for consumers.

articles.title: Bombs preventing rescue of kidnapped youths, Nigerian police say
articles.summary: The father of one of the 19 young abductees tells the BBC he hasn't eaten in three days out of worry.

blocks.text: Nigerian police say they have located a camp where 19 national youth service recruits are being held by gunmen but cannot move in as they believe the place is mined with explosives.

Police Commissioner Audu Bosso said drones helped locate the camp where the prospective National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) members were taken after being abducted last week in the south-eastern Imo state.
The exact location of the camp has not been disclosed and police have not identified those responsible for the kidnapping.
Omotosho Adewale, whose child is among those abducted, told the BBC that the kidnappers had demanded a ransom of 50m naira ($37,680; £28,440), which he could not afford.
"There's no peace of mind. I've not eaten in three days," he said in between tears.
Adewale appealed to the government for help.
Those kidnapped had been travelling from Ibadan in the south-west to NYSC orientation camps in Abia and Akwa Ibom states on Thursday when gunmen attacked their buses near Umunoha in Imo state.

The NYSC is a compulsory one-year programme for most Nigerian university and polytechnic graduates. Participants, known as corps members, are posted to different parts of the country to work and take part in community service, as well as to foster a sense of national unity.
Speaking to journalists, Bosso said they had tracked the kidnappers.
"The drone actually showed us exactly their location. But our predicament is that with the intel we have... the camp is mined with IEDs [homemade bombs]," he said.
Bulldozers and armoured vehicles are being deployed as police prepare for a rescue operation.
Kidnapping for ransom is a major security problem in Nigeria, involving both criminal gangs and armed groups.
The abduction in Imo state has caused widespread concern, with mass kidnappings less common in southern Nigeria than in some parts of the north.
Paying ransoms is illegal and authorities have repeatedly warned families against doing so, but relatives of kidnapped people are often under pressure to do so to secure their release.
The latest abduction highlights the risks faced by young people travelling across Nigeria to do their national youth service and has renewed calls for reforms.

The NYSC has previously said it would not deploy members to areas considered high-risk because of violence or the threat of abduction. Most parts of south-eastern Nigeria have not previously been classified as high-risk areas.

The co-pilot of FlyDubai flight ⁠FZ1073, which had been bound for Israel from ⁠Dubai, attacked the pilot with an emergency crash axe, the United Arab Emirates ‌prosecutor general has said, calling the incident a "terrorist attack."
