Vice President Sara Duterte said she expects the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) to file a perjury case against former cop Rodulfo Gracioso Jr. after the agency completes its investigation and determines that allegations against her were false.
In a statement, Duterte confirmed her office has received a copy of the Gracioso affidavit from the NBI along with identification documents, but without other attachments.

"Among several other pieces of my evidence, Jefry Tupas and I were nowhere near Marinduque during Mahal na Araw in 2019, nor were we in Manila on September 21, 2019," she said.

"NBI Director Melvin Matibag noted that a perjury case may be possible if the allegations are proven false. We expect a case to be filed by the NBI against Gracioso once the agency completes its investigation and the evidence is fully evaluated," she said.

Gracioso, who was part of the security detail of former House Speaker Lord Allan Velasco before, earlier said that he delivered suitcases containing cash to VP Sara Duterte, former president Rodrigo Duterte, and Davao City 1st District Representative Paolo “Pulong” Duterte on Velasco’s instructions.
Gracioso estimated that he had delivered a total of more than P2 billion to Sara Duterte.
The NBI said it is investigating the claims of Gracioso.
Matibag also said the NBI will invite VP Sara, Pulong Duterte, Velasco, and Velasco’s wife to get their comment on the claims of cash delivery by Gracioso.
Duterte, however, has said that she does not know Gracioso, and she did not receive any money from him.

articles.title: Teenager's hand blown off during confrontation between France school protesters and police
articles.summary: The prefect of Pas-de-Calais says the teenager's life is "not in danger" after the "very serious" incident on Monday.

blocks.text: A 15-year-old boy's hand was blown off during a confrontation between police and demonstrators near a school in France, an official has said, as student protests continue across the country.
The "very serious incident" happened in the north-eastern city of Lens on Monday morning, according to the prefect of Pas-de-Calais, François-Xavier Lauch.
"The student's life is not in danger," he said, adding that the teenager was transferred "very quickly" to a hospital in nearby.

Around 500 schools were partially or totally closed across the country on Monday amid student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing which have led to clashes with police in recent days.
There are mixed reports in French media about how the boy came to sustain the injury.
Regional newspaper La Voix Du Nord reported that they lost their hand after picking up a police stun grenade.
Officials have not yet provided details.
A regional prosecutor said an investigation would be carried out by the French police watchdog, the General Inspection of the National Police (IGPN), "so all light can be shed on what happened".
The incident took place close to the Auguste Béhal high school, the prefect said.
Lauch said a "larger gathering" of students than on previous days had assembled outside the school.

"At the start of the morning, they threw various projectiles at the local police officers who were on site initially. When I say projectiles, I mean stones, fireworks, and mortars," he told French media.

"Instructions were given by the interdepartmental director of the National Police, naturally with my approval, to deploy a company of riot police (CRS) here to maintain order, and it was in this context that this event occurred."

The school issued a statement on Monday morning, saying: "In light of the events that took place this morning and in order to ensure the safety of the entire school community, the institution is switching to distance learning from now on.
"In addition, to support everyone during this period, a listening and support unit has also been set up at the establishment."

articles.title: No10 insists UK military base RAF Fairford is safe after US withdraws bombers
articles.summary: US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed on Sunday, following an incident near the base last week.

blocks.text: Downing Street has insisted RAF Fairford is safe, after the US withdrew all of its bombers from the military base.
The Pentagon confirmed on Sunday it had removed its bombers - thought to be about a dozen B-1s - from the base back to their home stations in America.
US media reported a new threat led to the bombers being removed, which follows a major incident on 27 September when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase.

A Number 10 spokesperson said he would not comment on "foreign nations' military operations", but said the base was safe, and pointed to US President Donald Trump's comments last week, where he "praised our police, defence and security services" in relation to the base.
He added that Defence Secretary Wes Streeting had said last week, "we have tried and tested approaches to defend our bases around the country and throughout the world".
RAF Fairford - in the Cotswolds in Gloucestershire - is at the centre of an incident being investigated by counter-terror police.
Five men were initially arrested on suspicion of terror offences and subsequently released on bail. A sixth man, a UK-Iranian national, was also later arrested and released on bail.
Whitehall sources have not disputed that the decision from Washington to remove the bombers was in response to the incident at the airbase in Gloucestershire.
The BBC has also been told it was a military rather than a political decision - taken at an operational level - and communicated from the US military to its British counterparts.
Earlier on Monday, the New York Times reported US commanders had received new threats about an Iran-backed plot against RAF Fairford according to two US officials.
The newspaper wrote the new information was part of the same threat warnings from three weeks ago, but officials acted quickly after specific details emerged in the past 24 hours.

Days after the incident at RAF Fairford, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said there were "strong indications" that Iran had played a part in the incident but did not provide further details, while US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Fox News that it "clearly involve[d] the hands of a foreign actor" without going into further details.
Tehran has strongly denied any involvement.
In July, Iran said "any base used for aggression against Iranian territory constitutes a legitimate target for our forces".
RAF Fairford, near the village of Whelford in the Cotswolds, has been used as a forward operating location by the USAF for decades.
In recent months, the US has flown B-1 and B-52 bombers from the base for the Middle East, after the UK approved a US request to use it for defensive strikes on Iran.

articles.title: Georgia officials hunt for suspect in shooting that killed two and injured 35
articles.summary: A homecoming celebration turned into a scene of deadly violence, as dozens of shots were fired into a crowd.

blocks.text: Investigators in the US state of Georgia are on the hunt for a suspect in a mass shooting that erupted in the early hours of Sunday, killing two people and injuring 35 more.
A crowd of roughly 1,000 people had gathered for a block party in the southern rural community of Vienna when, according to officials, more than 50 shots were fired.
Two of the victims were pronounced dead at the scene, while another 25 were transported to multiple nearby hospitals, some in critical condition.
No known arrests have been made and authorities have not given a possible motive for the violence. Victims ranged in age from 14 to 51.
The incident occurred on Sunday morning around 01:30 local time (05:30 GMT), during a Dooly High School homecoming celebration, though it was not a school-sponsored event.
"Our hearts are with the families grieving the loss of loved ones, those who were injured, and everyone affected by this tragedy," the school said in a statement.
Anticipating a large gathering, authorities from the Dooly County Sheriff's Office were already positioned at both ends of the crowd as gunfire rang out.
"Some people were reporting fireworks and then someone said somebody been shot," Dooly County Sheriff Craig Peavy told local media.
Peavy said officials then worked their way through the crowd, as people ran scrambling in different directions, while authorities made their way towards victims.
Ashley Gee, who was there, told the Atlanta Journal-Constitution news outlet that the barrage of gunfire sounded "like a machine gun".
Authorities arrived and found several people injured. The two deceased victims were found several blocks away from the scene of the shooting on Pine Street.
Dooly County Coroner Brett Walls told the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the two killed were both men, ages 20 and 23.
The Georgia Bureau of Investigations Medical Examiner's Office said it would conduct an autopsy in each case.
The bureau also said it would join the investigation at the request of the Dooly County Sheriff's Office, describing operations as "active and ongoing".

articles.title: Guardian readers fund life-changing surgery for Somali boy injured in US airstrike
articles.summary:
After Guardian investigation uncovered drone strike that killed 12 civilians and injured many more, seven-year-old Abdiqadir Salah underwent vital operation in Mogadishu

On the rickshaw ride…

blocks.text: On the rickshaw ride to the hospital, Marian Haji Abdi Guled felt a mixture of joy and apprehension: the day they had been waiting for had finally arrived.

Almost a year earlier, her then seven-year-old son, Abdiqadir Salah, had been seriously injured, alongside his two siblings, in what a Guardian investigation found was a US drone strike on the village of Jamaame in Somalia that killed at least 12 civilians, including eight children.
Abdiqadir’s small body had been impaled by shrapnel in the attack, and several chunks remained embedded in his back.

Doctors feared that without an operation to remove them, the boy would lose his ability to walk, but Guled had no money for an operation. For 10 months, the family had languished in Mogadishu with growing expenses and no income – unable to afford surgery, but unwilling to let the boy return to the village without it.
After the investigation, which told the story of Guled and other civilians affected by the attack, a group of Guardian readers from across the globe fundraised for Abdiqadir’s surgery and recovery.
Within a few hours, enough money was raised to cover his treatment and rehabilitation, as well as any medical expenses and treatment for her other two children, who sustained less extensive injuries.
“I was so happy when I found out that Guardian readers raised the money needed for my son’s surgery. I didn’t know people like this existed,” Guled said.
“The people who contributed to the surgery – I really appreciate their support and how they stood by our family when we needed it the most.”
On a Saturday morning in September, Guled waited anxiously as Abdiqadir was finally taken for surgery at Kaafi hospital in Mogadishu.

“Other patients were taken into surgery after him and came out before him – so I worried maybe something went wrong,” she said. “I got to a point where I knocked on the operating room door asking if my son was still alive, then was held back by other patients.”

Finally, her son emerged. Doctors told Guled the surgery had been successful, but complex. While the first two pieces of shrapnel from the missile had been successfully removed, taking out the final piece was considered too risky, possibly resulting in paralysis, so they concluded that it was safer to leave it and monitor his condition.

When the Guardian visited Abdiqadir a few weeks later, he appeared bright, energised and visibly happy. “I have one piece of metal still in me, and if they touch it, I might become paralysed,” the seven-year-old said. “[But] I don’t have any problem with the last piece of metal in my body, because I’m no longer in pain.”

The Guardian investigation into the US airstrikes that injured Abduqadir raised myriad questions about US military intelligence, such as how the targets were selected and why children were hit while they were clearly visible and out in the open. The US has not responded to any questions about the Jamaame attack.

In the months since then, US attacks on the area have continued: from December 2025 to July 2026, it carried out at least three airstrikes around Jamaame, according to research by New America, a security thinktank that documents US military operations abroad. Residents say drones continue to fly above the town.

“We cannot return to Jamaame because what caused my children to be hurt is still there,” Guled said. “I fled Jamaame with my wounded children because of the drones, and the drones are still [flying].”

With the remaining financial support she received from Guardian readers, Guled plans to relocate with her children to the government-controlled port city of Kismayo, which has not been the target of drone strikes, and where Abdiqadir can receive further surgery if needed.
She still wants answers from the US government, nearly a year after they were bombed. “My son has been left scarred for life,” she said.
“I want the US government be held accountable for what they did to my family and for the US to stop bombing our community.”

articles.title: Suspected pneumonic plague in Siberia: What we know about the disease
articles.summary: A worker at a plague research institute in Siberia has died, and nearly 200 of her contacts are under medical observation. Russian authorities deny a link to the bacterial infection. The US is…

image.caption: Image: Britta Pedersen/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What you need to know about plague

items: There are three forms of plague, all caused by the bacterium, Yersinia pestis.
The three forms of plague are bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.

Bubonic plague is the most common form; it does not spread from person-to-person. If untreated, the bacteria can move through the body and bloodstream, causing septicemic plague, which causes internal bleeding and organ failure, and if they reach the lungs, they cause pneumonic plague.
Pneumonic plague is highly contagious as it can pass from person to person through the air, via coughing, for example.
If untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.

blocks.text: Speculation over the death in a Russian plague laboratory

Following the death of a Russian laboratory worker, there is speculation about an outbreak of pneumonic plague, a highly contagious bacterial infection of the lungs. Russia denies there is a broader risk to the community.

Russian officials have said the laboratory worker's death was not caused by a plague pathogen. The 28-year-old died of "pneumonia of unknown origin," according to Russia's Interfax news agency, citing Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's disease-control agency. According to that agency, samples taken from the woman showed no microorganisms "related to her professional activities." This contradicts earlier information.
Local media had previously reported that the woman, who worked at an institute dedicated to fighting plague, had dropped a test tube.
She reportedly died on Friday, October 2, 2026, at the district hospital in Shelekhov, a town near Irkutsk in Siberia.

According to official Russian figures, two hospitals and a children's clinic were placed under quarantine. Local reports said staff at the institute were being quarantined at their workplace. The US news site Axios has reported that around 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under observation. There were no further reported infections.

Even so, distrust of how Russia handles information persists. On one of DW's Russian-language social media channels, a user wrote: "It wouldn't surprise me if this turns into a disaster now, both in terms of the spread and the quarantine measures."
Pneumonic plague: a fast-moving lung infection
All that is known for certain, at time of writing and first publication (October 5, 2026), is that pneumonic plague is highly contagious.

Pneumonic plague is a form of plague that infects the lungs. Like every form of the disease, it is caused by Yersinia pestis, a bacterium usually found in small mammals, such as rodents and in the fleas that feed on them.
The World Health Organization describes the pneumonic form as the most virulent type of plague.

Its incubation period can be as short as 24 hours, and it is the only form that passes easily from person to person through respiratory particles released when a sick patient coughs. This is why, according to the WHO, it can trigger severe epidemics.
Symptoms appear quickly: high fever, headache and weakness, followed by a rapidly worsening pneumonia with shortness of breath, chest pain and a cough that often brings up blood.
A person can catch pneumonic plague by breathing in the bacteria directly, or by developing it when bubonic and/or septicemic go untreated and spread to the lungs.
What is the difference between bubonic and pneumonic plague
Pneumonic plague is not a separate disease. It is one of three forms of plague: bubonic, septicemic and pneumonic.
All are caused by the same bacterium.
What sets them apart is where the infection settles in the body, and that shapes how the disease spreads and how deadly it is.

Bubonic plague is the most common form and the one most people think of when they hear "plague". It usually follows a flea bite. The bacteria travel to the nearest lymph node, which swells into a painful lump known as a bubo. According to the WHO, it rarely spreads between people.

If bubonic plague goes untreated, the bacteria can move further through the body. If they spread into the bloodstream, the disease can become septicemic plague, which causes bleeding under the skin, tissue death in the fingers and toes, and organ failure. If the bacteria reach the lungs, the illness becomes pneumonic plague, the form that can pass from person to person through the air. Both septicemic and pneumonic plague can also develop directly, without a bubo appearing first.
Left untreated, bubonic plague kills between 30-60% of patients. The septicaemic and pneumonic forms are always fatal without treatment.
Pneumonic plague treatment: antibiotics within the first 24 hours
Pneumonic plague is curable, but only if treatment starts quickly. The WHO warns that without treatment it can kill within 18 to 24 hours of the first symptoms.
Common antibiotics can cure the infection, and recovery rates are high when patients are treated within about a day of falling ill.

Speed is what decides the outcome. Doctors are advised not to wait for laboratory confirmation and to start antibiotics as soon as plague is suspected, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

The drugs themselves are not rare or specialized. They are standard, widely used antibiotics, and patients usually need a course of up to two weeks. To stop the infection spreading, patients are kept in isolation, and wearing masks helps protect those around them, the WHO says.
Preventive antibiotics and isolation for close contacts

People who were close to a patient are treated as well, even if they have no symptoms. Both the WHO and the CDC recommend a seven-day course of preventive antibiotics for close contacts of anyone with pneumonic plague.
The WHO does not recommend a plague vaccine for the public. It reserves vaccination for high-risk groups, such as laboratory staff who work with the bacterium and health workers.

articles.summary: The Omani national was a "lone wolf" extremist, according to the reports.

blocks.text: More details about the co-pilot of the flydubai flight – whom multiple reports have named as Hamam al-Hammami – emerged over the weekend as he continued to be questioned in the UAE, with Israeli representatives being updated.

Israeli media cited sources with knowledge of the probe as saying the co-pilot told investigators that, having attacked Capt Smit Machchhar, he intended to continue flying the plane as normal into Israeli airspace and receive landing clearances from Ben Gurion airport.

He then planned to crash the Boeing 737 MAX – with more than 180 passengers on board – into the airport or into a tower block in central Tel Aviv, in the style of al-Qaeda's 11 September 2001 attacks in the US, according to the reports.
The sources are quoted as saying he was most likely to have acted alone rather than on behalf of a radical organisation or foreign government.
The co-pilot also reportedly told investigators that he had intended to hijack and crash a previous flight to Tel Aviv but changed his mind because he knew someone on board.
There was no immediate comment from Emirati or Israeli authorities.

UAE Attorney-General Hamad al-Shamsi said on Saturday that his country's investigations would establish the full circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident, and that the results would be announced upon their conclusion.
Questions are also being asked about major security lapses, including how the attacker was recruited by flydubai and given clearance to fly a plane filled with Israelis to Tel Aviv.
Regional officials said the co-pilot was barred from flying by Oman's national carrier, Oman Air, and moved to an administrative job because of concerns about his extremist views.
He was later hired by UAE-based flydubai after undergoing standard security checks that did not examine his background for potential signs of radicalisation, according to the officials.
Israeli aviation regulations also state that pilots who are citizens of countries without formal diplomatic relations with Israel, like Oman, are not permitted to operate flights to the country.
Regional officials told the Associated Press on Sunday that Emirati authorities had shared with Israel a list of passengers and crew ahead of flight FZ1073's departure.
Israel's Shin Bet domestic security agency said the transport ministry was responsible for vetting such lists from foreign airlines.

But Transport Minister Miri Regev said her ministry was not given passenger and crew lists, and that security oversight for flights operated by foreign airlines fell under the remit of the Shin Bet and the Mossad foreign intelligence agency.
Israel's Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has told the head of the National Security Council to review "all security aspects regarding foreign civil aviation to Israel".
Australian authorities are investigating the co-pilot's links to Australia. Sources have told local media that he studied there between 2015 and 2017.

articles.title: Indian singer Anuv Jain on finding success without the Bollywood boost
articles.summary: The star reveals why he is "very selective" about releasing music - and shares his future collab hopes.

blocks.text: Can you find success as an Indian artist, outside of the Bollywood machine, while making music that feels like you?
Well according to Anuv Jain it's possible - and you can even create something "beautiful".
The singer-songwriter's soft vocals have gained hundreds of millions of views on YouTube - not an easy feat as an independent artist in India's music scene.
BBC Newsbeat met Jain as he prepared for the final shows on the European leg of his first world tour to find out why he's taking his time and "hoping for the best".
"It's not about the numbers," Jain tells us backstage, ahead of his sold-out performance at London's Roundhouse.
But they do tell a story.
Jain is from Ludhiana in the Punjab region of India and began singing as a teenager.
His tracks have since racked up hundreds of millions of views on YouTube with their emotional storylines about relationships and heartbreak.
Jain primarily sings in Hindi, with his pieces often exploring deep emotions like love and longing.
Fans talk about feeling like his music soundtracks their lives, external and is personal to them.
His accessible style has attracted 3.9 million followers on Instagram and more than 20 million monthly listeners on Spotify.
According to Jain, the secret to his success is simple.
When writing music, he says, he imagines how someone listening in the car, going for a run or sitting alone at night would feel hearing the song.
"I just try to make a good song and something that I would like to listen to, something my mum, my sister and my wife would like to listen to," he says.
"For some reason, the taste that we have in music is gentle enough that when we put it out there, there are millions of people who are wanting to consume all of this."
Jain has attracted a sizeable fanbase without the backing of Bollywood, which has traditionally dominated the Indian music industry with opportunities and significant funding for artists.
He's one of a growing number of independent musicians offering something different to the rollicking film scores and dramatic ballads that are synonymous with the country's movie industry.
Jain describes artists like him as existing in an "alternate space".
"We release music ourselves and hope for the best," he says.
Jo Tum Mere Ho and Afsos, Jain's track with AP Dhillon, both reached number one on the Asian Music Charts, but the singer says there's no recipe to his success.
Jain says he's "very selective" about the music he releases, only putting out one song a year until recently.
But he plans to change that - and insists he has new songs coming "very soon".
"They're done and I think they're beautiful songs so technically you might have more music this year," he says.
"It's not like it's gonna be just one release, let's see how it works out."
The singer explains that seeing a project through is key - which might be why he limits what he puts out.
"There are no projects like right now for me that are half or that I haven't completed them yet.
"When I start a project, I always finish it. I mean, I might have ideas, but as soon as I start writing, I finish it."
Simplicity seems to do the trick, with certain passages , externalof Jain's songs, like Arz Kiya Hai, becoming hugely popular among his fanbase and going viral on TikTok and Instagram.
There have been high-profile collaborations between some of western music and Indian music's biggest names in recent years.
Jain says he'd be open to working with bigger stars, but only if his own identity can be preserved and things are done "the right way".
"The storytelling cannot get diluted just because there's a bigger name attached," he says.
But, he adds: "I'm not there yet".
However, Jain does admit he could see himself joining forces with former One Direction star Zayn Malik, who's enjoyed success in both the Official Singles Chart and Official Asian Music Chart.
"He would be somebody who would definitely work very well with the kind of music that I make," says Jain.
"Maybe the universe will just make it happen."

articles.title: German and US scientists win Nobel medicine prize for work on optogenetics
articles.summary: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel were selected for their 'discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics'

blocks.text: NOBEL PRIZE. Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel are awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, as announced during a press conference at the Nobel Forum at Karolinska Institute in Stockholm, Sweden, October 5, 2026.
TT News Agency/Pontus Lundahl/via REUTERS
Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann, and Georg Nagel were selected for their 'discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics'

items: American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discoveries in light and optogenetics, which enhance understanding of brain function.
Optogenetics allows researchers to control nerve cell activity in living brains and is being used in clinical trials to restore vision in patients with retinitis pigmentosa.
The laureates expressed surprise and delight at receiving the award together, highlighting the collaborative nature of their work in advancing neuroscience.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

STOCKHOLM, Sweden – American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine on Monday, October 5, for their discoveries on light and optogenetics that have helped understand how the brain works.

The Nobel Assembly of Sweden’s Karolinska Institute medical university said Deisseroth, 54, Hegemann, 71, and Nagel, 73, were selected for their “discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.”

Optogenetics “makes it possible to switch on, or off, the activity of individual nerve cells in a living brain,” said Thomas Perlmann, Secretary-General of the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet.
“This method is now being used in laboratories around the world to reveal the brain’s mysteries,” Perlmann said.
In clinical trials, researchers are restoring vision to people blinded by a condition called retinitis pigmentosa by inserting a light-sensitive protein in the retina.
Researchers also hope optogenetics could improve cochlea implants, allowing more precise stimulation of the auditory nerve than current electrical devices.
The physiology or medicine prize traditionally opens the annual Nobel announcements, with awards in physics, chemistry, literature, peace and economics to follow over the coming days.
Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel will share a prize sum amounting to 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.2 million).

In the early 1990s, Hegemann investigated how the alga Chlamydomonas reacts to light in half a millisecond. He hypothesised that a single protein captured light and acted as an ion channel. Nagel tested this by injecting Chlamydomonas genes into frog eggs, discovering channelrhodopsin-2—an ion channel that opens when exposed to light.

In 2003, they published that this protein could be introduced into human and hamster cells to generate electrical impulses using light. In 2005, Deisseroth at Stanford demonstrated the technique in rat nerve cells and the method was named optogenetics a year later.
Perlmann said he had talked to all three laureates this morning, and that they were surprised and delighted.

“All three said the same thing, that they thought it was absolutely wonderful to receive the prize with the other two and they call them my friends. That it’s such an honor to receive them together. So that’s something they conveyed,” Perlmann said.

The five original Nobel Prizes were created under the terms of Swedish inventor and industrialist Alfred Nobel’s will and have been awarded since 1901, with only limited interruptions, chiefly during World War One and World War Two.
A sixth award, the economics prize, was established in 1968 by Sweden’s central bank, the Riksbank.

The medicine prize has honored some of the most influential scientific discoveries of the past century, including Alexander Fleming’s work on penicillin, recognised in 1945, and Karl Landsteiner, who won in 1930 for his discovery of human blood groups.

Last year, American scientists Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell and Japan’s Shimon Sakaguchi won the prize for work shedding light on how the immune system spares healthy cells, creating openings for possible new treatments of diseases such as cancer.

Nobel laureates are chosen by expert committees appointed by the prize-awarding institutions. The awards are presented in Stockholm, with the exception of the Peace Prize, which is handed out in Oslo, a tradition often linked to the union that bound Sweden and Norway during Nobel’s lifetime.
More than 125 years after Nobel signed his will, the prizes retain many of their longstanding traditions.

The celebrations culminate on December 10, the anniversary of Nobel’s death, when laureates receive their awards in ceremonies attended by Sweden’s and Norway’s royal families and are feted at gala banquets held in their honor. – Rappler.com

articles.title: AMLC: Cale88 received P319M from China, HK
articles.summary: Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura confirmed Monday that Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte"s husband, lawyer Mans…

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 7:05pm

Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura confirmed Monday that Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company linked to Vice President Sara Duterte’s husband, lawyer Mans Carpio, received P319 million from China and Hong Kong.

Buenaventura, a witness presented by the House prosecution panel, said this on Day 33 of the impeachment trial, when asked by private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia about the total amount of the remittances from China to Cale88, based on the covered transaction reports (CTR) and suspicious transaction reports (STR).
“Ang kabuuang halaga po, Your Honor, ‘yung aggregate amount…ang naka-indicate sa aming tabular summary ay P319,326,770.41 po, Your Honor. Based on our tabular summary record,” Buenaventura answered.
(The total amount, Your Honor, the aggregate amount…indicated in our tabular summary is P319,326,770.41, Your Honor. That’s based on our tabular summary record.)
Of the amount, it was indicated in the table presented that P315.93 million came from Mainland China, while P3.39 million was from the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region of China.
Divinagracia then asked the AMLC official the nature of such a transaction.
“Ang title ng Table 5 is the CTRs and STRs pertaining to inward remittances to Cale88 Foods Corporation from a) China and b) other countries,” Buenaventura said.
He said that the AMLC no longer included the figures for the outflow of remittances involving Cale88 because it was not requested in the letter of the prosecution.
Divinagracia then asked the witness what basis, if any, the AMLC has to say that Duterte and Carpio deliberately concealed the true origin of the transactions.
Defense counsel Mark Vinluan objected to the line of questioning, saying it has “no basis.”

The prosecutor rephrased her question and asked Buenaventura if, based on the documents assessed by the AMLC, he could say that the transactions of the couple had the intention to conceal the source of the remittances.
Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero allowed the witness to answer despite the objection by the defense.

“I am unable to answer, Your Honor. I was only given the portion, and even then, it’s difficult to ascertain at this point because it’s just numbers, Your Honor… ‘Yun lang po (that’s it), unable to answer. It’s not in our records submitted,” Buenaventura said.
Divinagracia pressed the witness about what the transactions showed, if any, regarding money laundering. Vinluan objected, saying the question was “vague and has no basis.”

“Your Honor, I am unable to provide a comment or answer because I am only testifying based on the records and insofar as I was confronted with the documents submitted, there was nothing that could make me conclude that one or make an opinion on that,” Buenaventura added.
To recall, former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV accused Duterte and Carpio of respectively accepting P150 million and P319 million from China through their separate companies.
The Vice President’s camp has denied Trillanes’ claims, calling them "malicious and fabricated."

The Chinese Embassy in Manila also branded the allegations that China has funneled funds to a political faction in the Philippines as a " false narrative," calling them "malicious rhetoric and actions.” —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: On Teachers’ Day, they still don’t hear what they want to hear from Marcos
articles.summary: Quezon City has good news for its public school teachers on Monday, October 5, but others are left wishing 'sana all'

blocks.text: TEACHERS' DAY. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. delivers a speech during the Department of Education's National Teachers' Day Celebration at the Smart Araneta Coliseum in Quezon City on October 5, 2026.
Marcos' Facebook page
Quezon City has good news for its public school teachers on Monday, October 5, but others are left wishing 'sana all'
Teachers could only say “Sana all (I wish I had the same experience)!” after learning that their peers in Quezon City would have a higher monthly allowance in 2027.
Quezon City Mayor Joy Belmonte said their city government is set to increase the supplemental allowance for teachers and non-teaching personnel to P2,000 next year, up from the previous P1,500.

Belmonte made the announcement during the 2026 National Teachers’ Day celebration of the Department of Education (DepEd) on Monday, October 5, saying that they recognize the dedication of public school workers.
The crowd of 10,500 Luzon-based public school teachers at the Smart Araneta Coliseum, located in Belmonte’s turf, cheered.
But what about other teachers all over the Philippines?
In his speech at the same event, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. said other mayors may now have to raise allowances for teachers after Belmonte’s announcement.
“Mayayaman naman kayong mga city eh (Your cities are rich),” Marcos quipped.
Just as September ended, the Caloocan City Council approved an increase in the additional augmentation allowance of its teachers and staff to P2,555.56, effective October this year.

But on Monday, even the President might have felt the pressure. “Mayor Joy, kasama ako do’n sa [napasubo], dahil ako kaagad ang nilapitan. ‘Pahingi ng pondo para makapagbigay din kami ng allowance.’” (Mayor Joy, I’m among those who were put on the spot, because some mayors immediately approached me. “Please give us funds so that we can also provide allowance.”)
Not every local government unit provides a separate allowance for their teachers.

“Sana gano’n din ‘yong sa buong Pilipinas…. ‘Yong monthly allowance, napakalaking tulong ‘yon (I hope it’s the same experience across the Philippines. A monthly allowance would be a big help for us),” said Ronald Ventura, a teacher from Batac City, Ilocos Norte. He said their province — the Marcoses’ bailiwick — does not provide the same allowance.

Under the Kabalikat sa Pagtuturo Act, the government provides teachers with an annual tax-free teaching allowance of P10,000. The national budget also includes a P1,000 World Teachers’ Day incentive benefit.

Marcos mentioned this incentive in his speech, along with teaching and medical allowances, updates on the over 82,000 teachers and school heads who have been promoted under the Expanded Career Progression System, and the expedited process for the still-unreleased 2024 performance-based bonus.
But some teachers wanted to hear more from the President, such as a higher World Teachers’ Day incentive. Someone also shouted “Sahod!” (wage).

blocks.caption: On Teachers’ Day, they still don’t hear what they want to hear from Marcos

blocks.text: “Parang pahaging lang ‘yong nangyari (It’s like he just dropped indirect hints),” said Noliver Viray, a public school teacher from Valenzuela City.

Viray, who has over two decades of teaching experience, told Rappler that teachers who attended the DepEd event wanted to hear good news. “Wala kasing nailatag kung ano ba ‘yong dapat na benepisyo na mabibigay sa mga teacher, ‘yong mga increase,” he added. (The benefits that teachers truly need, including salary increases, were not outlined.)
The Teachers’ Day celebration highlighted Marcos’ seeming silence on calls for a salary increase for teachers. Even during his recent State of the Nation Address, the topic was left untouched.
“I was hoping he would make a public announcement in front of all the teachers,” Novie Ann Varias, a public school teacher from Cardona, Rizal, said in a mix of Filipino and English.
She believes that there should be a P15,000 across-the-board wage hike, which is the same plea of the Teachers’ Dignity Coalition.

In the streets, members of the Alliance of Concerned Teachers, along with other progressive groups, marched toward Mendiola in Manila on Monday, in a bid to bring close to Malacañang their call for a P50,000 starting salary for teachers.

In his written message, Marcos said the government recognizes the sacrifices of teachers, and reaffirms its “shared responsibility to cherish and uplift those who shape our lives.” For many, however, those words may remain empty unless their requests for higher wages are granted. – Rappler.com

articles.title: ‘Unintended consequences’: Poll shows UCP independence referendum boosting Alberta NDP
articles.summary: Premier Danielle Smith's efforts to satisfy the party faithful with an independence referendum may have unintentionally breathed life into the opposition NDP.

image.caption: Calgary-Shaw candidate Kyle Campbell and Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi celebrate the party's byelection win at a pub in southeast Calgary on Sept. 14. The NDP won by a margin of 582 votes. (Nate Luit/CBC)

blocks.text: Jessica Fallis initially feared getting doors slammed in her face canvassing for Alberta’s New Democratic Party in Calgary-Shaw during the 2023 general election campaign that propelled the United Conservative Party to its second majority.
But door-to-door canvassing for the NDP in the far south Calgary riding was a lot easier in the recent byelection, Fallis says.
“Some of the [voters at the] doors,” said Fallis, “would be, ‘I'm going to vote for anything but Danielle Smith and the UCP.’”
New Democrat Kyle Campbell defeated the UCP’s Mike Derry in September by nearly 600 votes in a constituency with a long history of electing conservative politicians.

items: Alberta NDP win in Calgary-Shaw byelection

blocks.text: UCP Premier Danielle Smith may have triggered the independence referendum, according to one longtime Alberta political watcher, because she “wanted to prove to her hardcore base she was committed to direct democracy,” but her efforts to satisfy the party faithful may have unintentionally breathed life into the opposition NDP.
“The referendum has meant we are attracting people from across the province who want to get involved,” said Heth Wilson, president of the NDP, in an interview with CBC News.

items: Follow all of our Alberta referendum coverage

blocks.text: Political trouble for UCP

A recent CBC News poll suggests Alberta voters’ impressions of Smith personally and support for her governing UCP have slipped in recent months, with the UCP now essentially neck-and-neck with the opposition NDP. New Democrats lead by eight points in battleground Calgary.
This past spring, the UCP and Smith still enjoyed the longest honeymoon period since the Ralph Klein era.

On top of losing the conservative stronghold of Calgary-Shaw, Smith faces simmering frustrations within her party surrounding the political “hot potato” that has become the Oct. 19 referendum asking if Alberta should remain a province of Canada.

“One of the unintended consequences is that it's given the NDP increased capacity. It's given the NDP a chance to get their ground game together one full year ahead of a general election,” said Calgary-based pollster Janet Brown, who conducted the random survey of 1,200 Albertans for CBC News.
The UCP, stressed Brown, usually has the better ground game to get out their vote than the NDP.

The referendum, likely in concert with the ongoing trade war between Canada and the U.S., and tensions with U.S. President Donald Trump, has also dialled up Albertans’ attachment to Canada in recent months.

“For those who are paying close attention,” said University of Calgary political scientist Lisa Young, “there's a real intensity of preference here, and that often turns into a desire to do something.”
For some, that something has turned into volunteering for the NDP.
“It seems to me that the NDP is well positioned to benefit from that,” said Young.
And the referendum offered the party a springboard of sorts to talk about issues other than separation.
Connecting referendum to affordability concerns

NDP door knockers in Calgary-Shaw say the independence referendum — and its ballooning cost — gave them an opportunity to talk about what voters care most about: affordability, education and health care.

“That's something that really resonated with the people,” said Wilson. “Where's our elementary school? How are our children being taken care of? How are my parents being taken care of in the health-care system?”
“The referendum seems to be a distraction and a cost we just can't afford as a province at this time, is what we heard on the doors when the referendum came up,” added Wilson.

The contrast between the cost of the referendum and “shovels are not in the ground to start building schools” proved an effective message, said David Cloutier, who door knocked for the NDP as a volunteer in the recent byelection and as the NDP candidate in the 2023 provincial election.
“We talked to a lot of folks who feel like their needs have been ignored for a long time,” he said.
The NDP’s president stresses the referendum was not a top-of-mind issue for voters in Calgary-Shaw when the byelection was called in August.
“We've certainly seen the referendum as an issue ramp up through the fall and toward the end of the byelection,” added Wilson, who said it breathed momentum into the party.
The NDP hopes to capitalize on that momentum in the looming provincial election expected next October.
But longtime political watchers warn against writing off the UCP too soon.
UCP retains structural advantages
The UCP may be facing tough headwinds now, but the governing party has a year to recover before facing voters in a general election.
Also, the province is flush with energy royalties because of high oil prices, meaning it can spend big on schools and the provincial health-care system in the coming months.
“I think we've already seen the UCP switching into pre-election mode,” said Young, highlighting the recent provincial pause on its fuel tax.

“They're clearly trying to shift the focus away from the issues that matter to their base toward the issues that matter to the electorate,” she said. “The UCP is well positioned to use its very significant budget surpluses to do things that make it more popular in electoral terms.”

“The challenge for the NDP,” Young thinks, “is going to be that once the referendum is over, it will be easy for Albertans to forget that there was a referendum. These things fade in people's minds relatively quickly.”

“For the NDP, there's going to have to be really razor-sharp focus on keeping people reminded that they weren't happy about the referendum, that the NDP is the party of Canada, and to the extent that Trump remains problematic, I think that's probably helpful,” said Young.
The NDP might also benefit from continued infighting in the UCP.
Smith could face a leadership review in the coming months amidst simmering tensions over the referendum.
New ridings, new problems for the NDP
There’s another structural advantage of being in power.
The UCP could use its majority in the legislature to redraw riding boundaries to create new so-called “rurban” ridings that include both rural and urban areas.
Data analysis done by CBC News suggests that proposed hybrid ridings in the Calgary area favour the governing UCP.
“The NDP is well positioned under this current seat model,” said Brown.
But the new hybrid ridings will be tougher for the party, given the UCP’s traditional dominance in the province's rural areas, said the pollster.
Still, with some wind in its sails from the recent Calgary-Shaw byelection and recent stronger public opinion polling, NDP volunteers say they’re feeling confident a year out from the election.
“We are hyped and inspired,” said Fallis. “We're on fire. We want to do this. We need to do this.”

The CBC News random survey of 1,200 Albertans was conducted using a hybrid method between Sept. 8 and Sept. 21, 2026, by Edmonton-based Trend Research under the direction of Janet Brown Opinion Research. The sample is representative of regional, age and gender factors. The margin of error is +/- 2.8 percentage points, 19 times out of 20. For subsets, the margin of error is larger.

The survey used a hybrid methodology that involved contacting survey respondents by telephone and giving them the option of completing the survey at that time, at another more convenient time, or receiving an email link and completing the survey online. Trend Research contacted people using a random list of numbers, consisting of 30 per cent landlines and 70 per cent cellphone numbers. Telephone numbers were dialled up to five times at five different times of day before another telephone number was added to the sample. The response rate among valid numbers (i.e., residential and personal) was 11.3 per cent.

blocks.text: SARA DUTERTE. Accompanied by her brother, Davao City 1st District Rep. Paolo Duterte, Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Quezon City RTC on September 11, 2026, to attend arraignment proceedings for a grave threat case.
Jire Carreon/Rappler
'To be fair to the AMLC, they simply received this report from a covered institution.... They are merely mirroring the report submitted to them by a covered institution,' Escudero clarifies

items: The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) has flagged financial transactions of Vice President Sara Duterte related to flood control issues and illegal drugs.

Duterte has a total of 373 covered transaction reports (CTRs) and 34 suspicious transaction reports (STRs), amounting to P4.4 billion, while her husband has similar reports, raising concerns about the context of these transactions.
The AMLC's reports do not imply that the flagged transactions are illegal, as they are part of the monitoring process under the Anti-Money Laundering Act.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) has flagged financial transactions of Vice President Sara Duterte allegedly related to the flood control issue and illegal drugs, the House prosecution team said on Monday, October 5.
During his direct examination, AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura testified on AMLC’s Suspicious Transaction Reports (STRs) related to the couple’s financial transactions.

blocks.caption: Flagged transactions of Sara Duterte ‘linked’ to flood control, drugs – AMLC

blocks.text: Asked by prosecutor Mae Divinagracia, Buenaventura read the reason cited in an STR dated November 15, 2019: “Based on records, as reported by the covered person, the reason indicated is graft and corrupt practices” related to the Department of Public Works and Highways’ (DPWH) flood control issue. Another STR for Duterte, dated August 1, 2024, mentioned alleged “shabu (metampethamine) importation.”

The AMLC is the Philippine government’s financial intelligence unit tasked to implement Republic Act No. 9160 or the Anti-Money Laundering Act (AMLA). AMLC specifically looks into two types of transactions and issues corresponding reports: covered transaction reports (CTRs) and STRs.
CTRs are automatically triggered if a financial transaction reaches P500,000 within a single day. Meanwhile, STRs are triggered not because of amount threshold, but because of certain conditions.

The law lists down the circumstances that include cases where customer cannot be properly identified; the amount is inconsistent with the person’s financial capacity; transactions appear structured to avoid reporting requirements, and the transaction appears connected to an unlawful activity, among other reasons.

However, it must be noted that transactions flagged or reported by AMLC do not automatically mean that money was illegal or if a crime has been committed. The reporting is just part of the AMLC’s mandate to monitor financial transactions and implement the AMLA.

blocks.caption: EXPLAINER: What makes a transaction ‘covered’ or ‘suspicious’ under AMLA?

blocks.text: Based on the summary of reports submitted by the AMLC to the Senate impeachment court, Duterte has 373 CTRs and 34 STRs, while her husband has 363 CTRs and 30 STRs. When combined, the transactions amount to P4.4 billion, based on the summary.

blocks.caption: Screenshot/Senate impeachment court

blocks.text: During the presentation of the STRs, some senators interjected and raised concerns on the context behind the STRs. Specifically, why covered persons or bodies — like financial institutions — use media reports for the STRs.
“We don’t even know the context of that. We don’t even know. Honestly, we don’t even know that banks do that,” Senator-judge Pia Cayetano said.
Senator-judge Alan Peter Cayetano raised the same concern.

“To be fair to the AMLC, they simply received this report from a covered institution. As earlier asked by the Chair, this did not come from them. They are merely mirroring the report submitted to them by a covered institution. And that covert institutions at times do submit it based on available information, whether from news or media reports or other information,” presiding officer Chiz Escudero clarified.

blocks.caption: Flagged transactions of Sara Duterte ‘linked’ to flood control, drugs – AMLC

blocks.text: Divinagracia also asked Buenaventura about the CTRs related to Cale88, a firm allegedly connected to Carpio. The prosecution alleged that there were inward remittances to Cale88 from China and other countries.
Based on the summary, there were 141 CTRs and 3 STRs involving China remittances. The total remittance reached P319 million, including remittances from Hong Kong.

On Friday, October 2, former senator Antonio Trillanes IV claimed that Cale88 allegedly got P319 million from “Chinese government and corporations.” Trillanes made this allegation the same week the prosecution dropped him from its list of witnesses.

blocks.caption: Mans Carpio’s firm got P319 million from ‘Chinese government and corporations’ — Trillanes

blocks.text: But during the Monday hearing, defense lawyer Mark Vinluan, during his cross-examination of Buenaventura, reiterated that the issuance of CTRs do not necessarily mean that the transactions were illegal per se.
“For the record, transaction that is reported as a covered transaction is not necessarily an illegal transaction, correct?” Vinluan asked.
“Tama po (Correct),” Buenaventura replied. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor challenges validity of search warrants in his Epstein-related arrest
articles.summary: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking the police to court to challenge his February arrest on suspicion of misconduct in public office over allegations he sent confidential government documents to…

image.caption: Britain's Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, formerly known as Prince Andrew, has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Jeffrey Epstein, and said he regrets their friendship. (Kirsty Wigglesworth/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor is taking the police to court to challenge his February arrest on suspicion of misconduct in public office over allegations he sent confidential government documents to Jeffrey Epstein.
Hearing set for Thursday to hear Andrew's challenge after being accused of leaking info to Epstein

Britain's Judicial Office, part of the non-political civil service which supports the courts, ​said a hearing would take place ​on Thursday after the former prince sought to quash the search warrants that were issued as part of the arrest.
Thames ​Valley Police, which carried out the arrest, confirmed it ⁠was engaged in ⁠legal proceedings and declined further comment.
Andrew, 66, was arrested in February on suspicion of leaking government documents to Epstein when the former royal was a special representative for trade between 2001 and 2011.
The second son of the late Queen Elizabeth and younger brother of King Charles ⁠has denied any wrongdoing in relation to Epstein and said he regrets their friendship.
Arrested: The fall of Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor | About That
Questioned for hours
Andrew ‌was questioned all day by detectives, and a Reuters photograph, which captured the former prince as he left the police station, showed him looking in a state of shock.
The Judicial Office said ⁠the hearing on Thursday regarded an effort by the police to restrict access to court documents. The hearing will begin in private.
News of the legal challenge was first reported by the Daily Telegraph.

items: CBC GEM: The Secrets of Prince Andrew
After former prince Andrew's arrest, the Royal Family tries to keep calm and carry on

blocks.text: Andrew's lawyer did not respond to a request for comment.

He was forced to ​quit all official royal duties in 2019 over his ties with disgraced financier and ⁠convicted sex offender Epstein, and was then stripped ⁠of his titles and honours last October by his older brother after further revelations about their relationship. ⁠

Andrew was accused by Virginia Roberts Giuffre of sexual assault when she was 17 and employed by Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell, whose London residence was the site of a now-famous photograph of Andrew and Roberts Giuffre standing together. Andrew denied her allegations but reached a financial settlement with Roberts Giuffre after she filed a civil lawsuit.
Epstein ⁠was found dead in ​his Manhattan jail cell in August 2019 in what was ruled a ​suicide.
Maxwell was convicted of federal sex trafficking charges in New York and sentenced to 20 years in prison in 2022.
Roberts Giuffre died at her Australian residence last year in a death that was ruled a suicide.

A U.S. congressional committee since last year has interviewed several prominent individuals, including former president Bill Clinton, who in the past had dealings with Epstein or Maxwell. While some members of the committee expressed a desire to speak to Andrew, the committee has no legal authority to compel him to appear before the panel.
With files from CBC News

articles.title: Nobel Prize awarded for showing how nerve cells shape feelings
articles.summary: US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded for their work.

blocks.text: US psychiatrist and neurologist Karl Deisseroth and his German colleagues Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel have been awarded this year's Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their work in the field of optogenetics.
Their research has helped scientists learn more about the workings of the mind, to better understand how the human brain works.

The Nobel Committee praised the trio for laying the foundation of a new era in neuroscience and revealing the neural circuits behind "specific memories, feelings, and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders".
In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method to try to restore sight in people with visual impairment.
"Optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain," the Nobel Assembly said.
"Every day brings new discoveries, helping to solve one of humanity's great mysteries: how our incredible brain works."
The winners said it was "absolutely wonderful" to get the award, and that it was an honour to share the accolade with friends.
The three men will also share the £900,000 (12 million Swedish kronor) prize money.

articles.title: Spanish PM Sánchez calls snap election after mounting housing crisis
articles.summary: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called an early election for Nov. 29 on Monday, in a bid to strengthen his mandate after a fragmented parliament rejected the government's key housing decrees…

image.caption: Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of campaign promises. (Susana Vera/Reuters)

blocks.text: World

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez called an early election for Nov. 29 on Monday, in a bid to strengthen his mandate after a fragmented parliament rejected the government's key housing decrees last week amid widespread protests.
Election call seen as risky move as Sánchez's Socialist Party is trailing in opinion polls

"We need to renew people's support," Sánchez said in a televised address. "We need to mobilize and win a much larger progressive majority in parliament, one that will allow us to overcome vested interests, deliver new social advances and continue transforming Spain."
The premier also acknowledged having made mistakes and falling short of campaign promises.
"I also know that part of that social majority is dissatisfied today," he said.

items: Pope Leo gives Spain’s 'phoenix' prime minister another turn in the global spotlight

blocks.text: Sánchez, 54, has stood out globally for taking a strong stance on progressive issues, from Palestinian statehood to defending multilateral institutions and cracking down on "tech oligarchs," even as a series of setbacks and scandals weakened his position at home.

Senior members of Sánchez's own Socialist Party, as well as his wife Begoña Gomez, have in the past year faced allegations of graft, dragging down the party's already weak approval rating. Sánchez has called the cases politically motivated.
Trails in polls

Facing the electorate now is a risky move as Sánchez's party is trailing in opinion polls. However, he has been boosted by proposals to tackle a mounting housing crisis that were well received but were struck down by right-wing MPs on Friday, leading to planned new public protests about housing.

An election defeat would spell the end of one of Europe's last few left-leaning governments at a time when the far-right is making unprecedented gains across the region as a growing swathe of European voters desert the centre ground.

Opinion polls suggest a coalition led by the conservative People's Party (PP) with the support of Vox is the most likely outcome in Spain, ushering a far-right party into central government for the first time since the return of democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco.
Still, Sánchez, a wily political operator, has proven time and again his ability to surprise those who had long written him off.

Despite never winning enough votes to form a majority government, he has cobbled together a series of fragile and seemingly impossible coalitions, including voices from the far-left to the separatist right, to remain in power for three successive terms lasting eight years.

But growing fragmentation among his partners has meant the government has passed little in the way of legislation in its third term and failed to pass a budget since 2023, even as Spain's economy has continued to be one of the best performing in the developed world.
Bucks European trend on migration, defence spending

Sánchez took office after leading a move to oust centre-right Mariano Rajoy in the wake of major ‌corruption scandals within Rajoy's People's Party. Against the odds, he won a second four-year term in office in 2023 despite heavy losses in earlier regional and local elections by negotiating support from a loose alliance of parties in parliament.

That was achieved after promising a highly controversial amnesty ​for pro-independence Catalan leaders in exchange for their support, a move still bitterly remembered by many voters as a betrayal of Spanish unity.

Sánchez won early plaudits for moves including the exhumation of Franco from a mausoleum the dictator built for himself ⁠outside Madrid, and the reform of a labour law that has seen unemployment fall to its lowest level in almost two decades.

He cemented his humanitarian and pro-immigration credentials early ⁠by saying in June 2018 that Spain would accept the Aquarius migrant rescue ship and its 629 passengers, after Italy and Malta both refused to let the ⁠ship dock ⁠in their harbours.

items: Canadians reaching out to Spain after Trump's 'sadly familiar' threats
'Absolute chaos' as thousands of Moroccan migrants breach Spain's Ceuta border

blocks.text: As other European countries have toughened their policies towards ​foreign arrivals, Sánchez has consistently argued that immigration is essential for sustaining Spanish growth by plugging labour gaps in key sectors such as construction, agriculture and hospitality.

More recently, his ⁠refusal to agree to U.S.-led demands to increase defence spending to five per cent of GDP while pivoting toward China has rattled U.S. President Donald Trump and some European leaders concerned about the threat of the bloc being flooded with Chinese goods.

articles.title: Banks flagged Sara Duterte transactions over alleged graft, drug links --AMLC witness
articles.summary: Multiple bank accounts under the name of Vice President Sara Duterte were flagged by banks over alleged links to graft and corruption, drug trafficking, and malversation of public funds, Executive…

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 6:37pm

Multiple bank accounts under the name of Vice President Sara Duterte were flagged by banks over alleged links to graft and corruption, drug trafficking, and malversation of public funds, Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura of the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) said Monday.

Buenaventura made the testimony during Day 33 of the impeachment trial of the Vice President, saying that at least two transactions of the Vice President involving premium payments to Mercantile Insurance Company Inc. in July and November 2019 were reported by the banks as suspicious transactions.

“Based on records, Your Honor, as reported by the covered person, the reason indicated is graft and corrupt practices, Your Honor,” Buenaventura said when asked by private prosecutor Mae Divinagracia why such transactions were reported suspicious.

“Several news outlets recently released a list of individuals and corporations identified as being involved in the Department of Public Works and Highways flood control issue, prompting the filing of a Suspicious Transaction Report,” he added.

Buenaventura also said that an August 1, 2024 transaction with Philippine Savings Bank and a December 5, 2024 transaction with BDO Life Assurance Company Inc. were also reported by the banks as suspicious transactions due to “drug trafficking and related offenses” and “malversation of public funds and property," respectively.

The suspicious report on the December 5, 2024 transaction with BDO Life Assurance Company Inc. also stated that “the client is alleged to have misappropriated confidential funds to her office in the OVP.”
Asked whose account these transactions were registered under, Buenaventura said, “Sara Z. Duterte.”
Defense counsel Mark Vinluan objected to the presentation of these documents, saying that the banks merely based their suspicious report on news reports that unfairly harm the Vice President.

Senate impeachment court presiding officer Francis Escudero overruled Vinluan, citing that the court will always clarify and set the record straight on testimonies to prevent misinterpretation by the public.

The prosecution is presenting evidence for Article 2 of the impeachment case against the Vice President, alleging unexplained wealth due to alleged failure to truthfully disclose assets in her SALN and failure to divest in businesses as required for the President and Vice President under a constitutional provision.—LDF, GMA News

articles.title: German soccer: Can new coach Klopp turn things around?
articles.summary: Jürgen Klopp has done things a little differently since becoming Germany coach. Casting a wider net for talent and trying to connect with players and country haven't made an immediate impact, but he…

image.caption: Jürgen Klopp handed debuts to a number of young players in his first internationals Image: Sven Hoppe/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Four games, three goals, two draws, one loss and one win. Jürgen Klopp would have hoped for better results from his first international break as Germany coach. But though the comfortable win over Serbia (2-0), draws against the Netherlands (1-1) and Greece (0-0) and a shock loss to Greece (0-1) in Germany leave them third out of four in their Nations League group, Klopp saw mostly positives.

"Everyone showed what they're made of; everyone earned their place. We've shown signs that we can do some things better than people gave us credit for. I wanted to get something going, and I definitely saw that happen," he said after Sunday's 0-0 draw in Thessaloniki.
For all the positivity of the former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach, the four matches have, in reality, been a mixed bag for Germany.
It's a long road back to the top
Having fallen in the last 32 of the 2026 World Cup and exited in the group stage in 2022, Germany's footballing stock has never been lower.

Klopp tried to address this by casting his net wider, announcing a 44-man squad that split over the matches. He then said this would be a one off, but that his strategy of trying to find a diamond in the relative rough who could adapt to the international game had given him valuable insights.

blocks.caption: Germany have exited early at the last two World CupsImage: Uwe Kraft/IMAGO

blocks.text: "Hard work, lots of information — these guys are brimming with talent," he said of those given a surprise opportunity.
"People were saying that German soccer was at rock bottom and that there was no talent. ... They're not lacking in talent."
While Klopp may have seen potential, and has credit in the bank from his past work, he will need to turn that into results before too long.
Klopp leans on emotion and unity

While much has been said about Klopp's success in imprinting his trademark Gegenpressing (counter press) style early on, he is also a coach who places a high value on connection. Throughout the international break, he has worn a cap emblazoned with the slogan "Einer von 83 millionen” (One of 83 million) in a reference to the German population and an attempt to unify in a country divided by the rise of the far-right AfD party.
He addressed the issue in his opening press conference and then reiterated his position after some social media users branded the team "not white enough" after their loss to Greece.

"There is no reason to give these people any thought. They aren't getting any of my attention. I have little time for stupidity in real life and none on social media either," Klopp said in answer to a question posed by DW.
As well as speaking honestly about his country, Klopp has been open with his new players.

"He has a very good rapport with every player. He tries to reach out to every player and make them feel good, that they're important and that they deserve to be here," said Florian Wirtz, who went on to label his coach as a "master" at managing relationships.
With limited time together, forming bonds between player, coach and country can elevate a national team. It may prove to be more important than any tactical plans.
Havertz injury highlights lack of striking depth

One of the key men in the more senior squad that started the opener against the Netherlands, Kai Havertz limped off after 29 minutes. He was replaced by Eintracht Frankfurt's Younes Ebnoutalib while Nick Woltemade (on loan at Juventus from Newcastle) and Jonathan Burkhardt, also Frankfurt, were also tested up front over the four games.

None of the replacements scored, with Woltemade guilty of a particularly bad miss against Serbia and Burkhardt having a goal disallowed against Greece on Sunday. While all have potential and have enjoyed strong patches of form in their careers, none is tried and tested at the top level, and none is playing in the Champions League. With Havertz being somewhat injury prone, Klopp needs someone to emerge as a viable backup.
Musiala and Wirtz key but both have question marks

Injury is also, sadly, beginning to be a major feature of Jamal Musiala's career. He picked up a thigh injury in the warmup to the Netherlands game that may keep him out for a month. He's also missed games this season due to a neurological condition and missed the first half of last season with a broken leg which came soon after another lengthy spell out. At his best, he is probably Germany's brightest attacking spark, but it's been a while since that level has been seen.

blocks.caption: There are signs that Florian Wirtz could thrive in Jürgen Klopp's systemImage: Tom Weller/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Wirtz, the issue is slightly different. He was excellent in the win over a limited Serbia team, scoring one and creating the other. It was a reminder of a talent that has been largely dormant at Liverpool where he's shown his creative best only in glimpses. He followed it up with a decent display against Greece but saw Burkahrdt inadvertently block his goalbound header. There were signs Klopp's system may suit him.
"He's really gotten us on board with his philosophy," said Wirtz of his coach. "I enjoy it myself, too. I get to show my strengths when we have possession."
Klopp will need more of the same from Wirtz, who captained the side in Greece, if Germany are to move forward.

articles.title: AMRO further cuts PH growth outlook as flood control issue slows investment
articles.summary: ‘The Philippines also had some domestic issues that they need to deal with. Remember, there was this flood control-related issue, and that's significantly slowed down public investment,’ AMRO chief…

blocks.text: HAZE. Metro Manila experienced hazy air conditions on September 1, 2026, due to smoke from forest fires in Kalimantan, Indonesia, blanketing the sky. The Manila local government advised residents to take precautions and wear face masks when going outdoors.
Rappler

‘The Philippines also had some domestic issues that they need to deal with. Remember, there was this flood control-related issue, and that's significantly slowed down public investment,’ AMRO chief economist Dong He says

items: AMRO has revised its Philippine growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027 down to 3.3% and 4.6%, respectively, due to the impacts of the Middle East energy shock and a slowdown in public investment linked to flood control issues.

The Philippines is experiencing significant economic challenges, including high inflation and reduced private consumption, exacerbated by domestic issues and delayed infrastructure projects following corruption allegations.
Despite these challenges, there are positive factors such as remittances and a stable IT-BPM industry, but recovery will depend on the speed and quality of public investment and government spending.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – The ASEAN+3 Macroeconomic Research Office (AMRO) cut its Philippine growth forecasts for 2026 and 2027, pointing to the combined negative impacts from the Middle East energy shock and a slowdown in public investment linked to the flood control controversy.

AMRO now expects the Philippine economy to grow by only 3.3% in 2026, down from its 4.1% forecast in July. Its 2027 growth forecast was cut to 4.6% from 5.5%. In contrast, the wider ASEAN+3 region is expected to grow 4.1% in both years, with Vietnam showing particularly strong growth at 8.0% in 2026 and 7.6% in 2027.

blocks.caption: NEW OUTLOOK. The table shows that AMRO has cut the Philippines’ growth outlook for 2026 and 2027. Photo from AMRO briefing.

blocks.text: The October update is yet another downgrade from AMRO’s assessment after its annual consultation with Philippine authorities in August, when it expected growth of 3.4% this year and 4.8% next year. At the time, it already flagged weaker private consumption due to higher prices alongside subdued investment.
In its latest update, AMRO also pointed to persistent high global oil prices and its effect on energy.

“The Philippines is one of the economies that was hit harder by the energy shock,” AMRO chief economist Dong He said during a briefing on Monday, October 5. “Growth did slow down significantly and the inflation went up very quickly.” (READ: DOE sees ‘no signs’ oil prices will fall as excise tax relief goes on table)
But AMRO said the slowdown cannot be blamed on external conditions alone.
“The Philippines also had some domestic issues that they need to deal with. Remember, there was this flood control-related issue, and that’s significantly slowed down public investment,” He said.
“So the growth outlook is very dependent on how fast public investment and construction-related activities can pick up,” he added.

blocks.caption: From ghost projects to growth slump, Marcos now faces a spending dilemma

blocks.text: In a July analysis, AMRO said infrastructure projects had been delayed or cancelled following corruption allegations that emerged in mid-2025. It estimated that public construction contracted 31.5% year-on-year in the first quarter of 2026.

The financial stability report similarly said foreign investors had pulled money out of Philippine equities, reflecting what AMRO said were “investor concerns over the Philippines’ widening current account deficit, delayed infrastructure implementation, and the potential implications for growth and corporate earnings.”

There are still buffers. He pointed to remittances and the country’s IT-BPM industry, while saying the Philippines has clear monetary and fiscal policy frameworks. But he stressed that the recovery would also depend on the quality and pace of government spending.
Authorities should ensure that “public investment, well-governed public investment, can pick up speed,” He said, calling this important for the economy to return to its potential growth rate.

The World Bank likewise warned that the fallout from the flood control corruption controversy was weighing on the economy through weaker investment. In August, the World Bank said heightened scrutiny and audits of infrastructure projects had delayed spending and made private investors more hesitant, contributing to its decision to cut its 2026 Philippine growth forecast to 3.7% from 5.3%. – Rappler.com

blocks.caption: Flood control corruption cleanup spooks investors, drags PH growth – World Bank
