articles.title: Bosnia election: New steps to prevent electoral fraud, but nationalist parties remain on top
articles.summary: New technology has stopped votes being cast on behalf of dead or absent voters, and turnout has fallen to a record low. But it was a case of deja vu in Bosnia's elections with the same parties…

image.caption: Voter turnout in the Bosnian elections reached a record low of just over 40% on SundayImage: AFP

blocks.text: Bosnia and Herzegovina went to the polls on October 4 with new technology that was meant to end years of vote-rigging.
Chief among the abuses was the casting of ballots in the name of deceased voters who had lingered for years on outdated voter rolls.
At just over 40%, turnout was the lowest since the Bosnian War ended in 1995, in part because the old tricks no longer worked.

In earlier elections, allegations kept surfacing that votes were being cast in the name of people who had died or long since moved abroad. Others said voters cast their ballot multiple times or that blank ballots were added after polls closed to make the turnout look higher.

blocks.caption: New technology was introduced in these elections in an attempt to stop vote-riggingImage: Dragan Maksimović/DW

blocks.text: The voter registry, packed with names of people who had passed away or left the country, was the perfect tool for all of this.
New technology, same old politics
This time, however, every polling station used biometric fingerprint checks.
This represented a clear step forward in making voter identification far harder to manipulate.
Still, the biggest story of this election is not technical. Three nationalist parties won, each within its own community: the SNSD among Serbs, the SDA among Bosniaks and the HDZ BiH among Croats.
The dead may have been struck from the voter rolls, but political trends have not shifted.

For readers who know Bosnia only vaguely, a little background helps: The 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement ended the war, but it also split the country into two entities: Republika Srpska, which has a Serb majority, and the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which has a Bosniak-Croat majority.
A three-member presidency runs the state, and each of the three peoples elects its own member.
That is why elections here are rarely about wages and prices and are instead almost always about who is perceived to be a threat.
Republika Srpska and the return of a fallen leader
For Milorad Dodik, the most powerful Serb politician in Bosnia, this election was a political resurrection.
In 2025, Dodik was barred from holding public office for six years after being convicted of defying the high representative, the top international envoy overseeing the 1995 peace process.
He was sanctioned by the US in 2022, although those sanctions were lifted late last year. Even so, his party, the SNSD, virtually swept the board in Republika Srpska.
Savo Minic became president of Republika Srpska, and Zeljka Cvijanovic kept the Serb seat in the presidency. Both are members of the SNSD.

The party also did very well in the entity's parliament. Neither the sanctions nor Dodik's conviction and the loss of his mandate hurt the party. Voters were not choosing an individual. They were choosing their "side."

blocks.caption: Milorad Dodik, the former President of Republika Srpska, says his party has retained power in the majority-Serb entity and its seat on the shared presidency at national levelImage: AFP

blocks.text: Dodik lost no time in declaring what comes next.

He announced a return to what he refers to as the "original Dayton." In practice, that means undoing the powers the state has gained since 1995 — from the judiciary to the army. To an outside observer, that sounds like a technical phrase. In reality, it is a program for dismantling the state step by step.
"That means we are returning the army to Republika Srpska, the border police, the intelligence service and everything that the high representatives once took away," said Dodik.
A deal between Serbs and Croats?
The opposition offered no serious resistance. It was divided and had no convincing message.
Voters who did not want Dodik had nowhere to turn, so most stayed home. Low turnout favored the side with the most disciplined party machine.

That raises a question that will shape what happens in Bosnia in the coming year. Dodik's conviction kept him out of the direct race in these elections. But for months, there has been talk of a way out.

If representatives of the SNSD and the HDZ BiH enter the presidency, they could pardon him — whatever the third member decides. Bosnian media have reported that this was a pre-election deal between Dodik and the HDZ BiH leader, Dragan Covic. Dodik could then return as prime minister of Republika Srpska, a post he has held before.
Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina: Troika defeated
The picture in the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina is different, but the outcome is the same.

blocks.caption: 'The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU: Help Bosnia,' said Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats after the preliminary results were announcedImage: Amel Emric/REUTERS

blocks.text: The parties of the so-called "Troika," a multi-ethnic liberal political alliance, suffered a defeat. They came to power at this level after the international high representative, a foreigner with the authority to impose laws, changed the election law.
Voters saw no benefit from that experiment. The SDA, the largest Bosniak nationalist party, won the most seats and did well.

The paradox is that SDA president Bakir Izetbegovic lost the race for the presidency. He is the son of Alija Izetbegovic, Bosnia's first president and one of the signatories of the Dayton agreement. The winner was Denis Becirovic of the Social Democrats (SDP), who kept the Bosniak seat.
So, the party won the election, but its leader lost. The son of the man who signed Dayton is now shut out of the institution Dayton created.

"The future of our region lies not in adopting the Russian model but the European one. The message to the EU: Help Bosnia. Let the will of the people be the law of the land," Becirovic said as he declared victory.
A Croat surprise

The same pattern holds among Croats. Darijana Filipovic of the HDZ BiH, their strongest nationalist party, won the Croat seat in the presidency for her party. Filipovic spent years as an aide to Covic, the Bosnian Croat leader.
"HDZ BiH has shown it is brave enough to take a road others would not dare. Who would have dared to nominate me? To some too young, but a surprise to everyone," Filipovic said after the vote.

blocks.caption: Darijana Filipovic, a candidate of the Croat Democratic Union of Bosnia and Herzegovina (HDZ BiH) won the Croat seat of the presidency on SundayImage: Amel Emric/REUTERS

blocks.text: Three peoples, three nationalist parties, three victories, and not one conversation about how to keep people in the country.
What this means for the state

The most important thing about these elections is not the numbers but the makeup of the presidency. Two women will sit in it: Cvijanovic of the SNSD and Filipovic of the HDZ BiH. Anyone who tries to sell that as a breakthrough for women in politics has missed the point.
Both come from parties that, in different ways, do not want the state in its current form. Both could also decide the fate of a man convicted of defying the international oversight of Dayton.

The HDZ BiH has long demanded a third, Croat entity. The SNSD wants autonomy for Republika Srpska. One side wants to split the state into three, the other into two, but they share the aim of making it smaller.
So, the presidency, which should symbolize a shared state, is again made up of people who feel like guests in it.

All of this is happening as the Western Balkans again becomes a stage for rivalry between Russia, the EU and the US. Dodik openly thanked both Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump after his party's victory.

Bosnia has entered a new electoral era with new technology and old politics. Young people are leaving the country in droves. The dead no longer vote, but the living have stopped believing that anything can be different.

articles.title: FACT CHECK: No, Malabon congressman Oreta did not slam Sara Duterte’s travels
articles.summary: Malabon City Lone District Representative Lenlen Oreta did not make such a statement, according to his office’s email response to Rappler. It added that public conversations should be based on…

blocks.text: Claim: Malabon City Lone District Representative Antolin “Lenlen” Oreta III pointed out Vice President Sara Duterte’s multiple travels to The Hague, Netherlands while bringing up President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s modernization plan for the Philippines.
Why we fact-checked this: The quote attributed to the congressman was posted on Facebook on August 5 by Malabon Standard, which has 10,000 followers.

The post has already garnered more than 43,000 reactions, more than 14,000 comments, and 376 shares as of this writing, alleging that Oreta said: “Puro kasi pagpunta sa the Hague ang inaatupag ni VP Sara habang si PBBM gumagawa ng paraan para sa modernization ng bansa.”
(VP Sara is busy flying to The Hague while PBBM is doing the work for the country’s modernization.)
The quote has also been reposted across various social media platforms, including Instagram.
The facts: Oreta did not issue such a statement as confirmed by his office in an email to Rappler on September 30.

“We would just like to clarify that the statement currently being attributed to Rep. Lenlen Oreta is not supported by any verified source or official record. Rep. Oreta has not made such a statement in any interview, speech, Facebook Live, or other official recording,” his office said.
“We believe that public conversations should be based on verified information and reliable sources, especially when statements are being attributed to a public official,” it added.

Rappler previously fact checked a false statement attributed to the congressman from the same Facebook page. In such a post, Oreta allegedly wished for Sara Duterte’s death. This has since been labeled by Meta and Oreta himself as false information.
As of this writing, Oreta still has not flagged the August 5 post as false information.
Oreta was one of the 257 lawmakers who voted for Duterte’s second impeachment. In 2019, he was threatened with arrest by Sara’s father then-president Rodrigo Duterte over the drug problem in Malabon.
Personal trip: While Oreta did not criticize the vice president’s trips abroad, another lawmaker has expressed statements relating to this.

On July 22, Manila 6th District Representative Bienvenido Abante Jr. criticized Duterte’s personal trip to five countries Qatar, Germany, United Kingdom, Northern Ireland, and The Netherlands from July 16 to July 31, amid her impeachment trial. Abante added that Duterte’s travel abroad is “betrayal of public trust.”

The Vice President is on trial for her alleged death threats against high-ranking Philippine officials, including Marcos, First Lady Liza Araneta-Marcos and former House speaker Martin Romualdez, alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, and alleged bribery of public officials. – Eunicito Barreno/Rappler.com

Eunicito Barreno is a 2026 Aries Rufo Fellow. He is a senior journalism student at the University of the Philippines Diliman, where he is also a news staffer at the Philippine Collegian, the university’s official student publication.

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

articles.title: Gasoline, kerosene prices rise on October 6, diesel gets slight rollback
articles.summary: The mixed adjustment comes after price cuts last week, while China’s suspension of refined fuel exports threatens to tighten Asian supply further

The mixed adjustment comes after price cuts last week, while China’s suspension of refined fuel exports threatens to tighten Asian supply further

items: Starting October 6, gasoline and kerosene prices will increase, while diesel prices will see a slight rollback due to volatile fuel markets.
Recent adjustments follow a previous rollback in fuel prices after three weeks of increases, influenced by international market dynamics and China's export policies.
China's suspension of refined fuel exports and increased crude oil purchases may further elevate fuel prices in Asia, impacting the Philippines, which relies heavily on imported petroleum products.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Gasoline and kerosene prices are going up again starting Tuesday, October 6, while diesel prices are set to fall slightly, as fuel markets remain volatile after the previous week’s rollback.
The Department of Energy announced the following fuel price adjustments for the week of October 6 to 12:

items: Gasoline – increase of P1.93 per liter
Diesel – rollback of P1.30 per liter
Kerosene – increase of P3.30 per liter

blocks.text: Before the latest adjustment, the Department of Energy’s price monitoring showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P94.10 per liter for gasoline RON95, P87.20 per liter for gasoline RON91, P95.70 per liter for diesel, and P125 per liter for kerosene for the week of September 29 to October 5.
The mixed movement follows last week’s rollback, which saw gasoline, diesel, and kerosene prices finally fall after three consecutive weeks of steep increases.

“Gasoline prices increased due to a combination of regional supply constraints, refinery operatingconditions, and sustained demand in key consuming countries. In particular, Chinese gasolineexports were expected to decline during the October 1–7 Golden Week holiday due to the laterelease of export quotas, while South Korea was expected to reduce gasoline output for four to fivedays,” the DOE said in a press release on Monday.
The diesel rollback is still a carry-over from the previous week’s drop in international diesel prices, so it does not yet fully capture the more recent developments pushing fuel costs higher again.

“Diesel prices in the region were affected by changing supply and shipping conditions. Asian dieselprices remained generally high but were volatile as shipping costs stayed elevated and pricedifferences between regional markets changed. These developments contributed to the decreasein diesel prices during the monitoring period,” the DOE said.

Worryingly, however, those pressures are building as China suspends refined fuel exports, while disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandab continue to threaten major oil and fuel shipping routes.
Chinese refiners have temporarily suspended exports of petroleum products outside Hong Kong and Macau as Beijing seeks to rebuild domestic fuel inventories.

At the same time, China has also stepped up its purchases of crude oil as refiners seek to replenish supplies and replace disrupted Iranian and other Middle Eastern barrels. Chinese independent refiners have snapped up cargoes from Russia, West Africa, Canada, and South America in recent weeks, adding competition and supporting even higher spot premiums.
The combination of China buying more crude while withholding more of its refined fuel output from overseas buyers could add further upward pressure on Asian fuel markets in the coming weeks.

China is the world’s largest oil refining market by capacity and an important source of fuel for the Philippines. In 2025, it supplied 3.78 billion liters, or about 20% of the country’s imported finished petroleum products, second only to South Korea.

Local pump prices also remain well above levels seen before fighting involving Iran and US-Israeli forces broke out on February 28. In the last full week before the conflict, DOE data showed common retail prices in Metro Manila at P56 per liter for gasoline RON95, P54.70 per liter for gasoline RON91, P55 per liter for diesel, and P83.47 per liter for kerosene.

The Philippines is a net importer of petroleum products, making local pump prices vulnerable to global oil price swings, foreign exchange movements, regional refined fuel prices, and disruptions in international supply routes. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
articles.summary: Sánchez says Spain will head to the polls on 29 November after recent defeats on measures aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.

blocks.text: Spanish PM Sánchez calls early election after housing protests
Image source, Getty Images
Sánchez's announcement comes after a series of measures to tackle the housing crisis was defeated in parliament on Friday
ByBen Hatton and Sergi Forcada Freixas
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called an early election for 29 November after recent defeats on legislation aimed at addressing the country's housing crisis.
Speculation about a snap election had been building over the weekend after parliament rejected two decree laws put forward by the minority government to protect tenants in the rental market.
The eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home after she was unable to afford a sharp rent rise has sparked nationwide protests and increased pressure for housing reform.
In a televised address on Monday, Sánchez said that to push reforms through he needed "a broader progressive majority" that can "overcome the resistance of the elites".

Housing has not been the only issue causing problems for Sánchez's leadership in recent months, with his party having been caught up in numerous corruption scandals and facing pressure on other cost-of-living issues and immigration.

"We have made mistakes and have not achieved everything we had set out to do," Sánchez said, acknowledging there were still "a lot of problems to solve, particularly in the areas of inequality, of public services and access to housing".
Sánchez's left-wing coalition government is made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, and does not have a majority in parliament.
Spain was not due to hold a general election until the summer of 2027 at the latest.
Sánchez has been prime minister since June 2018. His Socialist party finished second in the last election, in 2023.
Although the conservative People's Party won the most seats, it fell short of a majority.
Sánchez remained in power after striking agreements with left-wing parties and securing support from Catalan and Basque nationalist and pro-independence groups.

Most opinion polls suggest the conservatives are likely to emerge as the largest party in the next election. However, they would be expected to need the support of the hard-right Vox party to form a government.
Speaking after Monday's announcement, the leader of the People's Party, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said: "At last, Spaniards will be able to decide".

The opposition leader said it would not be "just another election", but a chance for voters to choose between "decline or change, lies or change, incompetence or change, division or change, corruption or change".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid home led to public outcry

blocks.text: Image source, Europa Press via Getty Images
The eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from her Madrid home led to public outcry
On Saturday, tens of thousands of people took to the streets in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona, calling for greater protections for tenants.
Maricarmen Abascal, 87, became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis when she was forcibly evicted from her Madrid home on 23 September.
A legal glitch allowed her landlord to raise her rent from €500 (£428; $572) to €2,650. It was later lowered to €1,650 - still €300 more than her monthly pension.
She was removed on a stretcher from her apartment of more than 70 years, and was later admitted to hospital.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Protests over housing took place in Madrid on Saturday

blocks.text: Image source, EPA/Shutterstock
Protests over housing took place in Madrid on Saturday
Her lawyer has since said she will be able to return to her home, but the incident has prompted widespread anger over housing.
The left-wing coalition government responded with two decree laws in an effort to defuse the protests.

The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the tenants' organisation Sindicato de Inquilinas.
The political right argued the government's attempt to intervene in the housing market would have led to fewer homes being rented and would have raised prices further.
Juan Bravo of the People's Party said last week "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".

blocks.caption: Image caption, The Spanish prime minister currently doesn't command a congressional majority

blocks.text: The Spanish prime minister currently doesn't command a congressional majority
Sánchez's leadership has been marred by numerous corruption scandals in recent months.
In April, his wife Begoña Gómez was charged with corruption after a two-year criminal investigation.
She is accused of using her relationship to advance her private career - allegations she denies, and which have been dismissed by Sánchez as a right-wing attempt to undermine his coalition.

In May, police raided the Socialist party's headquarters in Madrid as part of an investigation into allegations an operative was paid to carry out a misinformation campaign. The party has denied the allegations.

And in June, Sánchez's former transport minister, José Luis Ábalos, was jailed for 24 years after he was found guilty of being involved in a network that received kickbacks from the sale of face masks during the Covid-19 pandemic.

The Spanish prime minister also came under scrutiny for his handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer, when tens of thousands of people entered the territory from Morocco without authorisation.

articles.title: Trump heads to Nebraska in attempt to shore up GOP’s midterm vote – US politics live
articles.summary: President to visit Grand Island as his plan to allow more foreign beef imports proves unpopular in agriculture-rich state

blocks.text: Key events

items: 24m agoTrump heads to Nebraska in attempt to shore up the GOP's midterm vote

blocks.caption: Robert Mackey

blocks.text: Robert Mackey
The White House has defended a newly hired press aide who posed for a holiday photograph in 2021 wearing a “Fuck Joe Biden” T-shirt and holding a rifle.

Beni Rae Harmony, the new assistant White House press secretary, revealed on Friday that she was going to work for Donald Trump just days after covering him as a correspondent for Real America’s Voice, a partisan rightwing outlet originally created as a video podcast platform for the president’s former adviser Steve Bannon.

According to a LinkedIn profile, Harmony, 24, previously worked as a producer for the far-right Turning Point USA host Jack Posobiec – and as a press aide “focusing on crisis management” for two far-right Republicans: congressman Paul Gosar of Arizona and former congressman Matt Gaetz of Florida.

In 2021, when Gosar was censured by the US House for posting an animated video that depicted him killing Democratic congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and attacking Joe Biden, Harmony recorded an outraged defense of her boss for his YouTube channel.

The photograph of Harmony and an older man posing with rifles in matching anti-Biden shirts, in front of Christmas decorations, was reportedly posted on Instagram in November 2021 by a far-right Republican House candidate, Jarome Bell, who mounted a failed campaign for Congress in 2022.
Trump heads to Nebraska in attempt to shore up the GOP's midterm vote
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
Donald Trump will be in Nebraska later today, campaigning alongside Republican senator Pete Ricketts, in an attempt to salvage the GOP’s dwindling midterms campaign.

The president is headed to Grand Island, located in the solidly conservative south-central part of the state. It’s part of what Trump says is a 32-day blitz of rallies ahead of 3 November that so far has taken him to ruby-red territory such as Oklahoma and Alabama.
On Wednesday, he will make his second stop in two weeks in Texas with a rally in San Antonio.

“The president’s coming to Nebraska to help me campaign, so I can get reelected,” Ricketts, who is running against an independent candidate backed by national Democrats, told the Associated Press last week on Capitol Hill.

The administration’s plan to allow more imports of foreign beef has particularly roiled the agriculture-rich state of Nebraska. Trump wants to lower beef prices for consumers but ranchers have rebelled against the import proposal, arguing it would undercut them.

“The plan to import low-quality foreign beef is not helping Nebraska ranchers,” Ricketts told the AP. “I would advise the White House to change that policy and look for longer-term things that will help us build the size of the herd and ultimately bring the price of beef down for consumers.”

This campaign is set against the president’s plummeting approval ratings, the unravelling of his Maga movement and an affordability crisis escalated by his unpopular war on Iran. But Trump supporters are also among the most motivated to vote and Republicans have far deeper coffers to mobilise their base.
Meanwhile, vice-president JD Vance will rally in Alaska for senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican locked in a tight reelection campaign.
In other developments:

Trump on Sunday named Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, to also serve as the new White House AI czar. Clayton, who leads the US’s 18 intelligence agencies, previously served as the top federal prosecutor in Manhattan and led the Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump’s first term.

The United States has removed ⁠its B-1 bombers from a ⁠British air base one ​week after five men were arrested nearby on suspicion of preparing terrorist acts, a suspected plot that British prime minister Andy Burnham said was likely backed by Iran. The planes had been stationed at ⁠RAF Fairford, the preferred European base for US bombers 90 miles west of London, which had recently been used for US strikes on Iran.

articles.title: Nobel Prize in Medicine awarded to scientists who pioneered work in optogenetics
articles.summary: Scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg ‌Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or ​Medicine for "discoveries concerning light-gated ​ion channels and optogenetics," the…

image.caption: Thomas Perlmann, professor at Sweden's Karolinska Institute and a member of the Nobel committee for physiology and medicine, speaks to reporters in Stockholm on Monday as the three winners are projected on a screen behind him. (Pontus Lundahl/TT News Agency/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·New

Scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg ‌Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or ​Medicine for "discoveries concerning light-gated ​ion channels and optogenetics," the award-giving body ​said Monday.
Winners lauded for discoveries that enhance understanding of the brain

Scientists Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg ‌Nagel won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physiology or ​Medicine for "discoveries concerning light-gated ​ion channels and optogenetics," the award-giving body ​said Monday in Stockholm.
Optogenetics "has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain," the committee said on social media.

"Using optogenetics, researchers have been able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings and behaviours relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders," the committee said. "In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment."

Deisseroth, a 54-year-old American, Hegemann, a 71-year-old German, and Georg Nagel, a 73-year-old German, were all surprised to learn they had won, Thomas Perlmann, professor at Sweden's Karolinska Institute and a member of the Nobel committee for physiology and medicine said.
The Nobel Prizes come with a prize amount of 12 million Swedish crowns ($1.7 million Cdn).

items: Mark Carney for Nobel Peace Prize? Probably not, but his name's out there

blocks.text: Prizes for chemistry and physics will be awarded Tuesday and Wednesday, literature on Thursday and the peace prize on Friday. The economics prize will be announced Oct. 12.

The Nobel Prize was created by wealthy Swedish chemist and entrepreneur Alfred Nobel, who in his will dictated that the bulk of his estate should be used to fund "prizes to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind."

Nobel is best known as the inventor of dynamite, but also wrote poetry and drama and could speak Russian, French, English and German by the age of 17. The five original prize categories reflect the interests closest to his heart.
Nobel ‌died in 1896, with the first prizes bearing his name following five years later.
The Nobel prizes are presented to the laureates on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Nobel's death.

articles.title: ‘No toilet, tiles?’ Estrada office stripped bare ahead of Sotto turnover
articles.summary: The unusual state of the vacated office has caught several senators by surprise

blocks.text: The unusual state of the vacated office has caught several senators by surprise
Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III was in for a surprise when he prepared to move into Senator Jinggoy Estrada’s former office.
Sotto was set to take over the office this week, but ahead of the move, he found that his new room had been stripped bare.
Videos obtained by Rappler showed the office, located in the sixth floor of the Senate building, empty, with its fixtures including toilet bowl, sink, tiles, and carpet removed.
The unusual state of the office caught several senators by surprise.
“Where will Jinggoy bring the toilet?” a senator quipped.
Sotto’s move to Estrada’s office is part of a reshuffling of offices following the last Senate leadership change.
Sotto is expected to vacate his current office, which will be occupied by Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian. Offices in the sixth floor are usually reserved for Senate leaders.
Senate practice allows senators to take furniture and appliances when they vacate their offices, but prohibits them from damaging the premises.
Sotto was elected Senate president pro-tempore in June, following a leadership change that installed Gatchalian as Senate president.
Estrada has been detained at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas since June 2 for plunder charges in relation to alleged flood control corruption. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Southern Manitoba First Nations condemn newspaper for column questioning deaths at residential schools
articles.summary: A column questioning the deaths of children at residential schools has led the Southern Chiefs’ Organization to condemn the Winnipeg Sun and express concern that the newspaper’s CEO is running for…

image.caption: People march through downtown Winnipeg on the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation on Sept. 30. (Prabhjot Singh Lotey/CBC)

blocks.text: Manitoba

A column questioning the deaths of children at residential schools has led the Southern Chiefs’ Organization to condemn the Winnipeg Sun and express concern that the newspaper’s CEO is running for mayor of the Manitoba capital.
Column published days after National Day for Truth and Reconciliation; Kevin Klein disavows responsibility

A column questioning the deaths of children at residential schools has led the Southern Chiefs' Organization to condemn the Winnipeg Sun and express concern that the newspaper's CEO is running for mayor of the Manitoba capital.

On Oct. 4, the Sun published a column entitled "Grave misdirection: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence," suggesting the deaths of Indigenous children at residential schools have been mischaracterized.
"Each death is a tragedy, but none is evidence of an atrocity," the column states, citing as examples the death of one child from bronchitis and another by lightning.

The National Centre for Truth and Reconciliation documented the deaths of at least 4,200 Indigenous children over the course of 165 years at Canada's residential schools. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission of Canada defined the deaths and widespread abuses within residential schools as cultural genocide.

The publication of the column four days after the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation led to a formal statement of condemnation from the Southern Chiefs' Organization, which represents 33 Anishinaabe and Dakota First Nations in Manitoba.

"Survivors and their families should not be forced, yet again, to prove what happened to them or defend the children who never came home," SCO Grand Chief Jerry Daniels said in a statement. "Thousands of children died while attending residential schools. Children were forcibly removed from their families and Nations, stripped of their languages and cultures, and subjected to systems of abuse, neglect and assimilation.
"These are not allegations or political talking points. They are part of Canada's documented historical record."

The co-author of a book about residential school denialism called the column disgusting because, he said, it perpetuates the notion the deaths of thousands of children who were forcibly removed from their families is less horrific because many died of disease, malnutrition and neglect as opposed to murder.

"A lot of people will say, oh, it was just tuberculosis. Lots of kids died of tuberculosis in the early 20th century," said University of Manitoba history professor Sean Carleton, the co-author of Truth Before Reconciliation: Confronting Residential School Denialism.

"That, in fact, is true, except for the fact that, you know what spreads tuberculosis faster? Overcrowding, poor nutrition. Lack of proper sanitation, overwork. All of these issues that were known to be systemic to the residential school system."
Carleton said the column perpetuates what he describes as far-right misinformation about First Nations making claims about mass graves or clandestine murders.

"This is a distraction tactic. It's an attempt to move the goalposts, to make it extremely difficult for Indigenous nations, to explain the complicated nuanced understanding of what we already know, thanks to church and state records, that at least 4,000 children died in these institutions for a variety of different reasons," he said.

items: Why these Sask. writers contributed to a new book about residential school denialism

blocks.text: As criticism of the column mounted Sunday, the editor-in-chief of the Klein Group, the company that owns the Winnipeg Sun, dug in her heels. Heather Klein defended the column in a followup entitled "Disagreement is not denial."
The Southern Chiefs' Organization also criticized her husband, Klein Group CEO Kevin Klein, the candidate who is running for Winnipeg mayor.

Daniels called it "deeply concerning" someone seeking public office provided a platform for someone to use residential schools and the deaths of First Nations children as the basis for political commentary.

"Winnipeg is home to a large and vibrant First Nations population. Anyone asking to lead this city has a responsibility to understand the history of residential schools and the ongoing responsibilities of reconciliation," Daniels said.
Kevin Klein said in a statement he is not responsible for the content of the Winnipeg Sun while he runs for mayor.

"From the day I entered the race for mayor, I stepped away from every editorial decision at the Winnipeg Sun, and I have kept that commitment. The paper stands on its own," the mayoral candidate said.
Heather Klein alone is responsible for the content, he said, adding he does not assign stories, edit copy, approve pieces, or stop them from running.
"Any suggestion otherwise is reckless and without foundation," he said.
Other mayoral candidates criticize Klein
Several mayoral candidates also criticized the newspaper CEO-turned-candidate.
Mayoral candidate Noah Redden said in a statement there is a difference between upholding freedom of speech and tolerating hate speech.
Redden called residential-school denialism inflammatory and said Klein needs to explain to Winnipeg's Indigenous population why his newspaper echoed attacks on residential-school survivors.
Mayoral candidate Scott Gillingham told reporters Sunday he's spoken to enough Indigenous families in Winnipeg to hear firsthand the impact of residential schools.

"What is not deniable in my mind is the impact, the lasting, devastating impact of residential schools on our country," said Gillingham, who attended TRC Day events in an official capacity on Wednesday.
Klein said Friday he did not attend TRC Day events but called the national holiday important.
"Canadians ought to know what took place in the residential school system and what it has meant for Indigenous families and communities ever since," Klein said Sunday in a statement.
"The wrongs of the past should not be forgotten. As a father and a grandfather, I cannot begin to imagine the pain those families carry."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Bartley Kives joined CBC Manitoba in 2016. Prior to that, he spent three years at the Winnipeg Sun and then 18 at the Winnipeg Free Press, writing about politics, music, food and outdoor recreation. He's the author of three books — two of them Canadian bestsellers — and the winner of a Canadian Screen Award for reporting.

articles.title: Here are the 5 books on the 2026 Giller Prize shortlist
articles.summary: The Giller Prize annually recognizes the best in Canadian fiction. The five authors shortlisted are Tara Gereaux, Michelle Good, Nicholas Herring, Nazanine Hozar and Patmeena Sabit.

image.caption: The five books shortlisted for the 2026 Giller Prize. (Graphic by CBC Books)

blocks.text: Tara Gereaux, Michelle Good, Nicholas Herring, Nazanine Hozar and Patmeena Sabit are the five writers shortlisted for the 2026 Giller Prize.
The $100,000 award annually recognizes the best in Canadian fiction.

The 2026 shortlist features five novels, covering a wide range of material, from a historical fiction set in 1940s Saskatchewan (Gereaux's Wild People Quiet) to a contemporary story about a road trip from New Brunswick to Toronto (Herring's Your Breath in Charcoal) and a harrowing novel about child soldiers in the Iran-Iraq war (Hozar's The Small Ones).

Good, on the list for Eliza Sunshine, is the only author on the shortlist who has previously been recognized by the Giller Prize. Her debut novel, Five Little Indians, was on the 2020 longlist and won Canada Reads in 2022.
Unlike the other shortlisted authors who have had books published before, Sabit is a finalist for her debut work of fiction, Good People.

items: The 2027 CBC Short Story Prize is open!

blocks.text: The books on the 2026 Giller Prize shortlist are available in accessible formats through the National Network for Equitable Library Services and the Centre for Equitable Library Access.

The shortlist was chosen by a jury made up of independent booksellers from across the country: Dan Macdonald and Lori Cheverie of the Maritimes' Bookmark, Danielle and Rupert McNally from Toronto's Ben McNally Books, Sarah Klassen from Mosaic Books in B.C., Chris Hall of McNally Robinson Booksellers in Winnipeg, Jenn Baerg Steyn of Yellowknife Books, Sean Liburd of Knowledge Bookstore in Brampton, Ont., and Carmela Vedar of The Book Wardrobe in Mississauga, Ont.

items: Independent Canadian booksellers to represent the Giller Prize jury in 2026

blocks.text: The winner will be announced on Nov. 16 at the Giller Prize award ceremony in Toronto.

The ceremony, hosted by comedian Rick Mercer, will be broadcast on Monday, Nov. 16, at 9 p.m. ET (11:30 p.m. AT, 12 a.m. NT) on CBC TV and CBC Gem, with a livestream also available at 9 p.m. ET on CBC's YouTube channel. It will also be broadcast on CBC Radio One and CBC Listen.
The Giller finalists will also appear at live events in Calgary, Ottawa, Halifax and Toronto as part of the Between the Pages series.

After a few years of controversy surrounding the prize's funding, the Giller Prize cut ties with its former sponsor, Scotiabank, in 2025. The Giller Prize will now be supported by a recent multi-year gift of $4 million from the Hilary and Galen Weston Foundation.
Last year's winner was Souvankham Thammavongsa for Pick a Colour.

Other past winners include Anne Michaels for Held, Sarah Bernstein for Study for Obedience, Suzette Mayr for The Sleeping Car Porter, Esi Edugyan for Washington Black, Michael Redhill for Bellevue Square, Margaret Atwood for Alias Grace, Mordecai Richler for Barney's Version and Madeleine Thien for Do Not Say We Have Nothing.
You can learn more about the five shortlisted books below.
Wild People Quiet by Tara Gereaux

In Wild People Quiet, set in Saskatchewan in the 1940s, a Métis woman named Florence is hiding her true identity while living in a primarily white town, dyeing her hair blonde and doing what she can to blend in. When she meets a group of Métis farm workers in town for the season, she's forced to come to terms with her hidden past and must decide how she wants to move forward.

"A stunning exploration of colonial trauma, self-acceptance and the sacredness of community, Wild People Quiet follows an agonized Florence forced to choose between the community that birthed her and the life that she has built for herself," wrote the jury in a statement.

"An intimate and resonant tale filled with quiet intensity, Wild People Quiet invites readers to reflect on their own family histories, the parts of themselves they choose to hide and the hardships that have made them stronger."

items: How curiosity about her own heritage led to Tara Gereaux's novel about hidden Métis identity

blocks.text: Gereaux, a citizen of the Metis Nation-Saskatchewan, lives in Regina. She is also the author of Saltus and Size of a Fist.
Eliza Sunshine by Michelle Good

Eliza Sunshine is a family saga following three generations of Cree women: Eliza Sunshine, her Nôhkom, Swan, and her daughter, Ella. As the three of them face suffering and adversity in different ways, from violent contact with settlers to residential school, they stay grounded in telling their stories and staying true to themselves, while recognizing that freedom doesn’t have the same meaning to everyone.

"Lovingly written to evoke a rich oral storytelling tradition, Eliza Sunshine guides readers through memories of adversity and triumph, illustrating the power of storytelling as a means of healing and overcoming struggle," wrote the jury.

"Drawing heavily from the author’s own family history, Eliza Sunshine is a masterful, deeply personal snapshot of a tragic chapter of Canadian history, navigating readers with unflinching honesty through a story of hope and strength."

items: How Michelle Good weaves her family’s truth through her fiction

blocks.text: Good is a Cree author and a member of the Red Pheasant Cree Nation in Saskatchewan. Her debut novel, Five Little Indians, won Canada Reads 2022, when it was championed by fashion journalist Christian Allaire. It also won the Governor General’s Literary Award for fiction, the Amazon First Novel Award and the Rakuten Kobo Emerging Writer Prize. Good is also the author of the nonfiction book Truth Telling.
Your Breath in Charcoal by Nicholas Herring

In Your Breath in Charcoal, Knickle, an Islander with no direction, is tasked with picking up an acquaintance’s brother from a mental health hospital in northern New Brunswick. When he gets there, the two decide to take this opportunity to go west and see if they can make a life in the big city of Toronto.

"Your Breath in Charcoal is a deeply philosophical narrative filled with pop culture references, literary allusions and mordant, quotable witticisms," wrote the jury. "With Knickle’s distinctive voice at its centre, Your Breath in Charcoal is a character study of a young man learning how to live his life, facing the complexities of the modern world in a riotously funny working-class odyssey filled with love, loss and profound hope."

items: ‘It doesn’t feel real’: P.E.I. writer Nicholas Herring reacts to Giller Prize longlist nod

blocks.text: Herring is an author, fisherman and carpenter based in Murray Harbour, P.E.I. His debut novel, Some Hellish, won the Atwood Gibson Writers’ Trust Fiction Prize.
LISTEN | Nicholas Herring on his second novel making the Giller longlist:
Mainstreet PEI10:52Nicholas Herring - Giller Prize
The Small Ones by Nazanine Hozar

The Small Ones is a novel about a group of boys and one small girl who are forced to become soldiers and martyrs in the Iran-Iraq war of the 1980s. The ragtag bunch find friendship and community in each other, even as they desperately hope to return home and back to safety.

"Using an intricate three-part structure, The Small Ones shifts the question in readers’ minds from what will happen to these children to how these children arrived in their circumstances, confronting us with the toll that war takes on the world’s most innocent citizens," wrote the jury.

"Restrained in its telling yet expansive in its meaning, The Small Ones transforms the experiences of children caught in conflict into a deeply affecting examination of sacrifice, power, survival and the enduring humanity of those whom society deems expendable."
Hozar is also the author of the novel Aria. She lives in Vancouver and teaches at Simon Fraser University.
Good People by Patmeena Sabit

Good People is a novel that follows the Sharaf family, who have finally achieved the American dream. They arrived years ago as refugees and worked hard to live in the fancy neighbourhood and send their kids to the best schools. But when a horrific tragedy befalls the family, people begin to wonder what is actually happening behind closed doors.

"Instead of telling their own story, it is left to a rotating cast of relatives, neighbours, friends and even strangers to account for the Sharaf family’s movements and motivations, chronicling the Sharafs’ rise to success from desperate, distrusted refugees to members of the wealthy and exclusive gated community of Virginia," said the jury.

"Using these observers to speculate on the pressures and dynamics endured by an immigrant family, Sabit ultimately leaves it to the reader to determine what has brought the Sharaf clan such scrutiny and attention. Are they victims of a tragic accident? Or are they the perpetrators of a terrible crime?"
Sabit is an author born in Kabul who currently lives in Toronto. Good People is her debut novel. It won the 2026 Westport Prize for Literature.

articles.title: NMC flags destructive fishing as 'serious threat' to PH food, livelihood security
articles.summary: The National Maritime Council (NMC) raised concern over reported destructive fishing in the country, saying it threatens not only the enforcement of fishing laws but also food and livelihood security.

blocks.text: Published October 5, 2026 5:53pm

The National Maritime Council (NMC) raised concern over reported destructive fishing in the country, saying it threatens not only the enforcement of fishing laws but also food and livelihood security.
“This is serious because fishing, especially when explosives are used, is not just a one-day problem,” NMC spokesperson Undersecretary Alexander Lopez said on Bagong Pilipinas Ngayon.
“It can damage the marine ecosystem, destroy our coral reefs, harm juvenile fish and affect our overall fish stocks, which our fisherfolk depend on for their livelihood.,” he added in Filipino.
On Sunday, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) said it received a report of dynamite fishing near Pag-asa Island.

However, Rear Admiral Jay Tarriela, the PCG spokesperson for the West Philippine Sea, said Philippine authorities were unable to respond to the suspected vessel after Chinese vessels blocked their operation.

The NMC acknowledged that the Philippines must uphold its sovereignty and rights over its territory, adding that a regular presence and enforcement operations are necessary in the West Philippine Sea to protect the country's rights and livelihoods.

“So this is not just about enforcing fishing laws. It is also a matter of food security, livelihood and the protection of our marine resources. That is why it is important to maintain a regular presence and conduct enforcement operations in the West Philippine Sea,” Lopez said.
Upholding rights
The NMC said the Philippines does not have to choose between firmly upholding its rights and maintaining diplomacy with China.
Lopez said what is needed is proper coordination, professionalism and keeping diplomatic channels open to report and resolve disputes.

“We do not need to choose between being firm and being peaceful. We will enforce our laws and defend our maritime rights, but we will do so with professionalism, restraint and proper coordination,” Lopez said.
“And in the same way, we use diplomatic channels and mechanisms to resolve concerns or disputes and prevent unnecessary escalation,” he added.

To strengthen and expedite responses to suspicious activities within the Philippines' exclusive economic zone, the NMC advised authorities to sustain maritime domain awareness and monitoring, strengthen coordination among concerned agencies, and document incidents to guide appropriate future responses.
The NMC assured the public and fisherfolk that it would continue to protect marine resources and local livelihoods.

“Our position is clear: we will not abandon our rights, we will not allow our marine resources to be destroyed, and we will not neglect our responsibility to enforce our laws, whether local or international,” Lopez said. — MCG, GMA News

articles.title: Mixed start for pre-Cop as just two non-Pacific leaders accept Australian invitation to climate summit
articles.summary: Anthony Albanese joins about 4,000 people in Fiji for preparatory meeting for year-ending Cop31 UN climate summit

blocks.text: The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, has declared it is “important that Pacific voices are heard” after landing in Fiji on Monday to attend his first UN climate summit since becoming prime minister more than four years ago.

Albanese joined about 4,000 people in Nadi for a preparatory meeting for the year-ending Cop31 UN climate summit in Turkey while facing criticism from his political opponents at home. Pre-Cop meetings are usually small and bureaucratic affairs, but this meeting has a double purpose: it is being held in the Pacific after Australia and regional leaders argued it would help bring global attention to the plight of countries most at risk from the climate crisis.

In achieving the latter goal, the meeting has been a mixed success. The Australian government invited national leaders to visit the low-lying atoll nation of Tuvalu, but distance, geopolitical ruptures and the expectation that leaders would prioritise a trip to the Turkish Mediterranean resort city of Antalya for more significant climate talks in a matter of weeks made that a difficult sell.

After declining to comment for days, the Australian government acknowledged on Monday that only 14 national leaders would make the trip to Tuvalu on Tuesday, and just two of those – Timor-Leste’s José Ramos-Horta and Mauritius’ Navin Ramgoolam – have travelled from beyond the Pacific.

The climate change minister, Chris Bowen, said they would be joined by EU climate commissioner, Wopke Hoekstra; the heads of the Asian Development Bank and the Green Climate Fund; UN climate chief, Simon Stiell; the incoming Cop president, Turkey’s Murat Kurum; and international journalists.

Australian opposition energy and emissions reduction spokesperson, Dan Tehan, said the number of leaders attending showed the Fiji conference was a waste of taxpayers’ money, a “farce” and Bowen’s “vanity project”.

Albanese said it would be an important meeting leading up to the Cop31 summit. “It is important that Pacific voices are heard, because the Pacific is the frontline of action on climate change,” he said. “For many of the nations represented by leaders here it is literally a threat to their very existence, which is why the world must act.”

At a welcome event on Monday night, the Fijian prime minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, said it was important that Pacific stories were told. He said the Pacific Ocean covered about a third of the Earth and “was the engine room of the world’s weather”. When the water was warm and an El Niño was gathering, it could cause “havoc in every country”.
“I’m not asking you to look at the Pacific with your sympathy,” Rabuka said. “I’m asking you to look at us as a bellwether, indicating the scale of the challenges that will come.”
after newsletter promotion

The Australian government has faced criticism for approving large new coal and gas developments, and calls for it to reject the largest coalmine development in New South Wales history after it received state approval last week.

Bowen told journalists on Monday the path transitioning away from fossil fuels was “to build more renewable energy to replace the need for fossil fuels”, and gave a speech arguing for greater electrification.

Fiji’s environment minister, Lynda Tabuya, said the country’s aim this week and at Cop31 was to keep the goal of limiting global heating 1.5C within reach, unlocking “faster, fairer” access to climate finance for developing countries and making ocean health a focus of climate action.

The UN Environment Programme warned last month the world would overshoot the 1.5C global heating goal included in the Paris agreement, and said every fraction of a degree of temperature rise would intensify destructive extreme weather, glacier melt, ecosystem loss, and coastal submersion.

articles.title: As rising seas threaten low-lying Pacific Islands, regional leaders call on the world to take climate more seriously
articles.summary: From rising seas to a growing pressure for climate justice, Pacific island nations have invited world leaders to Tuvalu to highlight the very real consequences of burning fossil fuels that heat the…

image.caption: Climate-driven sea level rise is posing an existential threat to Pacific Island nations.Image: Ashley Cooper/Global Warming Images/picture alliance

blocks.text: For Pacific islanders, the ocean provides food, jobs, and a deep connection to culture and identity. But climate change is turning it into a threat, because as global temperatures rise, so do sea levels.

"When there's a low tide, you'll actually see foundations of homes, you see burial grounds of your ancestors...," said Anne Rasmussen, lead climate negotiator for the Association of Small Island States (AOSIS), adding that higher seas are making some land uninhabitable.

This week, a handful of world leaders are in Fiji with ministers and climate negotiators from around 60 countries to discuss the outstanding issues surrounding the UN-led international climate conference that kicks off in Turkey next month.
Pacific leaders see these talks ahead of COP31 as an opportunity to highlight the increasing urgency facing their low-lying islands.

"It's actually to bring the people who are continuing to turn a blind eye and deaf ears to the communities of the vulnerable islands to these effects," Rasmussen told DW, emphasizing the importance of holding these talks in the Pacific.

"It showcases the vulnerability. It showcases the impacts that are already happening. And it also brings the community, the real people at the front line, to participate in these pre-COPs," she added.
On the frontlines of climate change

Leaders attending the event will first travel to the island of Tuvalu, which scientists predict could be one of the first countries to become inhabitable due to rising sea levels caused by human-driven climate change.

blocks.caption: Tuvalau Prime Minister Feleti Teo addressed delegates at the United Nations General Assembly about the fate of his country due to climate changeImage: Seth Wenig/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: At the UN General Assembly last month, Tuvalu Prime Minister Feleti Teo told delegates that sea level rise is a "present reality."
"Tuvalu's message is clear: the world must act now decisively, collectively and with urgency to protect the future for generations to come."
At an average of just two meters above sea level, the archipelago has faced more frequent and severe flooding as water levels have risen.

"Having back-to-back hurricanes and storms, having back-to-back significant floods...it really sets back countries and affects communities,” Rasmussen, who comes from the Pacific island of Samoa, told DW. "People are losing their homes."

She also said rising sea levels are contaminating freshwater sources with salt, which threatens crops. In addition, hotter oceans mean corals lose the algae they rely on to survive, causing them to bleach and become less able to accommodate the diverse marine life that local populations rely on for their income.
Tuvalu is sinking — what's next for residents?
Overshooting agreed limits on temperature rise

Although only few leaders from outside the region are expected at the conference, negotiators from countries including Germany, Mexico and South Korea will be present. Efforts to limit planetary heating are expected to be high on the agenda.

Pacific leaders are pushing for a renewed commitment to keep global temperature rise capped to 1.5 degrees (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) — a limit that was agreed on by world leaders at the Paris climate conference in 2015.

A UN report released in September said under a best-case scenario, temperatures were likely to reach at least 1.8 degrees Celsius (3.2 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels. The study added that it is still possible to "bring temperatures down".

Natasha Green, Australia country lead for climate think-tank E3G , said small island and least developing states are calling for countries to work together to enable vulnerable nations to "adapt and build resilience to the worsening impacts of climate change".
Tricky questions of climate finance

A key issue at this week's talks will be climate finance. Poorer nations, which have done little to contribute to rising global temperatures, yet are feeling some of the worst impacts, have long called on richer, higher-emitting countries to provide more money to help them adapt to a hotter world.

Laura Schäfer, international climate policy head of division at environment and human rights nonprofit, Germanwatch, said she would like to see Australia, who holds the COP presidency, "address tricky questions."
Such as "how to include carbon majors, including the big fossil [fuel] industry in paying for climate damages like the ones we have just seen in Nepal."

blocks.caption: Thousands of people are still missing in Nepal following climate-fueled severe floods.Image: Tyrone Siu/REUTERS

blocks.text: Also on the agenda will be a the non-use of fossil fuels for creating energy. At the 2023 climate conference, countries agreed for the first time to move towards a future that doesn’t rely on oil, gas and coal. Since then, however, there has been little progress.
Earlier this year just under 60 states took part in the first International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels.

Scientists say an end to burning these polluting sources of energy is the only way to bring global temperature levels back under agreed limits. And thereby prevent some of the worst impacts of climate change — like the rising sea levels affecting island states and coastline communities.
"It's really important that the COPs continue to progress and elevate the commitment [...] to transition away from fossil fuels," said Green.
Edit: Tamsin Walker

articles.title: German and US scientists win Nobel Prize in medicine for research on brain activity
articles.summary: The trio won the award for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics. This neurobiology tool has provided new insights into how we might treat blindness, depression,…

image.caption: Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann und Georg NagelImage: Hidenori Nagai/AP//Soeren Stache/dpa//Christian Wiese/Uni Würzburg/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: The Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine 2026 has gone to Karl Deisseroth, Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, the academy announced on Monday.

The trio won the award for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics, which combines the methods of optics and genetics to create a form of non-invasive stimulation of neurons.

The Nobel Assembly said that optogenetics has fundamentally altered our understanding of the brain, as researchers have been "able to reveal neural circuits governing specific memories, feelings, and behaviors relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders."

"The impact of optogenetics extends far beyond understanding the healthy brain, it has also helped revealed how brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression, addiction and dementia," Abdel El Manira, Nobel committee member and professor of neuroscience, said after the announcement was made.

In clinical medicine, researchers are using the method in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. Researchers hope that the field could lead to treatments for neurological and sensory disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
Who are the winners?

Peter Hegemann Hegemann is considered to be the leading expert in photobiology and one of the founding fathers of optogenetics. He is a professor of neuroscience at the Humboldt University of Berlin, Germany.

Georg Nagel is a biophysicist and professor at of neurophysiology at the University of Würzburg, Germany. Karl Deisseroth is a professor of bioengineering and of psychiatry and behavioral sciences at Stanford University in the US.

The trio came togther as Hegemann explored how a single-celled type of green algae could swim toward light. He and Nagel discovered a particular protein that, when illuminated by blue light, opens a channel to create an electrical impulse. Putting that protein into other cells makes them light-sensitive.
Deisseroth then joined in to work with the gene that controls that protein to create a light-controlled switch for nerve cells in the brains of living mice.
Medicine is the first of Nobels announced this week
The award for medicine is the first Nobel prize to be awarded this week, with laureates set to be named in physics, chemistry, literature and peace in the days up to Friday.
Last year's prize was awarded jointly to Mary Brunkow and Fred Ramsdell of the United States and Shimun Sakaguchi of Japan for "for their discoveries concerning peripheral immune tolerance."
The prizes will be presented at ceremonies in Stockholm, Sweden on December 10.
Each prize carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor, which is equivalent to just over €1 million or $1.2 million.

articles.title: Quebec poised to elect separatists to power for first time more than decade
articles.summary:
Parti Québécois promises to hold independence referendum in Canada’s French-speaking region by 2028

Voters in Quebec are going to the polls in provincial elections which will probably result…

blocks.text: Voters in Quebec are going to the polls in provincial elections which will probably result in victory for a party that has promised to hold a referendum on independence from Canada within the next two years.

If polls are correct, the Parti Québécois (PQ) will form the government of the province of roughly nine million, the first time that the separatist movement will have gained power in the French-speaking region for more than a decade.
A PQ victory in Monday’s election would also be likely to trigger a return to pitched battles over questions of language and identity between Quebec and the federal government.

Long considered a declining force in Quebec politics, the PQ owes its resurgence to party leader Paul St-Pierre Plamondon. The 49-year-old Oxford-educated lawyer and polyglot has positioned himself as a TikToking gen-X rebuttal to François Legault, Quebec’s long-serving Premier until he resigned early this year.

blocks.caption: Paul St-Pierre Plamondon is greeted by his children and partner ahead of a leaders debate in Montreal in September. Photograph: Canadian Press/Shutterstock

blocks.text: Analysts say that St-Pierre Plamondon’s electoral success is not because he is a separatist – the majority of voters do not support an independent Quebec – but because of his rightwing take on red-meat identity issues.

He has blamed immigrants for Quebec’s overflowing schools, increased crime and skyrocketing housing prices, while promising to slash immigration levels and ban “conspicuous” religious symbols from the bodies of teachers and their students. He has derided his critics from the leftist Quebec Solidaire party as “woke”, and has taken to repeating the talking points of hard-right columnists.

Many in the province agree with St-Pierre Plamondon’s rhetoric, even though it strays from PQ’s social democratic roots, according to radio host Patrick Lagacé. “Most Quebecers traditionally see themselves as being on the left. Increasingly, though, they are on the right when it comes to social issues like systemic racism and accommodation of religious behaviour. They’ve hardened on these issues, and don’t see themselves in the left’s recent fixation on identity issues,” Lagacé said.

The biggest drag on St-Pierre Plamondon’s popularity has been his oft-repeated promise to hold a referendum during the first mandate of a PQ government. An overwhelming majority of Quebecers don’t want such a thing any time soon – particularly with Canada locked in a trade war with the US. The province mostly voted for Liberal leader Mark Carney over the separatist Bloc Québécois in last year’s federal election, expressly because of Carney’s “elbows up” posturing against the Trump administration.

But for the PQ, Donald Trump was at first a curse, then a gift. Early in the campaign, St-Pierre Plamondon said he wouldn’t hold a referendum as long as Trump was in power, defusing the issue and allowing St-Pierre Plamondon to concentrate on attacking immigration and immigrants.

The party has also benefited from a four-way race for the right-leaning nationalist vote beyond the reliably Liberal fiefdom of Montreal – particularly around Quebec city, where the upstart Parti Conservateur du Québec has made significant inroads. “The Parti Québécois is benefiting from a massive vote split because those who don’t like the PQ don’t agree on who to vote for,” said poll analyst Philippe Fournier.

Though the PQ will probably form the next provincial government, it remains unclear what sort of mandate it will have. Polls have the party hovering at roughly 30%, somewhat below the likely threshold for a majority government.

In any case, St-Pierre Plamondon is laying the groundwork for confrontation with the federal government. He has mused about defunding the office of Quebec’s lieutenant-governor (the British Crown’s representative in the province) and promised to introduce a law to abolish the province’s ties with the monarchy, which separatists see as the ultimate symbol of oppression of Canada’s French minority.

St-Pierre Plamondon also tore into Carney, after the prime minister said the government will probably increase immigration rates in the country. Doing so, St-Pierre Plamondon said, was an “abuse of power” that would have further nefarious effects on French-language services in Quebec.
For a man who trades on his relative youthfulness, St-Pierre Plamondon’s attacks on the monarchy have the whiff of anachronism – the kind of thing the PQ did in its 1970-era heyday.

Attacking the federal government is similarly outdated, and potentially risky for St-Pierre Plamondon. Carney remains popular in Quebec, and is likely to remain so, at least until the existential threat of Trump recedes.

articles.title: Sass Jordan, Canadian rock singer-songwriter, dies aged 65
articles.summary:
Musician who had hit albums with Racine and Rats later became a judge on six seasons of Canadian Idol

Sass Jordan, the singer-songwriter who became a significant success in Canada’s rock…

blocks.text: Sass Jordan, the singer-songwriter who became a significant success in Canada’s rock scene in the 1990s before starring as a judge on Canadian Idol, has died aged 65.

No cause of death has been given. A statement on social media said she died on 2 October “surrounded by her loving family … She remains in our hearts, an inimitable force of nature. An irreplaceable being of light and joy!”

Born in Birmingham, England, in 1960, Jordan moved to Montreal as a child when her French academic father took a position at the city’s Concordia University. She began performing in her teens, and by her 20s was recording with a range of Montreal acts: she wrote a song for singer Michael Breen that became a Canadian Top 40 hit.

By 1988 she was signed to Atlantic Records, who released her debut album Tell Somebody, with two singles – the title track and Double Trouble – charting just outside the Canadian Top 10. The following year she won a Juno (the Canadian equivalent of the Grammys) for most promising female vocalist.

Her 1992 album Racine contained four Canadian Top 20 hits and, coupled with a move to Los Angeles, a new label in RCA, and an appearance on the bestselling soundtrack to The Bodyguard broke Jordan into a wider US market. Sun’s Gonna Rise, from 1994 album Rats, became her only US Hot 100 hit, and her biggest hit in Canada, reaching No 7. Taylor Hawkins, later the drummer for Foo Fighters, was her live drummer during this period.

Her RCA deal ended and Jordan later voiced disappointment in the glossy sound of her next couple of albums, but her career received a boost from being a judge on the six seasons of TV talent show Canadian Idol, and she returned to recording with 2006’s You Get What You Give. In 2001 she also performed as Janis Joplin in the off-Broadway musical Love, Janis.
She later embraced a bluesier sound, with 2020 album Rebel Moon Blues reaching the top five of the US blues chart, followed by her most recent studio recording, 2022’s Bitches Blues.
In September, Jordan cancelled tour dates, citing “a serious medical condition”.

articles.summary: More than a third of Israelis have shown symptoms of mental health conditions, a report found. Three years after the October 7 attack, the country's health system is still struggling to come to terms…

image.caption: Almost 400 people were murdered at the Nova festival in IsraelImage: Ronen Zvulun/REUTERS

blocks.text: Warning: This article contains references to death by suicide that some readers may find disturbing.
As October 7's third anniversary approaches, Ronen Shalev's body tells him something's coming.
"You start shivering," he tells DW. "It's not just one day and you move on. We have many graves to visit, many families to meet. It's a difficult time and you feel it in your body."

Both of his children attended the Nova Party in Israel's south, where almost 400 people were killed in a terrorist attack carried out by Palestinian militant group Hamas and its affiliates in Gaza. In total, roughly 1,200 people were killed in the attack and around 250 were taken hostage.
The attack triggered the war in Gaza, during which Israel has killed tens of thousands of Palestinians and displaced much of the territory's population.
Shalev's son, Roee, was shot and hospitalized, but he survived. Roee's partner, Mapal Adam, was killed in front of his eyes. Shalev's daughter, Lior, also made it out.
Shortly after that day, Shalev's wife Gavriela went missing, before her body was found in a burned car with a goodbye letter. "She couldn't handle the sorrow from that day," Shalev says.

At the same time, his son Roee's post-traumatic symptoms started emerging, mostly in the form of extreme mood swings. "He went to treatment to please me, but he didn't really believe in it. He thought he was OK, that he was strong," Shalev remembers.
Two years after Gavriela's death, Roee couldn't take it anymore, either.
"I'm alive, but I'm dead within," Roee wrote in his goodbye message, which he posted on his Instagram account. "I'm sorry."
A country in post-traumatic state
Since October 2023, Israel has been grappling with a mental health crisis of unprecedented scale.

According to a report by Israel's State Comptroller from February 2025, some 39% of the Israeli public reported suffering from post-traumatic symptoms, depression, anxiety or a combination of the three, on a medium or severe level.

This amounts to some 3 million people, 600,000 of whom could suffer severely. However, the report also found that the number of people receiving mental health treatment had only risen by 1% since October 7, 2023, a difference of around 60,000 people.
Among the affected groups are survivors of the attack, as well as people evacuated from their homes in Israel's south and north due to the war.

Noga Dagan-Buzaglo is a researcher with the Adva Center, a think tank focusing on inequality in Israeli society. She wrote an extensive paper about Israel's mental health system and its challenges post-October 7.
She tells DW that while the country's mental health budget did increase due to the war, it was too little, too late, as the health system faced an ongoing crisis that was not handled properly.
"The biggest challenge is convincing people to work in Israel's public mental health system, both due to lower wages in comparison to the private sector and due to an overload of work," she says.
Survivors mourn victims of October 7 music festival killings
Sedatives often the go-to solution

The current situation affects mental health professionals, too. Research by the University of Haifa found that 84% of the therapists who treated people affected by the October 7 attack showed traumatic symptoms themselves, and some 45% of them said they feel mentally exhausted.

Israel's Health Ministry has repeatedly said it has increased funding and job openings for the country's public mental health system, but staffing shortages remain, especially in peripheral regions in the far north and south.

Because of these issues, the report said waiting times for treatment through Israel's public healthcare system were longer than six months. In some cases, Dagan-Buzaglo says, patients had to wait more than a year before receiving help.

Mental health NGOs and volunteers try to fill the gaps, often struggling themselves under the workload. This also leads to an increased use of prescription medications. Some people turn to substances like alcohol and drugs.
The Israeli Ministry of Health said earlier this year that it had registered a rise of between 13% and 17% in the prescription of sedatives, sleep aids and antidepressants.

Those who suffer from the situation the most are the ones who cannot afford to pay a private therapist. Dagan-Buzaglo labels the Israeli public health system's response to the situation as "simply bad."

blocks.caption: Soldiers are one of the groups affected by Israel's mental health crisisImage: Avi Ohayon/REUTERS

blocks.text: Soldiers at risk
Combat soldiers have received a special focus when it comes to Israel's mental health crisis.

Statistics published by the Israeli parliament and the IDF suggest a sharp rise of suicide cases among reservists: from a maximum of one annual case in the six years preceding the war to 11 cases in 2024, as well as nine cases investigated as suspected suicides in 2025. This does not include ex-soldiers who committed suicide due to trauma after the end of their service.

Dagan-Buzaglo, a researcher at the Adva Center, says that while professionals receive better pay and conditions working for the army, the lack of personnel is still apparent. "In the army, too, the length and quality of treatment are by far not at an adequate level."

To start solving the problem for both civilians and soldiers, she believes the system needs more support. "We have to acknowledge the fact that trauma is not over after a year. This means investing money."
Breaking the taboo
Ronen Shalev holds regular lectures and talks about the importance of mental health, often to groups of soldiers. He believes this is the best way to continue his son's legacy of fighting to live on.
Shalev, who himself was diagnosed with post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), says he made a choice to live his life to its fullest.

His message: The taboo regarding suicidality — which still exists across Israeli society — needs to be broken. "This is especially true regarding those who say they are strong. They're the scary ones as they're less likely to receive treatment."
For Shalev, speaking publicly about his family's experience has become part of his own recovery — and a way to encourage others to seek help before they reach a crisis point.
"Life, with all its pain, is still worth deciding in favor of," he said.
October 7 survivors recall attacks on Kibbutz Nir Oz

If you are suffering from serious emotional strain or suicidal thoughts, do not hesitate to seek professional help. You can find information on where to find such help, no matter where you live in the world, at this website: https://befrienders.org/
