articles.title: Israel observes October 7 anniversary with national memorial day
articles.summary: Israel is holding memorial ceremonies nationwide for those killed in the October 7, 2023 Hamas terror attacks and soldiers who died in the ensuing war.

image.caption: The Hamas terror attacks on October 7, 2023, resulted in over 1,200 deaths and sparked nearly three years of an ongoing Israeli military campaign in Gaza [FILE: October 7, 2025]Image: Ahmad Gharabli/AFP

blocks.text: Israelis observing a national memorial day on Monday for those killed in the October 7, 2023 Hamas terror attacks and the soldiers who died in the Gaza war, Israeli media reported.

Two state ceremonies are being held at Mount Herzl in Jerusalem, where President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and other senior officials are expected to attend, The Jerusalem Post reported.
More memorial events, rallies and ceremonies are planned across the country with schools, municipalities and communities also holding events throughout the day.

Flags at state institutions, police stations, prisons and military bases were lowered to half-mast, reports said. The memorial fell on October 5 this year due to the Hebrew calendar, which is lunisolar.
October 7 terror attacks set of chain of events

The Hamas terror attack on October 7 killed some 1,200 people in Israel, with the Palestinian militant also taking another 251 hostages into Gaza. It was the single deadliest day for Jewish people since the Holocaust.
The October 7, 2023, attacks had massive consequences not only for Israeli society but also for Palestinians in Gaza, where Hamas had maintained power since the territory last held elections in 2006.

Following the Hamas attacks, the Israeli military began a war targeting Hamas in Gaza. The European Union, as well as the United States, Germany, and other countries, classify Hamas as a terrorist organization.
Israel's war on Hamas left more than 73,650 Palestinians dead in Gaza , most of them civilians, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.

articles.title: 'Not again': Arrest of US marine for murder reignites protests in Japan's Okinawa
articles.summary: For many locals on this island, the arrest has brought decades of frustration back to the fore.

blocks.text: For many Okinawa locals, the arrest of a US soldier accused of robbing and killing a woman in a hotel room has reignited decades of frustration over crimes involving US military personnel there.
"Honestly my first reaction was, 'Not again,'" 52-year-old longtime Okinawa resident Ai Sato told the BBC.

"Nothing has changed since I was a child. How many times are we going to repeat the same thing, create more victims, cause their families to suffer, and ultimately, cause the people of Okinawa to grieve?"
Akemi Oshiro, a 62-year-old Ginowan resident shared similar sentiments.
"I know we shouldn't get used to terrible things like this, but because they keep happening, I've stopped being surprised," she told the BBC.
Okinawa hosts the largest US military presence in Japan. It is home to several US military bases and tens of thousands of American troops.

US Marine Lance Corporal Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, was arrested by Japanese police on Sunday. Police say an investigation is underway and that Ballard is in Japanese custody because the alleged crime was unrelated to official military duties.

Whether a US service member is acting in the performance of official duty, external or not can determine which country has primary jurisdiction. When Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect is under US custody, they can retain custody until Japan brings charges.
Ballard was assigned to III Marine Expeditionary Force and stationed at Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City.
The Okinawa prefectural police say 39-year-old Anna Yagi was found dead early 3 October in a hotel room in Naha.

Security footage allegedly shows a man believed to be the suspect entering the hotel with the woman and leaving alone with her belongings. Local media citing police have reported that Yagi appeared to have been strangled with a cord.
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi registered an official protest with Washington. But residents like Sato feel that's far from enough.
"I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades -- that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously."

"I want Prime Minister Takaichi to call President Trump directly, someone with whom she has been emphasizing as having a close relationship with, and discuss concrete measures to prevent this from happening yet again," she said.

Following news of the suspected murder, people in Japan have been voicing anger with some 100 people protesting in both Naha and Tokyo. Others took to social media expressing their outrage and demanding justice with one user saying: "Enough is enough."
Over the past few years, a number of accidents and crimes have led to growing local opposition to the US presence on the island.

The 2016 rape and murder of a 20-year-old local woman saw tens of thousands of protesters demonstrate against the heavy US presence there. A former US marine subsequently received a life sentence for the crime.

The US currently has about 55,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, with the heaviest concentration based on the tropical island prefecture. Okinawa is one of the country's smallest prefectures by size, but 70% of the land used exclusively by the US military in Japan is located there.

In 1972, Okinawa prefecture was returned to Japanese control after United States forces occupied the islands at the end of the Second World War. Since then, there have been 6,409 arrests for criminal offenses related to US military personnel, according to Okinawa Prefectural Government.

Locals say the significant US presence has stirred resentment over a number of issues from crimes including rapes, assaults, and drunk-driving accidents to local disturbances such as noise and aircraft crashes.
In 1995, three US servicemen abducted, beat, and raped a 12-year-old schoolgirl as she walked home from a stationery store.
In 2025, a US Marine was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a Japanese woman.
"Even 80 yeas after the war, Okinawa where we live is a place that is so unnerving," 48-year-old mother of two boys Hitomi Miyagi told the BBC.
"We will not stop raising our voices hoping for an Okinawa, where we can live in peace."

articles.title: Extreme heat warnings issued for parts of southern California
articles.summary:
Temperatures in US state forecast to hit high 30s celsius this week, while regions in Indonesia grapple with wildfires

The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings…

blocks.text: The National Weather Service in the US has issued extreme heat warnings for parts of southern California, including Los Angeles, until Thursday, as temperatures are expected to hit the high 30s celsius. Burbank, a suburb north of Los Angeles, recorded 39C on Saturday, a few degrees shy of the October record for the region set in 1987. A persistent area of high pressure will remain in place this week, leading to further hazardous hot weather and increased fire risk.

Parts of Indonesia are in the midst of an extreme wildfire season, which has peaked over the past month. Western Kalimantan (Borneo) and southern Sumatra have been particularly badly affected. The lack of rainfall has dried the usually water-logged tropical soils, meaning that fires have been able to spread quickly, above and below the surface. Indonesia’s soils are also extremely rich in peat, meaning that the smoke produced from the fires contain higher levels of toxic gases such as sulphur dioxide and carbon monoxide. Cities in surrounding areas and as far as Malaysia and Singapore have experienced reduced air quality in recent weeks as a result. Drought and wildfires are more common in this part of the world during El Niño events owing to suppressed thunderstorm activity.

blocks.caption: Indonesian firefighters work to extinguish wildfires near a residential area in Palembang, south Sumatra. Photograph: Muhammad Fajri/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: On the flip side, El Niño is contributing to an extremely active period for tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean. After recent hurricanes in the eastern half of the basin, Super Typhoon Choi-Wan is now active and a category 4 typhoon to the south-east of Japan, while on a strengthening trend. After developing on 30 September, Choi-Wan moved through the Northern Mariana Islands as a tropical storm, causing power outages on the island of Tinian, forcing the closure of schools and government offices. Choi-Wan underwent rapid intensification after clearing the islands on Sunday, and as of Sunday night has sustained winds of 150mph, and gusts of up to 180mph. The system is expected to curve away from mainland Japan and areas affected by Typhoon Dujuan last month, while steadily weakening over the coming week.

articles.title: £800m in, £800m out - Why Man City scandal shines light on Man Utd finances
articles.summary: Manchester City's owners have been found guilty of injecting money into the club. At Manchester United, fans are frustrated at how much has been taken out.

blocks.text: United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."
This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.
Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.
Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.

In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn.
To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m.

Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027. United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.

When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.
Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.
Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.

In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.

While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.

Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.
When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.

Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.

It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.
In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.
Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.
The negativity around Manchester City's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.

Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.

In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a £10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.
When Carrick sends his team out against bottom-club Tottenham at Old Trafford on 10 October, they will be attempting to drag themselves up from 12th place in the table.
The overall target is undefined, but it is pretty clear Champions League qualification will be a significant part of it.

articles.title: Cold reality: Canadian troops struggle in Alaska as military relearns Arctic warfare

image.caption: Members of 3rd Battalion Royal Canadian Regiment attend to a casualty at Yukon Training Area, Alaska, in February. (Pte. Felix Chagnon/Department of National Defence.)

blocks.text: A series of internal Department of National Defence documents suggest Canadian troops were ill-prepared and occasionally ill-equipped for the harsh conditions they faced last winter during a major training exercise with American forces in Alaska.
The evaluation reports, obtained by CBC News, show the military has a lot to learn and a long way to go to rebuild its capability to defend the Arctic.

The training involved over 400 members of the 3rd Battalion Royal Canadian Regiment (3RCR) which was folded into a much larger U.S. Army brigade during Exercise Global Response in February at the Joint Pacific Multinational Readiness Center, north of Fairbanks, Alaska.

The Carney government has committed to an almost year-round presence in the Far North and the reports indicate, among other things, that troops will need to learn to rely less on technology and more on basic skills in order to fight and survive, according to defence experts.

items: Cold front: Inside NATO's race to secure the Arctic

blocks.text: Separate Canadian and American evaluations were prepared and both show a litany of concerns that raise questions about how prepared troops and their equipment are to fight in harsh conditions, where the temperatures plunge below –30 C.

"Throughout their stay in the waiting area the Coy [Company] consistently demonstrated a lack of preparations needed to live in Arctic conditions," said an undated Canadian evaluation, which assessed individual companies within the battalion.
Carney's $35B plan is 'a start' for Arctic security: former Canadian top soldier
The report was critical of a recent initiative which allowed the regiment to purchase off-the-shelf civilian equipment to augment military cold-weather gear — something that created problems.

"This was evident when observing soldiers attempting to remedy issues with a Coleman stove and lanterns or watching them attempt to set up a 10-man tent," said the evaluation, obtained by CBC News. It said that among some Canadian units there was a "lack of emphasis on basic winter soldiering skills."
In an interview, Lt.-Col. Aaron Corey, the commander of 3RCR, disagreed and said his troops trained for winter conditions for a year before the Alaska training deployment.
"Every soldier to go up on that exercise had to be a cold weather operator qualified," Corey said.
"All of our leaders from the sections and up, we received cold weather leader training and then we had Arctic operations advisers that were sprinkled into the battalion as well."

He added the battalion "put a lot of effort into preparations for this exercise in the year preceding it and to get back to a level of winter warfare — or Arctic warfare — that we haven't seen in a few years."
Canadian soldiers have wrestled with the problem of fighting in extreme cold for decades, and even prepared for the possibility of Soviet attack across the polar region during the early Cold War.

The Alaskan exercise reports did note that despite the challenges — and as many as 30 troops suffering various levels of frostbite — the battalion was successful in the exercise by capturing its training objectives.
Corey said troops learned valuable lessons, most notably how they have to slow down and take the weather into account, more so than when they are on operations in other parts of the world.

"We had the enemy and the weather, which was a greater enemy in most cases," Corey said. "So we had to slow down. We had to make sure that our troops had warming cycles. We had to slow down because the kit and equipment you're carrying is heavier. We had to slow down because there's more energy being exerted as you fight your way through the muskeg or up the mountains."
The Ottawa Citizen previously reported on the frostbite casualties. The documents obtained by CBC News, however, paint a broader picture of the challenges faced by the regiment.
One document noted how "several gaps emerged regarding the medical team's understanding of their required tasks" during the exercise.

items: Canadian Coast Guard tests Arctic surveillance drone as air force delivery stalls
Military satellite deal could set stage for new battle over cabinet secrecy

blocks.text: The medics thought they were only on standby to treat real casualties, not participate in the training scenario, said an undated evaluation prepared for the health services branch. On three occasions some of them were seen using personal phones for long calls, giving away their positions to the enemy.

It was also noted that the medical team was only given a four-hour professional development seminar on Arctic medicine principles rather than a five-day U.S.-led course at the Arctic medicine simulation centre.

Chief Warrant Officer Robert McSpadden, the regimental sergeant major for 3RCR, said he found the medical team to be outstanding, especially when it came to treating the frostbite casualties. He said he couldn't speak to the training decisions.

The Canadians also ran into problems with the rapid cold weather draining batteries for their drones, leaving in some cases only 10 minutes of flying time. There were problems with communications because of the absence of satellites so far north.

The separate American assessment, prepared by the Ted Stevens Center for Arctic Security Studies and published online, noted how U.S. units experienced similar difficulties. It pointed to basic preparation problems such as a lack of snowclearing equipment and a shortage of fuel to keep engines running in order to prevent them from freezing.

Retired colonel Pierre Leblanc, who served in the Far North in command positions in the late 1990s, said it's been almost a generation since Canadian troops were present in large numbers in the Arctic and many skills will have to be relearned.
Who’s defending Canada’s Arctic?
"It's a different world," said Leblanc, who noted the unpredictability of the weather and the vast distances made it the most challenging place to operate he'd ever encountered.
He used the example of having to dispatch a repair team to a North Warning System radar location during his tenure.
It was supposed to be a simple job, lasting only a few hours. The team was stuck there for 21 days, Leblanc said.
Today's high-tech, web-enabled, satellite-tethered military needs a serious back-to-basics approach in a place where technology can't be counted on, he said.
"If you rely too much on it, you're going to very quickly have a problem. Have to be able to work with very, very basic systems," said Leblanc.
Rob Huebert, an Arctic defence expert at the University of Calgary, said the Canadian military in the 1950s and 60s was expert at training and fighting in the Far North.
There was, at the time, the capacity to move more than 1,000 troops and their equipment at short notice anywhere in Canada.

For example, in February 1950, more than 5,000 Canadian and American troops took part in Exercise Sweetbriar along the Alaska Highway between Whitehorse and Alaska, specifically testing how combined forces could move, fight and sustain themselves in Arctic conditions.

Canadian troops subsequently trained for the possibility of Soviet airborne attacks in the North, while the military experimented with clothing, vehicles, communications, mobility and survival techniques. In the 1970s, the Canadian Airborne Regiment practised its own parachute assaults at places including Coral Harbour and Inuvik.
Huebert acknowledged the increase in winter exercises that the Carney government has enabled through its increase in defence spending. But he says they are a smaller scale.

items: Carney announces $35B for defence, infrastructure in Canada's North

blocks.text: "You can't just simply say, we know how to do this with small units and we can magically do it with big units," Huebert said.
It's also a mindset problem, he added.

Several years ago the country's former top military commander, retired general Walt Natynczyk, quipped that if the Russians ever invaded Canada's Arctic, the first thing he'd do is launch a search and rescue operation.
"I really think that that was a very unfortunate comment," said Huebert, who added it established the notion that troops wouldn't have to fight in the Far North.

"The Russians know how to fight in the North. We would be much better off if General Natynczyk, at that time, had actually said there are growing signs that the Russians are not the friends that we thought they were."

articles.title: The mental health of young men is declining. Experts warn it could get worse
articles.summary: The federal government launched a nationwide consultation earlier this year to try and determine why boys and men’s health is suffering. Data they reported on shows a country of young men…

image.caption: Nick Cholmsky, who grew up in Ottawa, experienced depression as a teen. He says online messaging encourages boys and men to stay silent about their psychological struggles. (CBC)

blocks.text: Young men are struggling. Can Canada fix the problem?
On the surface, Nick Cholmsky looked like a thriving teenager.
Growing up in Ottawa, he says he was athletic and heavily involved in basketball, had friends and a close relationship with his family.
But underneath all that he says he was deeply depressed. The symptoms began in middle school and became much worse by Grade 11.
At 16, he had begun entertaining suicidal thoughts.

Even as his depression and anxiety grew stronger, Cholmsky believed he couldn’t say anything, because "being a man" meant pushing negative thoughts down, and that any sign of weakness would cause him shame.
"Looking back, so much of that [congenial attitude] was for sure just a performance, me acting the way I thought I was supposed to act as a man," said Cholmsky, now 21.
There’s a common problem everywhere and it’s how men and boys are feeling. And they are not feeling great.- Federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel

Earlier this year, the federal government reported on a wide range of data showing that the mental health of young men has deteriorated since 2012. Between 2012 and 2022, the number of men aged 15 to 24 who self-reported mood disorders increased from 11 per cent to 16 per cent, while self-reported generalized anxiety disorders increased from four per cent to 10 per cent.
Those who reported their mental health as "very good" or "excellent" plummeted from 70 per cent to 52 per cent in that same time period.
A separate report shows that men are three times as likely as women to commit suicide and that it's the second-leading cause of death in boys aged 15 to 34 (after unintentional injuries).
"There’s a common problem everywhere and it’s how men and boys are feeling. And they are not feeling great," federal Health Minister Marjorie Michel told CBC News.
"There is a lot of anxiety [about] their role as men and boys."
Social media use, gambling major issues
Research implicates a variety of factors in men’s depression, most prominently social isolation, social media use and online sports betting.

Data from the Canadian Medical Association Journal shows a huge rise in young men calling helplines with gambling addictions. (Health Canada reports men are three times more likely than women to have a gambling problem.)
Canada legalized single-event sports betting in 2021. In 2022, Ontario became the first province to allow private companies to operate alongside government-regulated industry.

A separate report released this month by the Institute for Clinical Evaluation Sciences (ICES) showed that since 2022, emergency room visits for gambling disorders had doubled — largely with young men showing up in a psychological crisis, such as suicidal ideation or psychosis, as a result of gambling losses.
"The gambling stats didn’t surprise me at all when I heard them," said Cholmsky. "I saw kids in middle school gambling."
Scott Galloway on male potential
Whether the stress is the result of gambling or something else, Cholmsky says online messaging encourages boys and men to stay silent.
"When I was going through some of my worst mental health times, I was online a lot and it was really the height of Andrew Tate," Cholmsky said.

The U.S.-born Tate is one of the best-known influencers in the manosphere, famous for espousing strict rules for being an alpha male, such as maximizing fitness, maintaining control over relationships and emotions and making as much money as possible.
He retains a large following despite being in U.S. detention on multiple criminal charges, including sex trafficking.
"[Tate's] message, and a lot of that manosphere messaging for boys, is 'be a man, be tough, make lots of money,'" Cholmsky said.

There are also trends like "looksmaxxing." Influencer Braden Peters, also known as Clavicular, has amassed a huge following telling young boys sometimes to smash their own faces with hammers to be more conventionally beautiful. His content has more than 40 million likes. Peters was charged with rape last month.
Experts warn dangerous role models like this can have real-world impacts.

"The manosphere is radicalizing young boys who don’t know where they fit — and that should concern us all," said John Oliffe, Canada research chair in men’s health promotion at the University of British Columbia.

items: What to know about Cornell's alleged frat house gang-rape case and the 'Cornell 7'
What Cornell's alleged rape case and the Hockey Canada trial's striking parallels reveal

blocks.text: Oliffe says this was "amplified" by the earliest parts of the COVID-19 pandemic when global lockdowns increased isolation and the loss of social connection. Vulnerable teenagers often found themselves lost online.
"There continues to be a whole world of pain in some of that unregulated content," Oliffe said.

Adam Kunder, a 33-year-old former firefighter who lives in Toronto, says he also felt he needed to keep his problems quiet. He suffered mental health issues and hit "rock bottom" before beginning to find help in the summer of 2024.
"As a man, you think you are supposed to be strong, push any bad feelings down, suppress depression or sadness or fear," he said.
Kunder says he has lost multiple friends to suicide and says you never would have known they were suffering.
Gender roles and 'toxic masculinity'
Kunder said the world is changing in ways that are becoming confusing for many men.
The emphasis on women's parity in the labour force and society, as well as a greater acceptance of non-traditional gender identities, has upended expectations.

"At one point we knew we were supposed to be the provider and protector, and the idea of ‘toxic masculinity’ wasn’t a thing," he said. "I think men are really trying to figure out what it means to be a man in today’s world."
Why ‘manosphere’ influencers are appealing to young men
Oliffe pointed to other troubling patterns for young men.
"There are increasing lower rates of boys heading to universities, and very serious challenges in male-dominated industries such as construction, that as a society, we should not ignore."

Oliffe said that while the trades offer good careers, they often see high rates of substance use and mental health issues, as the necessary physical labour and harsh working environments can "heighten these risks."
Oliffe said that in the last decade, there has been "low government investment in men's mental health."

"I think the theme of silence is a very regrettable period in history, where on one side we talked about equity and inclusion, and then in effect ostracized 50 per cent of the population," Oliffe said.

Health Minister Michel said that when she brought this issue to the federal cabinet, she was met with some resistance. Some colleagues told her it took "courage" to broach the mental health of boys and men, given it could even be politically risky to talk publicly about the issue.
"I said 'courage'? This is not courage. We are ministers of health, it is our job to take care of the entire population," she said.
"Men don't know how to ask for help. And when they are struggling, they don't know how to express it."
Government strategy to come by early 2027
The federal government will soon launch its first-ever mental health strategy for boys and men.

The agency told CBC that some of what they hope to invest in will be "mentorship, peer support, sport and recreation," while "promoting healthy relationships, positive social norms and safer online environments."
For Robert Whitley, a men’s health expert and professor of psychiatry at McGill University in Montreal, part of the problem is the way society now views masculinity.
"Traditional masculinity has been denigrated in the popular mind whether it's through the media, through influencers, through commentators," he said. "The problem sometimes is a lack of masculinity."
He says there's a need for positive male role models.
"I’ve said many times before, it’s not a crisis of masculinity, there’s a crisis of mentorship," said Whitley.

For example, data from Statistics Canada shows only 25 per cent of teachers across elementary and high school systems in Canada are men. And at the organizations that step in to fill the mentorship gap — like the Big Brothers and Big Sisters of Canada — 70 per cent of volunteers are women.
"We're getting young men who are getting to the age of 18, 19, 20, who have never had a male role model in their lives," Whitley said.
Kunder and Cholmsky both say their mental health began to recover after they started asking for help, and they're now working to be role models for other young men.
"I feel like it’s my duty in a way to show up for men who are suffering and to hear them out and just let them know it’s all OK," said Kunder, who coaches and works with other men.
Last month in Ottawa, Cholmsky was awarded top 21 under 21 for his work in mental health advocacy and challenging "harmful stereotypes around masculinity and mental health."
"We all need to be doing our part to talk about this stuff," he said.

articles.title: It’s election day in Quebec: What you need to know to vote
articles.summary: It's Oct. 5, which means Quebecers are heading to the polls today to shape the province's political future and determine who will lead the next government.

image.caption: Voting day in the Quebec 2026 provincial election is upon us. (Gabriel Claveau/Radio-Canada)

blocks.text: Montreal
It's Oct. 5, which means Quebecers are heading to the polls today to shape the province's political future and determine who will lead the next government.
Polling stations open Monday at 9:30 a.m. and close at 8 p.m.
It's Oct. 5, which means Quebecers are heading to the polls today to determine who will lead the next government.

Polling stations will be open on Monday from 9:30 a.m. to 8 p.m. ET. Your employer is supposed to give you at least four consecutive hours to vote on election day, with no reduction in pay or other penalty.

Voters should have received information by mail on where to vote, including a reminder card that was mailed in both official languages, following a provincial judge's order. The back of the reminder card also features the names of the candidates running in your riding.
You can also find your polling station by entering your address on Élections Québec's website.
As part of Élections Québec's aim to make it easier for people to get to the polls, the BIXI and àVélo bike-sharing services are offering free rides across the province from 8 a.m. to 8:30 p.m. ET.
Here’s what to expect as an anglophone when casting your ballot in Quebec’s election
If you're still unsure of who to vote for, the following tools have been designed to help prospective voters:

items: Vote Compass: developed by political scientists to help voters see how their views compare to parties and candidates.
Platform Tracker: compares the promises of Quebec’s five major parties.

blocks.text: The last two general elections have seen about two-thirds voter turnout, with approximately 66 per cent of eligible voters casting ballots (66.15 per cent in 2022, and 66.45 per cent in 2018).
Ahead of this election day, just over a quarter (25.59 per cent) of electors voted at advance polls between Sept. 25 and Oct. 1.
Election night coverage
CBC's live coverage of the election will begin Monday evening at 7:30 p.m. ET, and will continue until it's clear who will form Quebec's next provincial government.

The coverage will be available on CBC TV, CBC News Network and CBC Radio One. It will also be streamed on CBC Gem, CBC Listen, cbc.ca/quebec, YouTube and the CBC Quebec News streaming channel. ASL interpretation will be provided on the stream.

Viewers will be given up-to-the minute results and expert analysis from host Debra Arbec, chief political correspondent Rosemary Barton and political panelists Emilie Nicolas, Rodolphe Husny and Robert Libman. Sudha Krishnan and Douglas Gelevan will also break down the results, and live reports will come in from communities across the province.
CBC Montreal News at 6 will air at its regular time at 6 p.m. ET.
Post-election analysis

On Tuesday, Oct. 6, CBC will air a provincewide morning show election special on Daybreak Montreal. Host Sean Henry will be joined live by Quebec AM’s Gordon Lambie and Rachel Watts to provide analysis and reactions from across the province.

You'll be able to find it on CBC Radio One, CBC Listen or on the CBC News app starting at 6 a.m. ET (5:30 a.m. ET in Montreal). Beginning at 6:10 a.m. ET you can also watch on our website, CBC Gem, YouTube or the CBC Quebec News streaming channel.

articles.title: After years of calls for data, study confirms Black Canadians face higher risk of maternal complications
articles.summary: The most comprehensive study yet of maternal health in Canada has found that Black Canadians face a much higher risk of serious complications during pregnancy, labour, delivery and postpartum than…

image.caption: A new study looking at maternal data in Canada from 2012 to 2023 has found that Black Canadians face much higher risks of several complications during pregnancy, birth and post-partum compared to white Canadians, sparking renewed calls for efforts to combat anti-Black racism in the health-care syste

blocks.text: The most comprehensive study yet of maternal health in Canada has found Black Canadians face a much higher risk of serious complications during pregnancy, labour, delivery and postpartum than white people — underlining the urgent need for better data tracking and tools to eliminate systemic anti-Black racism in our health-care system, researchers and advocates say.

The research, published Monday in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ), looked at more than 108,000 in-hospital deliveries to Black people, and more than 1.3 million in-hospital deliveries to white people across the country between 2012 and 2023.

Researchers found that severe maternal morbidity, encompassing complications such as pre-eclampsia, hemorrhage and sepsis, occurred at a rate of 47.8 out of 1,000 live births for a Black parent compared to 27.7 out of 1,000 live births for a white parent.

Even when researchers accounted for other factors like age, immigration status or other health conditions, Black people still had a 66 per cent higher chance of experiencing these potentially life-threatening complications.
The data lines up with what advocates have been saying for years — that Black women have their pain dismissed and routinely face barriers when navigating maternal care.

“It's huge to finally have this, you know, so-called proof and evidence that we've been told that we need to have in order to really prioritize Black communities and reproductive health,” said Cheyenne Scarlett, co-founder of the Black Birth Project, a non-profit aimed at improving reproductive outcomes for Black people in Canada.

She told CBC News that she has first-hand experience with the cracks in Canada’s maternal care: She once went to the ER with an ectopic pregnancy, and says she was sent home without receiving proper treatment.
“This report is not at all shocking to me,” she said.
'Less equitable outcomes'

Official data shows Black women in the U.S. are three times more likely to die in pregnancy or childbirth than white women. They are twice as likely in the U.K., while a 2021 study from The Lancet found that Black women had a 43 per cent higher risk of miscarriage.
But similar long-term demographic data has been lacking in Canada until now, despite years of calls for it.

“As Canadians … we’ve been able to distance ourselves from the very real reality of the fact that although universal health care is so important, it still doesn’t mean universal access for everyone,” Giulia Muraca, associate professor of obstetrics and gynecology at McMaster University, told CBC News.

items: Research highlights disparities in breast cancer care for Black women in Canada
More women are taking testosterone to treat menopause symptoms. Does science support that?

blocks.text: The higher rates of complications for Black people persisted when researchers controlled for conditions that occur in different rates in Black and white populations, such as sickle cell disease, with authors noting in the study that the consistent disparity “suggests broader structural influences on maternal health.”
Calls for more data about health risks to Black women in pregnancy

And while a higher income correlated with an improvement in maternal outcome for white parents, the study found that rates of severe complications increased for Black parents along with their income — an example of a "diminishing returns" phenomenon, Muraca suggested, in which those who experience structural marginalization don't receive the same advantages of an increased income.
The study didn't look at causes, but its authors stress that these differences don’t stem from race itself.

"Being Black is not the cause of these differences," Muraca said. The evidence that Black patients are experiencing "less equitable outcomes," she said, should prompt us to start examining "inequities in access ... differences in communication, in escalation of care, in differences in treatment, for example.
"These are things that we can start to now collect routine data on and hold institutions accountable for."
'We are dying'
The struggles Black people face in Canada just trying to access health care is something that community organizations have been studying independently for years.

"So me, as a Black woman, when I go into the hospital, when I'm in front of a practitioner, how are they responding to me?" Kearie Daniel, executive director and founder of the Black Women’s Institute for Health, said. "Are they going to see my pain the same way that they're seeing someone else's?"

A national survey released by the Black Women’s Institute for Health in 2025 looked at the experiences of nearly 2,000 Black women and girls with Canada’s health-care system. It found that 42 per cent avoid seeking medical care because they were afraid of how they might be treated.

When it came to maternal care, some women reported fearing their children might be taken from them after staff summoned social workers with no justification, Daniel said. Others dealt with miscarriages at home rather than risk poor treatment at the hospital. Many reported their pain was ignored.
"They're giving birth in the emergency bathroom, in the waiting room, they are being turned away," Daniel said.

items: Life-threatening complications overlooked in weeks after childbirth, researchers say

blocks.text: She said during her own pregnancy, her mother kept stressing she needed to dress well when going to the hospital, concerned that she wouldn’t be taken seriously.

"Having to go into a system that really isn't seeing your full humanity when you're depending on them to do so for your survival and the survival of your baby is just so — 'demoralizing' is not the right word. It's not a heavy enough word to really articulate just how excruciating it is."
Scarborough facility offers prenatal and postpartum midwifery care for Black families
Government action needed: advocates

Research has shown that Black people in Canada often suffer higher risks of negative health outcomes, including with breast cancer and during the COVID-19 pandemic. Enduring disparities have their roots in historical injustices that shaped modern medicine, according to a recent report set to publish this fall in the Canadian Ethnic Studies journal.
To ensure equitable maternity care, what’s needed now, Daniel said, is real action from governments and health-care organizations.

Better staff training is important, but it must be paired with the tracking of race-based data along with other socioeconomic differences, she said, to monitor if interventions are actually improving health outcomes for Black people.
Although some regions began tracking race-based health data after the pandemic, it's still fractured across the country.
"There has to be accountability," Daniel said. "We are dying as a result of not having that."
Canada’s health-care system also needs to work with community organizations to create truly informed care, advocates say.

Althea Jones founded Ancestral Hands Midwives in 2024, meant to help Black people get better pregnancy care. She said it's frustrating to have to prove what community members have known for years, but she's still hopeful this study might lead to more funding for interdisciplinary, Black-led care.
"I think people need care that reflects them," she said. "They need to be seen and heard."

Jenelle Ambrose Dash, chair of the Black Maternal Health Collective Canada, echoed the call. Every April, her organization runs Black Maternal Health Week in Toronto, bringing together groups like Ancestral Hands to share research and educate others.
She added that there needs to be more funding for health care in general, noting that the current “overwhelmed” system only exacerbates inequity.

When she heard about the CMAJ study, she saw her own story — a previous traumatic experience with pre-eclampsia — reflected in the data. She's determined to ensure that no Black parent has to go through what she did.
“There are real people behind the numbers,” she said.
“I hope that something will be done coming out of this study. We’re well past the point of awareness. We are looking for accountability now.”

articles.title: Build Canada Homes was launched a year ago. Can it scale up fast enough to meet demand?
articles.summary: Build Canada Homes promises to scale up the delivery of affordable housing at a time when industry leaders are raising the alarm about the lagging pace of housing development across the country.…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney launched Build Canada Homes last year to help scale up the construction of affordable housing, something the federal government had effectively stopped funding for decades. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

blocks.text: Business·New

Build Canada Homes promises to scale up the delivery of affordable housing at a time when industry leaders are raising the alarm about the lagging pace of housing development across the country. After one year of existence, the agency has only begun construction of about 2,000 units.
Of the 19,000 units slated for construction, only about 2,000 are currently being built

A little more than a year ago, Prime Minister Mark Carney stood in Ottawa in front of a backdrop of partly constructed, prefabricated houses to announce the launch of Build Canada Homes, the federal government's initiative to tackle the housing crisis and speed up residential construction.
The agency promises to scale up the delivery of affordable housing at a time when industry leaders are raising the alarm about the lagging pace of housing development across the country.
So far, Build Canada Homes has committed to supporting the construction of roughly 19,000 affordable units across the country — only about 2,000 of these are currently being built.

"I think we can always go faster," Dave Wilkes, president and CEO of the Building Industry and Land Development Association based in Toronto, said in an interview. "I like to say I work for an industry that measures patience in terms of seconds."

To be fair, the federal housing agency did only become a Crown corporation in July, shortly after the Build Canada Homes Act received royal assent. A large portion of the past year has been spent clearing bureaucratic hurdles, securing land transfers and signing intergovernmental deals.

"This is just the beginning," Build Canada Homes spokesperson Joshua Coke told CBC News in an emailed response to questions. "Canada's housing sector is under unprecedented pressure, with demand for affordable homes far exceeding current supply."

The housing agency primarily focuses on building non-market housing, where rents are typically linked to income rather than market rates, but it is also partnering with developers to build affordable homes for Canada's middle class.
"Combatting this housing affordability challenge requires more homes to be built, more quickly, and at greater scale," Coke added.
Ottawa's long absence from housing market

Kevin Fettig, president of CMI Financial, a mortgage lending and investment company, points out that the Canadian government — under both Conservatives and Liberals — effectively stopped funding and building new affordable housing for roughly three decades.

In the late '80s and early '90s, federal debt was ballooning as governments repeatedly ran deficits. Fettig, who worked on monetary policy for the Bank of Canada during that time, says home prices had skyrocketed, which pushed the central bank to increase interest rates. "We saw mortgages at 14 per cent, so there were high defaults in that period."

items: Toronto board of trade urges province to reform housing regulations

blocks.text: Shifting fiscal priorities saw Ottawa reduce spending on housing initiatives, cut the federal co-operative housing program and eventually pull the plug on building any new affordable housing units altogether.
"They basically decided to not finance that area anymore," Fettig said. "There hasn't really been a focus on affordability. It sort of crept up on us."
Federal Housing Minister Gregor Robertson agrees that Ottawa had been absent from the housing affordability picture for a long time.
"The leadership was not there. We're changing that now," Robertson said in an interview.
Ontario won't hit its new homes goal by 2031: Toronto board of trade
Fettig believes the approach of Build Canada Homes, providing tools to builders, developers and community partners to speed up residential projects, will yield positive results over time.
"It's hard to fill that gap in a hurry. We're on the right track, but it's going to be, more than anything, a question of time and effort and financing to get there," Fettig said.
Significant supply gap
Even the market-priced segment is lagging.

Over the past two years, housing starts have hovered around 250,000 annually, according to the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC). "We still need to keep doubling the pace of current housing starts if we are to restore 2019 affordability across the country," CMHC chief economist Mathieu Laberge said.
In its latest report, CMHC says roughly 417,000 to 469,000 units must be built every year by 2036 to reach that goal.
That supply gap is "putting future affordability at risk," according to Laberge. He notes a significant "pent-up demand" from younger Canadians and newcomers.
Even though non-market housing represents about five per cent of overall residential construction, Laberge says the entire housing spectrum is needed to address the ongoing affordability challenges.
"There's no wrong supply in this case."

Wilkes from the Building Industry and Land Development Association says the HST rebate and reduction in development charges in Ontario helped recalibrate some of the country's most overheated housing markets, such as Toronto and its surrounding suburbs.
"The combination of people not having to pay as much because of the HST [rebate on new homes] and builders being able to make sense of the numbers, we are seeing more and more supply come," he said.

Last month, Ottawa announced a partnership with the government of Alberta to build at least 1,460 affordable apartments and townhouses through Build Canada Homes — a new supply that's "much needed here in this province that's growing very fast," the federal housing minister said.

items: 4.8M new homes need to be built over next 10 years to restore affordability, CMHC says

blocks.text: When asked for more information on the planned developments in Alberta, Build Canada Homes said in a statement "it is not in a position to share details regarding individual projects under consideration at this time," including details about location, affordability mix or timelines.

Part of the new Crown corporation's mandate is to promote modern methods of construction, such as modular, factory-built, panelized and prefabricated housing, which can help shorten construction timelines.
"We're doing everything we can to modernize the industry and make sure that we can build faster and more affordably," Robertson said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Philippe de Montigny is a senior reporter covering business and economics for CBC News. He previously led a team as Radio-Canada's business bureau chief in Toronto. During his free time, Philippe enjoys playing board games, volleyball and music — he plays flute and piccolo in the Rosedale Symphony Orchestra and Toronto Concert Band. Email him at philippe.de.montigny@cbc.ca.
With files from Radio-Canada's Kim Taï Franco

articles.title: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez calls snap election
articles.summary: The Spanish prime minister had repeatedly insisted he would serve out his four-year term, with elections scheduled for 2027.

image.caption: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez speaks at a news conference in Madrid following the deadly Valencia floods (FILE 11/11/2024)Image: Burak Akbulut/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called an early general election on Monday, bringing forward a vote that had been scheduled for 2027.
Sanchez announced the decision in a statement at Madrid's Moncloa Palace after a weekend of consultations with his closest advisers.
What did Sanchez say?
"It is time for Spaniards to decide what future you want," Sanchez said.
The announcement of the November 29 vote follows a parliamentary defeat for his minority government on Friday, when lawmakers rejected measures aimed at tackling Spain's housing crisis.

Sanchez framed the election as a choice over Spain's future direction, saying voters must decide whether the country joins what he called a "far-right wave" or continues on a path of "openness, social justice and environmental responsibility."
He said he trusted Spanish voters to make that choice.
The decision comes despite Sanchez repeatedly insisting in recent months that his government would complete its four-year term.
The election follows mounting public pressure over housing costs, with large protests across the country.
This is a developing story. Please check back for more.

articles.title: Shadow chancellor to address Tory conference as he claims slashing red tape could cut cost of new houses by £50,000 – UK politics live
articles.summary: Andrew Griffith makes speech today as Reform UK accuses party of copying policies they ‘announced weeks and months ago’

blocks.text: Good morning. Yesterday Kemi Badenoch published a tract setting out the principles that a Conservative government would follow in office. It was presented as Thatcherism revived for the 21st century, and a key theme was that government should leave wealth creation up to business, and not get in the way with red tape.

Today Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, is presenting a plan that illustrates what this would mean in practice. Normally, at party conference, ministers and shadow ministers put out a press release in advance of their speeches highlighting just one headline policy idea, with perhaps one or two associated policies.

Overnight Griffith has published what is practically a manifesto. The press release alone runs to almost 5,000 words. Jessica Elgot had the task of reading them all for us yesterday and here is her write-up.
She has led her story on the plan to get rid of two environment quangos, the Environment Agency and Natural England.
But there are plenty of other proposals in the package too, including:
-Getting rid of net zero regulations and other planning laws, including section 106 agreements and the community infrastructure levy, that put up the cost of housebuilding.
-Getting rid of the EPR (extended producer responsibility), a law intended to make producers liable for waste disposal costs. The Tories call it the “grocery tax”.
-Backing a third runway at Heathrow.

-Leaving the Aarhus convention, an international treaty giving the public access to information relating to environmental decision-making. The Tories claim this enables the “lawfare hindering every major infrastructure project in this country”.
-Speeding up the delivery of more nuclear power stations.
-Simplifying the tax code.
The Tories claim the plans relating to housebuilding would “cut up to an estimated £50,000 off the price of a new home”.
There is more detail in what Griffith is proposing, and there is clearly a lot to discuss. Labour and Reform UK have both responded overnight – but taking different lines of attack.
Labour has said that Griffith has no credibility on these topics. In an overnight statement, Bridget Phillipson, the party chair, said:

double quotation markTrusting the co-author of Liz Truss’ disastrous mini-Budget with Tory plans on the economy and housing is like asking an arsonist to run the fire service. Kemi Badenoch is once again demonstrating her appalling lack of judgement. The Tories had 14 years in government to grow our economy and help people get on the housing ladder, but they completely failed at every turn.
But Richard Tice, the Reform UK deputy leader and business spokesperson, says that Griffith is copying ideas that his party has already adopted. He says:

double quotation markTories pledge to scrap some costs regulations and taxes they put in place! They are copying Reform policies we announced weeks and months ago! They are trying to fix problems they created 😡 Never forget Never forgive

One of the themes emerging at this conference is that, while there is far less talk of some sort of Tory/Reform UK pact than there was a year ago, the policy overlap continues. Yesterday the Conservatives announced two other proposals (excluding foreigners from the student loan scheme, and reducing aid spending to just £1bn a year) that were little more than cut-and-paste versions of Reform UK pledges.
Here is the agenda for the day.

9.45am: Andrew Bowie, the shadow energy secretary, speaks at the conference on the main stage (the smaller of the two halls the Tories are using at this conference for speeches). The other main morning speakers are Richard Holden, the shadow transport secretary, at 10.30am; Damian Hinds, the shadow health secretary, at 11.15am; and Andrew Griffith, the shadow chancellor, Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, and Laura Trott, after 12.15pm.
12.14pm: Victoria Atkins, the shadow environment secretary, speaking in the fanzone area on the Conservative’s rural vision.

2pm: Griffith takes part in “meet the team” event in the symphony hall (the conference stage being used for larger events) with Richard Fuller, chief secretary to the Treasury, Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, and Julia Lopez, the acting shadow business secretary.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

Spain’s prime minister Pedro Sánchez is about to hold a press conference shortly amid speculation he is about to call a snap election to address a national housing crisis, after parliament rejected two of his government’s emergency relief measures on Friday.
The vote prompted tens of thousands to march in the street on Saturday, in the capital Madrid and other cities. Protesters were calling for action on rent prices and tenant protections.
Spain’s next general election had been due next year, and Sánchez had previously said that he would complete a full four-year term.

But the defeats in parliament have raised questions on how effective his government can be in getting through key legislation, and analysts say while there’s the risk with an early election, it might be worth striking while the iron’s hot.

articles.title: Yemen launches major military operation against Houthis
articles.summary: Yemen's internationally recognized government announced a new military offensive to retake Houthi-held territory after rebels cut a key road linking the city of Taiz with Aden.

image.caption: The recent Houthi advance followed days of heavy fighting in and around the besieged city of Taiz [September 22, 2014]Image: Mohammed Hamoud/Anadolu Agency/picture alliance

blocks.text: Yemen's Saudi-backed government on Sunday announced a new military operation to retake territory held by Iran-backed Houthi rebels, as fighting intensified around the key southwestern city of Taiz.

"Today, I announce the start of military operations to retake the remaining territory of the republic and extend the authority of the state and its institutions across the entire national territory," Yemeni Presidential Council chief Rashad al-Alimi said in a televised address.
The announcement came after Houthi fighters captured a key road linking Taiz with the government-held city of Aden, effectively isolating Taiz. The rebels have besieged Taiz for more than a decade.
More than 70 people were reportedly killed in fighting around Taiz over the past day, according to AFP news agency.

blocks.caption: The escalation between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has revived Yemen’s civil war after a four-year ceasefire [FILE: September 27, 2026]Image: Social Media/REUTERS

blocks.text: How did the conflict between Saudi Arabia and Houthis escalate?

The latest developments come amid an escalation between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is supported by Saudi Arabia, reviving Yemen's civil war after a four-year ceasefire.
A 2022 truce between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia collapsed in July after the rebels allowed an Iranian plane to land in Yemen's capital Sanaa, which defied the Saudis' control over Yemeni airspace.
As a result of the escalation, the Houthis announced a maritime blockade on Saudi Arabia.

Last month, the Houthis seized Yemen's Red Sea coast and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait — a vital global shipping route — from government hands, even as Al-Alimi called for support from the international community.
The Houthis have controlled Sanaa and much of Yemen's more populous western areas since the start of Yemen's civil war in 2014.
Why can't the Saudis defeat the Houthis?

articles.title: India news: Top court hears petitions against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar
articles.summary: The Supreme Court heard pleas against India's beleagured poll body chief over alleged unilateral decisions related to the large-scale revision of voter lists. DW has the latest.

image.caption: The hearing comes after thousands of protesters and opposition supporters rallied in Delhi and Mumbai over the weekend to demand Kumar's resignationImage: Abiraj Kumar Arulgnanakumar/DW

blocks.text: October 5, 2026
Supreme Court issues notice to Election Commission of India, no suspension for Gyanesh Kumar

The Supreme Court on Monday issued notice to the Election Commission of India (ECI), seeking the poll body's response to petitions against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the revision of electoral rolls.

The pleas sought action against Kumar following an investigative news report which claimed that the poll panel, headed by him, took decisions on voter list changes despite objections from two of three election commissioners.

India’s top court said on Monday that after considering ECI’s response, if it finds that decisions were taken by the top poll official without the required unanimity, it would reconsider or recall those decisions, news agency ANI reported.
"If records show some decision was not unanimous etc., we will injunct those decisions," legal news portal LiveLaw quoted the court as saying.
The Supreme Court declined to pass any interim order to suspend Kumar, an action sought by one of the petitions.

articles.title: Hundreds of French schools shut, teen loses hand in protests
articles.summary: The student protests that rocked France last week have prompted authorities to keep up to 500 schools closed on Monday. A teenage boy lost his hand, seemingly while trying to pick up a police tear…

image.caption: The school protests have spread nationwide, as here in LyonImage: Laurent Cipriani/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Several hundred schools in France closed totally or partially on Monday amid security fears following a wave of nationwide student protests, the education minister has said.
The protests by pupils complaining of poor conditions began at one Paris school on September 17 but last week mutated into sometimes violent demonstrations across the nation.

A 15-year-old boy in the northern town of Lens sustained a severe injury to his hand amid one of the protests on Monday. French news agency AFP cited a police union source as saying he appeared to have picked up a sting ball grenade, another term for a type of tear gas grenade also often called a blast ball, and it exploded in his hand.
The demonstrations have started to dominate France's political debate just a few months before presidential elections that will choose a successor to Emmanuel Macron, who is approaching term limit.
France students protest school conditions
Why are the schools staying closed?
Education Minister Edouard Geffray said on Sunday that lessons would be totally or partly suspended in some 400 to 500 high schools on Monday, as the security conditions "have not been fulfilled."
According to Geffray, the schools were being closed mainly as a precaution, with more large protests planned for Tuesday.
Geffray said the number of schools remaining closed on Monday would be similar to that on Friday but that there was planned to be a "partial, progressive return to lessons."
He said 24 schools had been "burned or ransacked" and 78 education staff members injured since the protests began.

"There are activists — particularly from the far left — who have infiltrated the high school student movement, hijacked it from the students themselves, and engaged in extreme violence," Geffray said.
"Clearly, this poses a risk to both our staff and our students," he added.

blocks.caption: Several schools have been damaged amid the protestsImage: CLPRESS/ABACA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Valerie Pecresse, the president of the Ile-de-France region surrounding the capital, said that more than a third of the 468 schools in the region would be shut on Monday.
What are the school protesters saying?
The protesting teenagers at French upper high schools, called Lycees, have complained of high rates of absenteeism by teachers, school days that are too long and dilapidated facilities.

They have also protested at the lack of adequate cooling on hot summer days, with some towns seeing temperatures of 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) last summer in a country without widespread air conditioning.
Organizers have called for the protests to continue on Tuesday, saying the government was still failing to propose "concrete measures" to remedy the situation.
On Sunday, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu urged local authorities to make it a priority to fill gaps left by long-term absences and unfilled posts.
He also called a meeting for Tuesday with regional presidents to discuss renovating school buildings that are often in poor condition.
Violent incidents at the school protests
The protests have been marked by several violent incidents, with security forces sometimes using tear gas and batons to disperse the young protesters.
More than 5,000 people, 85% of them minors, have been arrested since the start of the movement.
On Sunday, a 16-year-old was detained after a 59-year-old teacher was hit and doused with gasoline on the sidelines of a protest in the southern town of La Ciotat.
Last week, a group of young people was filmed beating and kicking a policeman on the ground in the eastern town of Belfort.
The French branch of rights group Amnesty International last week described the action taken by police as "disproportionate."

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez has, however, defended security forces, saying they were "not cracking down on young people" but rather "protecting" school and university students wishing to "peacefully voice their demands."

articles.title: California woman arrested and accused of spying on Taiwan president’s son for China
articles.summary:
The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport before she left for China, the agency said

US authorities arrested a California ⁠woman on…

blocks.text: US authorities arrested a California ⁠woman on ​Sunday, accusing her of spying on the son of Taiwan’s president at the behest of Chinese officials, the FBI said.

The FBI ⁠arrested Wanying Zhang, also known as Heather, at Los Angeles International Airport on Sunday before her planned departure to China, the agency said in a ⁠statement. Authorities charged Zhang, 34, of Irvine, California, with acting as an unregistered foreign agent.

Zhang surveilled a ​son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, the ‌FBI alleged. The agency ‌did not directly name Zhang’s alleged target, but later shared a New York Post report ‌identifying him as Lai Ting-yu, a US resident.
Taiwan’s presidential office described Zhang’s alleged actions as a “typical case of transnational repression” and thanked the US government for protecting Taiwanese citizens.
“Our country expresses the strongest condemnation of such barbaric conduct that disregards human rights and the sovereignty of nations,” spokesperson Karen Kuo said in a statement.
China’s foreign ministry did not respond to ‌a request for comment.

The Justice Department alleged Zhang travelled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, video and licence plate information of the Taiwanese president’s son and his family.

Zhang used tradecraft to avoid detection ⁠and never notified Washington that she was acting for a foreign government, Bill Essayli, ​the first assistant US ​attorney for the Central District of ​California, alleged in a statement.
It was not immediately clear whether Zhang ​had a defence attorney. She ‌will appear on ​Monday in a ​Los Angeles federal court, Essayli said.

Lai and his Democratic Progressive Party champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing, which views the island as ​Chinese territory. Lai says only Taiwan’s people can decide their future.
Washington does not have formal diplomatic ties with Taiwan, but the US is the island’s most important international backer and weapons supplier.
