articles.title: Brazil presidential election 2026: first-round live results
articles.summary:
Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva is standing against Flávio Bolsonaro in the first round of the presidential race

The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son…

blocks.text: The incumbent, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is up against Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison for plotting a military coup. The president in Brazil is directly elected, and candidates need more than 50% of the vote to avoid a second round. Polls close at 17.00 BRT / 21.00 BST.
Live first round results
Guardian graphic. Source: TES
How the election works

Brazil’s president is directly elected: each voter’s ballot counts equally and there is no electoral college. If no candidate wins more than 50% of the valid votes cast in the first round, a second runoff election will be held three weeks later between the two candidates who polled highest.

According to opinion polls, there are two leading candidates. The first is the incumbent president, Lula, 80, a veteran of the Brazilian left who has served three terms. During his first two terms, between 2003 and 2011, he was credited with overseeing a historic period of commodity-fuelled growth and poverty reduction.

Brazilian presidents are limited to two consecutive terms, so if he wins this time he will not be able to stand in 2030. In 2018 Lula was jailed on corruption charges, although his conviction was quashed after 580 days behind bars.

Lula’s principal opponent is the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, son of Jair Bolsonaro, who is in prison. Flávio is a 45-year-old lawyer and a former senator from Rio de Janeiro. Bolsonaro senior is serving a 27-year sentence for masterminding a failed coup after losing the 2022 election but has endorsed his son’s campaign and hopes to regain his freedom if he wins.

Opinion polls suggest no other candidate will come close to the two frontrunners, but neither is there a clear leader in polling for the 25 October runoff. The new leader will take power on 5 January 2027.

One of the most important states to watch is Minas Gerais, a mountainous mining and agricultural region that is larger than France and has 21 million inhabitants, and is Brazil’s bellwether state. Since democracy returned in the 1980s, no candidate has won the presidency without triumphing in Minas. In 2018, Jair Bolsonaro beat Lula’s candidate there by more than 1.7m votes and was elected president.
Four years later, Lula reclaimed the state by fewer than 50,000 and also won the nationwide race. History suggests that whoever wins Minas, will win the election.

articles.title: Egyptian journalist faces terrorism charges after entire newsroom detained
articles.summary:
Calls for release of six Matsadaash staff after one is charged while whereabouts of other five remain unknown

An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days…

blocks.text: An Egyptian journalist has been charged with joining a terrorist group, days after an entire newsroom was detained in what rights groups have said is a crackdown on press freedoms.

Last week, authorities arrested six journalists from the independent fact-checking and investigative platform Matsadaash – literally meaning “don’t believe” – accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and publishing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The outlet’s six journalists, Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal, were arrested by security forces over the course of two days.

On Sunday, Egyptian authorities charged Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading false news, according to a statement by the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, a NGO. The charges came after an interrogation that lasted from 10pm to 8am and focused exclusively on material published by Matsadaash, the rights group said.
Ashraf was to be held for 15 days, pending investigation, while the whereabouts of the other five journalists were still unknown.

blocks.caption: Egyptian authorities have charged the journalist Mohamed Ashraf with joining a terrorist group and spreading fake news. Photograph: Matsadaash/AP

blocks.text: Abdelrahman Mansour, the co-founder of the platform, denied having any association with the Muslim Brotherhood, a transnational movement that was designated a terrorist organisation by Egypt in 2013 after the former president Mohamed Morsi, a senior Brotherhood figure, was ousted in a coup. Mansour called the arrests “one of the gravest attacks on journalism in Egypt’s modern history”.

“My colleagues were doing what journalists should do: asking difficult questions, uncovering facts, and reporting on issues that affect people’s lives. They deserve recognition for their work. Instead, their homes were raided, and all six were taken away,” he said. “The government must answer this question: why have you arrested six journalists? What have they done beyond doing their jobs?”
The Guardian contacted the Egyptian State Information Service for a comment but did not receive a reply by the time of publishing.

Dozens of journalists staged a sit-in outside the Egyptian Journalists Syndicate (EJS) in Cairo on Saturday, demanding the release of the Matsadaash staff. Members said they would keep the sit-in open ended until the journalists were released, and the EJS said it would convene an emergency meeting on Monday.
The EJS had filed a request with the ministry of interior and public prosecutor for the release of the journalists, as well as for information on their whereabouts.

More than 80 rights groups, including Human Rights Watch and the Committee to Protect Journalists, condemned the arrests as a violation of freedoms, and demanded the immediate release of the Matsadaash staff.

The arrests came little over a week after the US government waived its human rights conditions on $320m (£242m) in military aid to Egypt, citing Cairo’s “helpful role” to US national security after the US-Iran war.

The US gives about $1.3bn in aid to Egypt annually, but a portion is contingent upon the Egyptian government meeting certain human rights and democracy-related requirements. The US has withheld portions of aid several times since the 2013 coup owing to Egypt’s poor human-rights record, but has largely kept the majority of funds flowing.

This year, Washington waived the human rights requirement in total as doing so was “essential for the US-Egypt relationship and US national security priorities”, read a state department memo revealed by Reuters.

While saying that he was unsure whether the arrests were linked to the recent waiver, Mansour said: “The use of the national security waiver on human rights conditions by the US by many years, a willingness by other states to look the other way on Egypt’s human rights record … certainly enables violations like this to occur more easily.”

Cairo has for years faced criticism for its human rights abuses, with the rights monitor Freedom House saying Egyptian security forces “engage in human rights abuses and extrajudicial killing with impunity”.
Since the Egyptian president Abdel Fatah al-Sisi took power in the coup that ousted Morsi, civil liberties have been curbed and domestic political opposition has been violently crushed.

Egypt ranks 169th out of 180 countries on Reporters Without Borders Press freedom index. Freedom of the press is tightly restricted in the country and independent platforms such as Matsada2sh are rare. About 26 journalists are held in Egyptian prisons, according to the EJS.

articles.title: US marine arrested in Japan on suspicion of killing woman, police say
articles.summary:
Suspect allegedly killed woman at hotel in Okinawa as prime minister calls crime ‘exceptionally brutal and vicious’

A US marine stationed on

blocks.text: A US marine stationed on Japan’s southern island of Okinawa is accused of murdering a Japanese woman and has been arrested on suspicion of murder, police said on Sunday.
The suspect allegedly “killed [a] 39-year-old woman at a hotel in Naha and stole her wallet” as well as her backpack, local police told news media outlets.
Citing police, NBC News reported that the suspect charged in the case was identified Lance Cpl Devin Jacob Ballard, 20. Anna Yagi was identified as the victim.
Ballard denied the allegations, police said, according to NBC.

Crimes including rapes, assaults, hit-and-run and drunk-driving accidents by US personnel have long sparked protests on Okinawa. The island bears a disproportionate burden of hosting about 70% of US military facilities in Japan.

US ambassador George Glass posted on social media that he had spoken with Japan’s foreign ministry and Okinawa’s governor, offering “sincere condolences to the victim’s family” and pledging cooperation into the investigation of her death.
The Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, said Japan had lodged a protest with US authorities and called the crime “exceptionally brutal and vicious”.

The government has urged the US “to provide maximum cooperation with the investigation, enforce stricter discipline among US military personnel, and take thorough measures to prevent the recurrence of similar crimes,” Takaichi said.

Public broadcaster NHK and other Japanese media outlets, citing investigation sources, reported that CCTV footage from near the scene showed a foreign man entering a room with a woman and later leaving with her belongings.

Police then found a 20-year-old man who matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage and asked him to accompany them voluntarily to a local police station where he was arrested, NHK reported.

“We have lost a family member and are deeply saddened,” Yagi’s brother said through local police, according to the Asahi Shimbun daily newspaper. “My parents, in particular, are utterly devastated at the loss of their daughter.”
The US has about 54,000 military personnel stationed in Japan, mostly on Okinawa.
Crimes committed by US personnel in Japan have been a thorn in relations between the close security allies.
“Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen,” Japan’s defense minister Shinjiro Koizumi said.
In June 2025, a Japanese court sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton – then 22 – to seven years in prison after being convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.
Earlier, in 2017, former US marine and civilian military base worker Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local woman in Okinawa.
The same year, US forces in Japan banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated American marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing its 61-year-old local driver.
According to the Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper, about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since Okinawa was returned to Japan from the US in 1972 after the second world war.
The number of arrests in a year hit 80 in 2024, the highest in 20 years.

articles.title: UK car industry faces ‘difficult trade-off’ between Chinese and EU markets
articles.summary:
Britain under pressure to put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicle imports ahead of protectionist trade measures

Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China…

blocks.text: Britain’s car industry is grappling with a “difficult trade-off” between China and Europe, as manufacturers struggle to balance the benefits of both markets ahead of looming trade measures that could restrict UK exports to the EU.
The UK is an outlier in choosing not to put import taxes on Chinese vehicles, even as the US has shut them out almost entirely, and the EU imposes duties of up to 45%.

EU officials reportedly warned Andy Burnham last month that the UK must put tariffs on cheap Chinese vehicles otherwise Brussels would impose protectionist “made in Europe” barriers on British exports to the bloc, hitting British carmakers in their largest market.
Ministers have so far resisted such calls, with Jonathan Reynolds, the business secretary, arguing any levies would “probably be reciprocated” – costing UK manufacturers sales in China.

Tariffs would also raise prices for British drivers, who have flocked to cheaper Chinese models, and could deter brands such as Chery, which is in talks to build cars at Nissan’s Sunderland plant, from investing further in the UK.

“There is a difficult trade-off,” said Emily Sawicz, of the consultancy RSM UK, adding that the UK “cannot afford to drift between the two indefinitely”. Chinese investment could be a “lifeline” for carmakers, while access to Europe would also be “crucial” for smaller manufacturers.

“Being excluded risks UK suppliers becoming increasingly shut out of those European opportunities,” she added. “Manufacturers need clarity on which direction the government intends to take so they can make long-term investment decisions.”
Ian Plummer, commercial director at Autotrader, said competition from Chinese brands had made cars more affordable and “is encouraging more people to go and buy a new car”.
Brands such as BYD, Omoda and Jaecoo more than tripled their share of the UK new car market in the first eight months of 2026, reaching 12% of sales, according to industry figures.

Figures released on Friday showed that British new car ⁠registrations rose 12% in the year to September, the best month for annual growth since 2017. The preliminary data from the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT) showed the boom was powered by a demand for electric vehicles and Chinese brands, with the Jaecoo 7 and BYD’s ​Sealion ‌7 among the top sellers.

The trade body said on Wednesday that the European Commission’s made in Europe rules, which restrict subsidies, tax breaks and public procurement contracts to vehicles built within the EU, pose an existential threat to British car production. The EU accounted for 58% of UK car exports in the first half of the year, compared with about 4% for China.

Mike Hawes, the SMMT’s chief executive, said: “The UK and EU automotive industries are deeply integrated, so effectively excluding British-produced vehicles from their largest market would assure mutual damage.”
Massimiliano Messina, Nissan’s chair in Europe, said last month: “Europe cannot have a Trojan horse where the Chinese are going to flood the market through the UK.”
after newsletter promotion

Victor Zhang, the deputy UK chief of Chery, which owns the Jaecoo and Omoda brands, rejected that claim, saying: “Most of what we sell are super-hybrids, not the cars that those tariffs are about, and the cars we sell here stay here.”
He added: “Tariffs can come and go, but we won’t change our ongoing investment in the UK.”

Brussels raised its own tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024, triggering a decline in what was then an accelerating sales trajectory. It is now facing calls for fresh barriers to be imposed on importing hybrid electric vehicles, potentially quotas or price floors.
Imports of plug-in and battery hybrid cars rocketed after the EU tariffs were imposed on EVs, underlining China’s ability to pivot its export efforts when hit by trade barriers.
Others in the industry believe tariffs could help protect the UK’s manufacturers, whose market share in Britain continues to be eroded Chinese firms.
Tim Tozer, a former chair of Vauxhall, said that tariffs were “vital” to stop Britain’s car sector “atrophying”. He said: “We are at last knockings now, trying to save the industry.”

He added that Reynolds was “whistling in the wind” with hopes of continuing to export to China en masse, arguing the market had become “fiercely nationalistic,” with buyers increasingly loyal to domestic brands “because they’re bloody good”.

articles.title: Rare tornado whips through small Australian town
articles.summary: The twister was caught on camera in Ulladulla, New South Wales, damaging property and downing trees.

blocks.text: Several people in Ulladulla, New South Wales, filmed the moment a rare tornado came through the town on 3 October.
The Australian Bureau of Meteorology said the phenomenon was caused by "severe" thunderstorms and that it was "very uncommon to see one in such a populated place".
The weather incident caused damage to properties and knocked over some trees, it added.

articles.title: Why Canada is preparing for a (long shot) US invasion
articles.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the military is running scenarios in the unlikely case the US invades Canada.

blocks.text: Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.

Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.
"That's just risk management," Carney said.
Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.
In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.
"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.
Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.
But the issue is clearly weighing on Canadians' minds.
In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.

A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.
"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.
Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.
They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.
The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.
Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.
After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.

But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.
"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.
Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.
Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.

In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.
Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.
Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.
It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.
They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.
A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.
"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."

Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.

He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.
"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.
Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.
So what would it be like if it happened?
The first phase of a war could be quite short.
According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week
Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.
Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.
The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.
The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.

He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.
An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.
Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.
"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.
"They would see it as an illegal and immoral order."
Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.

But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.
"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.
Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.

articles.title: 'Heartbreaking reality': Crew, passengers of downed medical transport jet are likely dead, company says

image.caption: Rear Admiral Matthew Lake, commander of the U.S. Coast Guard Northeast District, is shown at a news conference Sunday morning addressing media on the search for the missing medical transport jet. The Coast Guard decision to end the search Sunday night means all four crew and the two passengers likel

blocks.text: Hamilton·New

The decision by the U.S. Coast Guard to end the search for the crew and passengers of a medical transport jet out of Hamilton, Ont., means it's time to accept that the four Canadians and two Bermudians on board didn't survive, says the company that operated the jet.
U.S. Coast Guard ends massive search for survivors off coast of Nantucket Sunday night

The decision by the U.S. Coast Guard to end the search for the crew and passengers of a medical transport jet out of Hamilton means it's likely that the four Canadians and two Bermudians on board didn't survive, says the company that operated the jet.
Latitude Air Ambulance issued a statement late Sunday night, saying hope of finding survivors from the downed Gulfstream G100 aircraft appeared to be gone.

items: Update: Crew, passengers of downed medical transport jet are likely dead, company says
U.S. Coast Guard suspends search for six aboard air ambulance

blocks.text: "It is with profound sadness that we acknowledge the decision by the United States Coast Guard to conclude active search and rescue operations and transition to recovery efforts," Latitude said in its statement.

"Given the information shared by authorities and the conclusion of the search and rescue phase, we must now face the heartbreaking reality that the four members of our Latitude team, our patient and the patient's family escort, who were aboard…are presumed to have died."

The Coast Guard and National Guard had used fixed wing aircraft, helicopters and ships to search a huge area of 4,445 square miles over about 66 hours since about 2 a.m. Saturday when the Coast Guard said it was contacted by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration that contact had been lost with the Gulfstream aircraft. The jet, which had flown out of Hamilton, was travelling from Bermuda to Boston with a patient and a family member along with the crew.
Sunday morning, the Coast Guard said debris from the jet had been found off Nantucket. Sunday night, the Coast Guard decided to end the search.

"Suspending a search is not an easy decision," Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, commander of the Northeast District, said Sunday night. We express our deepest condolences to the families and loved ones affected by the tragedy and our gratitude for our partner agencies who helped support search efforts.
Debris was recovered by Coast Guard

Sunday morning, Lake said the Coast Guard was in the process of working with Massachusetts authorities to get some craft out in the area that are equipped with sonar to be able to do some detection on the seabed floor. He said the water was about 80 to 90 feet deep in the area.
Latitude said its thoughts are first and foremost with the families, loved ones, friends, and colleagues of the people on the jet.

items: U.S. Coast Guard searching for missing air ambulance with 6 passengers on board
4 Canadians aboard missing Ontario-based air ambulance flying from Bermuda

blocks.text: "Our four crew members were valued members of the Latitude family. They dedicated themselves to providing care to people at some of the most difficult moments in their lives, and they were carrying out that mission when this tragedy occurred," the company said.
"We are grieving their loss deeply and will continue to support their families and our employees through the difficult days ahead."
The names of the crew and the passengers have not yet been released.

"We extend that same care and compassion to the family and loved ones of our patient and family escort," Latitude said. "We ask that the privacy of all of the families involved be respected as they grieve."

The company said it will continue to cooperate fully with the U.S. National Transportation Safety Board, the Transportation Safety Board of Canada and all other relevant authorities as recovery efforts and the investigation proceed.
"Determining the circumstances and cause of an aviation accident is a careful and methodical process, and we will not speculate about what occurred," the company said.

Latitude said it was "deeply grateful to the United States Coast Guard and to the air traffic controllers, search and rescue crews, first responders, government agencies and others in Canada, the United States and Bermuda who worked tirelessly in the search" for those aboard the jet.
"Their professionalism, determination, and compassion will never be forgotten."
Peter Byl, president of Latitude, said the tragedy is an "unimaginable loss for our Latitude family and for everyone who loved the six people" aboard the jet.

"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities. We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."
The company said it may provide further relevant information when it is confirmed by the appropriate authorities and can be shared with respect for the families involved.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Paul Forsyth is a St. Catharines-based CBC reporter covering communities in the Niagara Region. He has decades of reporting experience in Niagara, having worked for Niagara This Week, the St. Catharines Standard and the Welland Tribune before joining CBC. You can reach him at paul.forsyth@cbc.ca.

articles.title: UK remands 2 Iranians over alleged antisemitic terror plot
articles.summary: The pair were arrested on the eve of Yom Kippur and later charged with plotting to attack Jewish targets in Manchester.

image.caption: Police forces across the UK have stepped up patrols outside synagogues [FILE: October 2, 2025]Image: Andrew Matthews/PA Wire/empics/picture alliance

blocks.text: Two Iranian nationals charged with plotting acts of terrorism against the United Kingdom's Jewish community were remanded in custody by a court in London on Saturday.
The pair were detained on September 20, the eve of Yom Kippur, the holiest day in the Jewish calendar.
The case only came to light on Friday when the two men were charged, just days after another terror plot, which the UK has linked to Iran, was foiled.
What do we know about the case?

Prosecutor Mark Luckett told Westminster Magistrates' Court that Rahman S., 34, and Salam ‌A., 36, are accused of carrying out "hostile reconnaissance" on Jewish targets in Manchester, in northern England.
He said the two men planned to use a "homemade explosive device" and had allegedly been in contact with a third party, an Iranian national, most likely operating from within Iran.
The contact is alleged to have given the pair instructions on how ‌to put together a homemade device from chlorine and brake fluid, the court heard.
Luckett said the two suspects had used online resources, including images, plans and maps, to identify and research potential attack sites.
He told the court that the targets included the Manchester Jewish Museum and the Heaton Park synagogue, where two Jewish worshippers were killed in a knife attack a year ago on Friday.
The two Iranian suspects had arrived in Britain in small boats that crossed the English Channel from mainland Europe, Luckett added.
One had been granted asylum, while the other's application is still pending, the court heard.
The pair did not enter a plea and were remanded in custody until their next hearing at London's Old Bailey on October 23.
Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator of counterterror policing, said the plot was believed to be isolated and there was no ongoing public threat.

blocks.caption: Heaton Park synagogue was the scene of a deadly attack in October 2025 [FILE: October 2, 2025]Image: Ian Hodgson/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Police find no link to RAF Fairford plot

Evans also said the Manchester plot was "not connected in any way" to the suspected terror plot at RAF Fairford last weekend, which Prime Minister Andy Burnham said showed "strong indications" of Iranian involvement.
Also on Saturday, police said a dual British-Iranian national, arrested on Thursday in connection with the RAF Fairford plot, was released on police bail.
The 25-year-old was the sixth person arrested and then bailed as the investigation continues.
Police said the five other men held are all British nationals in their 20s and from London.
UK releases air base plot suspects

Police uncovered the RAF Fairford plot when a farmer spotted suspicious white vans near the base early on Sunday morning and called the authorities. Officers found petrol inside the vans, but no explosives.
UK media reported this week that one of the suspects dialled the police about an hour earlier, though that has not been confirmed.
Tehran has rejected as baseless accusations of targeting RAF Fairford, which lies 90 miles (145 kilometers) west of London and has been used by US bombers to strike Iran.
The UK remains on high alert for potential threats from Russia and Iran.
Iran has previously used proxies to commit crimes on British soil, including repeated attacks and plots against Jewish targets, as well as against dissidents.
Antisemitic attacks more broadly have risen sharply since Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023.

articles.title: Libyan unity talks upended as warlord’s son linked to drone attacks on fuel facilities
articles.summary:
Western Libya’s GNU say working with Saddam Haftar ‘impossible’ as US-backed merger plan breaks down

Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell”…

blocks.text: Allegations that the son of the Libyan warlord Khalifa Haftar oversaw a “terror cell” that launched drone attacks on fuel storage facilities and power stations in western Libya have upended plans for the Tripoli-based government of national unity (GNU) to continue cooperating with Haftar on a plan to unify the country.

Saddam Haftar, the deputy commander of the so-called Libyan National Army (LNA), has increasingly been seen by the US as an important figure in its plans to unify Libyan security, judicial and political institutions.
But a round of drone attacks in August worsened electricity blackouts in the west of the country, putting intense popular pressure on the GNU led by the prime minister, Abdul Hamid Dbeibah.

Libya has been split between the east, dominated by Haftar, and the west, governed by the GNU, since the fall of Col Muammar Gaddafi in 2011, leaving the oil-rich country at the mercy of corruption, militia, migrant traffickers and myriad external actors.

blocks.caption: Khalifa Haftar. Photograph: Esam Omran Al-Fetori/Reuters

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s Africa adviser, Massad Boulos, has hatched a plan to unify the two Libyan governments in which Haftar from the east would take on the role of president and a member of the Dbeibah family from the west would become prime minister.

Boulos has insisted he is not trying a quick fix that entrenches family elites in Libya. “It’s not about families or names,” Boulos said when asked about the reported Haftar-Dbeibah deal, before adding: “At the end of the day, those are individuals that have to be in one position or the other.”

But the drone strikes, it is claimed, were prompted by Haftar’s anger at Dbeibah apparently stalling on the Boulos merger plan and by Tripoli allegedly encouraging tribes in southern Libya to attack and kill his forces.

Over more than five days in August, drones attacked the Zawiya oil station and fuel storage facilities in western Libya. The drone strikes hit the gasoline-storage tank at the Zawiya oil complex, west of Tripoli, causing a large fire and the tank’s collapse. The tank held approximately 4.5m litres of fuel when it was struck, according to Libya’s National Oil Corporation.

On 5 September, three Libyans and one Spanish citizen were arrested in southern Tripoli by the GNU for their alleged role in a plot that was intended to include an attack on Tripoli airport. It was thought the whole group involved five Spaniards and four Libyans. The three arrested Libyans were allegedly affiliated with the Tareq ben Ziyad brigade, an LNA formation. Information that has emerged from interviews about the plot, and Saddam Haftar’s alleged role, not just in Libya, has been described as a goldmine, capable of weakening Khalifa Haftar.

Sources in the GNU said the alleged plotters were working for Saddam Haftar. “No formal decision has been made, but in light of what has been discovered it is impossible to work with Saddam,” the sources said.

The claims not only damage Saddam Haftar’s role in the Boulos plan but also the parallel UN sponsored 4+4 talks involving the main four political institutions in Libya that led to an August agreement to stage elections within two years. The deal endorsed by the UN security council overcomes previous obstacles to elections, and had been backed by the main actors capable of delivering the change.

Walid Ellafi, minister for state for political affairs in the UN-backed Libyan GNU and an enthusiast for elections, said: “Our support for the 4+4 process is rooted in its role as a UN sponsored framework offering a new approach to achieving practical results that pave the way for elections and institutions whose political legitimacy derives from the will of the people – not as a political settlement that overlooks violations or sets aside the rights of those affected.”
He opposes an elite east-west political deal that brushes aside longstanding grievances such as the displacement of 9,000 families in Benghazi during the 2014 war.
The allegations about the sabotage operation may intensify a power struggle between the three sons of Khalifa Haftar in the east.

Saddam Haftar is seen as his father’s most likely heir, possesses the most resources, enjoys the backing of the United Arab Emirates and has so far dominated the political tracks. But his brothers, Khaled and Belqasim – more allied with Egypt than the United Arab Emirates – have recently started to challenge his dominance.

articles.title: Bosnia and Herzegovina is still shaped by war, separatism, EU ambitions
articles.summary: Bosnia and Herzegovina is governed by a system established after the Bosnian war — more than 30 years ago. Ethnic divisions, a complex administration and European integration all shape the country's…

image.caption: Sarajevo, host of the 1984 Winter Olympics, was under siege for four years during the Bosnian war in the mid 1990sImage: Gabriele Thielmann/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: To call Bosnia and Herzegovina a complicated country is an understatement. The country in the Balkan Peninsula divides its economic, administrative and political responsibilities between the multiethnic central government, the self-governing neutral Brcko district and two semi-autonomous entities that, for the most part, operate independently — the Muslim-Croat Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Serb-run Republika Srpska.

Both semi-autonomous entities are further split into several cantons and communities, home to mostly Bosniaks and Bosnian Croats in the central-western federation and Bosnian Serbs in Republika Srpska, to the north and east.

This principle of ethnic nationalism is key to the country's central constitutional and political organization. The Bosnian constitution recognizes Bosniaks, who are predominantly Muslim, the largely Orthodox Bosnian Serbs and primarily Catholic Bosnian Croats as "constituent peoples" with equal rights.

Today, the country has a population of around 3.1 million people. Around half are Bosniaks, while 31% are Serb and 15% are Croat. The rest of the inhabitants belong either to one of the 17 officially recognized minorities, like the Roma and Jews, or chose not to identify with any ethnicity at the last official census. Bosnian, Croatian and Serbian are all recognized as official languages.

The central government is led by rotating three-way presidency, made up of one representative from each of the three main constituent groups. The upper house of parliament and key government offices are also divided according to this principle.
This strict balance between the three groups is always maintained, both politically and socially, often leading to ethnic interests and political gridlock dominating the decision-making process.
Dayton Peace Accords brought an end to war

This complex, convoluted and oft dysfunctional structure was set up during the 1995 Dayton Peace Accords, and then anchored in the constitution. It was intended to bring an end to the Bosnian war — sparked by the breakup of Yugoslavia in the early 1990s — and legally secure the balance of power between the three feuding ethnic groups.

During the war, from 1992 to 1995, the armed forces of the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats initially fought each other, before all three groups began to clash. Later, the Bosniaks and the Bosnian Croats joined forces to take on Republika Srpska. Throughout the war, neighboring Serbia and Croatia were actively involved in the fighting.
Bosnia-Herzegovina: 30 years after Srebrenica massacre

The fighting devastated wide swaths of the country, and resulted in countless war crimes — among them the nearly four-year siege of Sarajevo and the Srebrenica genocide, in which thousands of Bosniaks were killed at the hands of Serb forces.

By the end of the war, some 100,000 people had been killed. A further 2.2 million were displaced by so-called "ethnic cleansing," forced from their homes by expulsions and violence to flee to other communities or abroad.

The fighting only ended after the international community, especially the United States, stepped up its involvement, culminating in the peace deal agreed at a military base near Dayton, Ohio in November 1995.
International oversight — essential, or no longer relevant?

Although Bosnia and Herzegovina has been recognized on the international stage since the signing of the Dayton agreement, and is also represented at the United Nations, the country itself is still, in effect, only partially independent.

The Office of the High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina, an international institution responsible for overseeing the civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement, has been in place since a UN Security Council resolution in 1995.

The high representative — Christian Schmidt of Germany until this past June, and currently filled by acting head Louis J. Crishock of the US — has sweeping powers. He can dismiss elected officials, pass laws, establish new government agencies and overrule all the country's democratic institutions.
The Dayton Peace Agreement 30 years on

This authority is often referred to as the Bonn Powers, as they were negotiated during a meeting of the Peace Implementation Council in Bonn, Germany in December 1997. From 2002 to 2011, the high representative also acted as the EU special representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina.

In recent years, there's been much discussion over whether the office is still relevant. Supporters have said the high representative remains a necessary guarantor of the country's unity and functionality. But critics have pointed out the negative impact on Bosnia-Herzegovina's democratic culture, turning the country into a de facto protectorate that, to an extent, frees local politicians of responsibility for their actions.
Separatist ambitions surface once more

The sharpest criticism has come from the Republika Srpska and Milorad Dodik, its most influential leader. Dodik, in office as prime minister and president of the Serb entity until 2025, views the office and the international backing it provides for a unified Bosnia-Herzegovina as an obstacle to his separatist ambitions.

With strong support from the Serbian capital, Belgrade, Moscow — and, increasingly, the Trump administration — Dodik has flirted with several different scenarios to split his Republika Srpska from Bosnia-Herzegovina. In his interpretation, and that of Republika Srpska's political elite, Bosnia-Herzegovina is highly centralized and unitary, which undermines the independence and sovereignty of the Bosnian Serbs.

blocks.caption: Milorad Dodik (right, seen here meeting with Vladimir Putin in April 2025), continues to foster a close relationship with RussiaImage: press service of kremlin.ru

blocks.text: A similar sentiment prevails among the political representatives of Bosnia's Croats. Although they aren't considering separation, they are trying to squeeze more independence from the central government in Sarajevo — not least with the creation of a third, Croatian, entity. The plan, incidentally, also has the support of the government in neighboring EU member Croatia.
EU support aims to 'foster regional integration'

A potential path out of the current economic and political paralysis is rapprochement with the European Union — the "European perspective," as it's called in Bosnia-Herzegovina, officially supported by all the relevant political actors.

Bosnia-Herzegovina formally submitted its application for EU membership in 2016, and the European Council gave the green light for negotiations to begin in early 2024. But the actual start of membership talks hinges on the prior implementation of numerous reforms, notably in the areas of rule of law, fighting corruption, the prosecution of organized crime and the functionality of state institutions.
EU enlargement: Who's slowing? Who's advancing? Who's next?

The EU has been financially supporting Bosnia-Herzegovina since 2007 in the framework of pre-accession assistance, and the country is also expected to benefit from the European Commission's Economic and Investment Plan for the Western Balkans. The plan aims to "foster regional integration" — and as a result, infrastructure funding for the Republika Srpska has been partially suspended due to its ongoing separatist rhetoric and policies.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: North Korea launches ballistic missile after Seoul demands apology over wounded soldiers
articles.summary:
Pyongyang fires towards sea a day after Kim Jong-un sister denounces South Korea for claiming North’s mines wounded South’s soldiers in DMZ

North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the…

blocks.text: North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, ⁠a day ​after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.

The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s ⁠coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been ​a ballistic missile and appeared to have come ‌down, warning ships to take ‌precautions.

South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.

Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, ​issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.

South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.

South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured ⁠three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches ​across the Korean peninsula.

The missile ​test might be an attempt ​by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, ​said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president ‌at the Sejong ​Institute in Seoul, ​a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.
With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: German reunification: How inequality is shaping a new East German identity
articles.summary: A new study highlights persistent structural disparities in wealth and leadership positions between East and West Germany, 36 years after reunification.

image.caption: Thirty-six years after the end of the division, differences between East and West Germany remainImage: Soeren Stache/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: German reunification may be 36 years in the past, but when it comes to wealth, the divide between East and West Germany is far from history. East Germans still earn less on average, receive smaller pensions and own less property, according to Elisabeth Kaiser, the Federal Government Commissioner for Eastern Germany.

Kaiser, born in the state of Thuringia in the socialist German Democratic Republic (GDR) in 1987, has put the enduring wealth gap at the center of the debate. A study she presented in Berlin points to decades in which private entrepreneurship and opportunities to invest in one's financial future were restricted in the East. That meant, Kaiser said, that "families have not been able to acquire or pass on as much wealth." The consequences, she argues, have had a profound impact upward mobility.
How important are personal connections and social background?

But it is not only East Germans who see fewer chances of upward mobility these days. Kaiser pointed to the latest "Deutschland-Monitor," an annual survey she commissioned to make her point. Although this year's survey is still being analyzed, early findings reveal that about two-thirds of respondents across the country believe that financial and social mobility depend crucially on wealth, personal connections and social background.

This perception is reflected in the numbers. Even though the percentage of East German executives in the highest federal agencies has risen from 13.9% in 2022 to 16.3% today, Kaiser says, "The further up the management ladder you go, the lower the percentage of East Germans you find."
How much did the German reunification cost?
East German leaders remain scarce across the board

Based on these findings, the Commissioner for Eastern Germany calls for greater equality in decision-making. "And that is why I would like to see East Germans sitting at the table wherever decisions are made in the country," she said, "in the ministries, in government agencies, in business, academia, the judiciary, culture and the media."

With just under 20%, East Germans are significantly underrepresented in all sectors relative to their share of the population. To back this up, Kaiser cited the "Elitenmonitor," another study commissioned by her office. With over 3,000 top positions examined across twelve sectors over a long period of time, the Elitenmonitor study, conducted by the universities of Jena (Thuringia), Leipzig (Saxony), and Zittau/Görlitz (Saxony), can offer more than just a snapshot.

According to the report, the percentage of East Germans in leadership positions in both the public and private sectors only increased from 10.9% to 12.1% from 2018 to 2024. And in the business and cultural sectors, the percentage of East Germans has actually declined.

Most striking of all is that among the 100 largest German companies, all executives are from West Germany — and the same holds true for the military. East Germans are also severely underrepresented in top positions in the judiciary and the media.
Fact check: Fake campaign about alleged division of Germany
New stereotypes about East Germany

The insufficient representation of East German perspectives in nearly all areas of society also appears to have consequences for how East Germans are viewed. Kaiser says that her generation, born around the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, did not feel East German for a long time. It was only in school and during vocational training that she realized there were differences between East and West that would sometimes put her at a disadvantage.

This has also shaped stereotypes about East Germany, both past and present. "An East German identity is also being created politically to some extent because people are looking for some way to orient themselves, because they're looking for a common bond," Kaiser knows from her many experiences and conversations.
As an example, she cited the symbolic power of the Simson moped, produced in the millions during the GDR era — a symbol of mobility and freedom for many young people at that time.

Leading representatives of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party classified in part as far-right extremist by the domestic intelligence agency, frequently make public appearances riding on Simson mopeds. One of them is Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD candidate who recently won state elections in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.

Without specifically mentioning the AfD by name, Kaiser lamented the exploitation of cultural symbols for political purposes."It creates a very powerful emotional connection," said Kaiser regarding the use of the Simson brand.
How a Jewish family's moped brand became a far-right symbol

As for the AfD and its recent electoral successes in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, Kaiser said that these elections send a dangerous signal. She believes that international investors and skilled workers will ask themselves: Should I go there or not?

Kaiser specifically mentioned sectors that have played an important role as drivers of economic growth and innovation in eastern Germany, such as the semiconductor industry, battery cell research, healthcare, biotechnology and renewable energy. Her concern is that the economic upswing in these sectors could suffer as a result.
This article was originally written in German.

articles.title: Newly released video shows Luigi Mangione’s arrest
articles.summary: The bodycam footage also shows a police officer finding a gun in Mangione's backpack, days after the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.

blocks.text: Newly released bodycam footage shows the moment Luigi Mangione is arrested in a McDonald's restaurant, days after the killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson.
In one clip, a police officer can be seen finding a gun magazine in a backpack belonging to Mangione. Later, officers are also seen finding a gun in the backpack.
Mangione has pleaded guilty to federal charges relating to Thompson's killing.
